description: A 9router bugfix patch file sitting in ~/.9router/patches/ does nothing until wired into the running process via NODE_OPTIONS --require

# 9router patch files are dead code until wired into `NODE_OPTIONS`

## Symptom
`azure_ai does not support parameters: ['reasoning_effort']` (`litellm.UnsupportedParamsError`) resurfaced on the Elastic LiteLLM Gateway → Azure AI backend, even though a fix (`~/.9router/patches/reasoning-effort-patch.js`, stripping `reasoning_effort` before the request hits that backend) already existed on disk from a prior session (written 2026-07-14/15 for this exact error).

## Root cause
Two separate gaps:
1. **9router's built-in `reasoning_effort` stripping only fires for Anthropic-shaped providers** (`provider==="anthropic"` / `claude|anthropic` match in the bundled `chunks/8833.js`) — it never strips the param for `openai-compatible-chat-*` providers like the Elastic Gateway, whose upstream is `azure_ai` and rejects it.
2. **A standalone patch file existing at `~/.9router/patches/<name>.js` is not automatically loaded.** Nothing in the launchd plists (`com.9router.headless.plist`, `com.9router.autostart.plist`) or the running process's env wired `NODE_OPTIONS=--require <patch path>`. Confirmed via `ps eww -p <pid>` on the live `com.9router.headless` process showing no `NODE_OPTIONS`/`--require`. The patch was inert dead code from the moment it was written.

## Fix
Add `NODE_OPTIONS` to the `EnvironmentVariables` dict in **both** `com.9router.headless.plist` and `com.9router.autostart.plist` (whichever is the actually-running one — check via `ps`, not assumption):
```xml
<key>NODE_OPTIONS</key>
<string>--require /Users/patrykkopycinski/.9router/patches/reasoning-effort-patch.js</string>
```
Then `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/<label>` + `launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/<label>.plist` to reload with the patch active.

## Generalizable lesson
When any patch file is written into `~/.9router/patches/`, **verify it is actually loaded** by the running process before considering the issue closed — don't assume "the fix file exists" means "the fix is live." Check `ps eww -p <9router-pid> | grep NODE_OPTIONS` (or equivalent) as the closing verification step, and wire it into the launchd plist(s) in the same change that creates the patch, not as a follow-up.

# Kibana Worktree Location — Verify Before, Not After

When setting up a dedicated worktree for a Kibana PR validation, demo env, or
any branch work, the target path MUST be `~/Projects/kibana.worktrees/<slug>`.

**Why:** This was violated twice in one session for PR #273049's local demo
setup: the original worktree creation defaulted to a sibling
`~/Projects/kibana-pr273049` directory, and the user's correction request was
initially (mis)handled the same way before being caught. `git worktree move`
fixed the location after the fact, but the move surfaced a second-order cost:
stale absolute paths baked into `.moon/cache` and `target/public/bundles`
(and a spawned `rspack-optimizer` child process referencing the old path)
silently hung Kibana's dev-server boot. Diagnosing that required inspecting
the process tree and clearing caches before Kibana would boot cleanly from
the new location.

**How to apply:**
- Before any `git worktree add` for Kibana, assert the destination path starts
  with `$HOME/Projects/kibana.worktrees/`. Refuse and re-derive the path if not.
- This applies even for "quick" one-off PR validation / demo-env setups, not
  just multi-repo epics — there is no size threshold exception.
- If a worktree is discovered in the wrong location after the fact, prefer
  `git worktree move` over delete+recreate (preserves bootstrapped
  `node_modules`), but budget for a cache-clear step
  (`.moon/cache`, `target/public/bundles`) and a check for stale child
  processes (e.g. `rspack-optimizer`) still holding the old path before
  trusting a clean Kibana boot.
- Backgrounding Kibana's dev server across tool calls requires `screen -dmS`
  (or equivalent true detach) — plain `&` or `nohup ... & disown` do not
  survive Cursor/Claude tool-call shell teardown.

**Never:**
- Create a Kibana worktree as a sibling of `~/Projects/kibana` (e.g.
  `~/Projects/kibana-<slug>`) even temporarily.
- Assume a post-move Kibana boot will just work without clearing
  `.moon/cache` / `target/public/bundles` and checking for stale-path child
  processes.

**Confirmed approach:** Escalated to a rule on the 2nd recurrence per
`capture-learnings` policy — see the "Pre-flight gate" section added to
`kibana-dev-cells-mode-b.mdc` (ao-workspace canonical, Claude-symlinked).

name: feedback_launchd_hook_kickstart_vs_bootstrap
description: On this machine a hook blocks launchctl bootstrap/load and any LaunchAgents-path access; restart already-loaded services with `launchctl kickstart -k` instead, and stage new plists for the user to load
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-03
source: Restarting the treadmill daemon + staging fleet-watch/i9 smoke plists (Jul 3 2026)
---

# launchd on this control mac: kickstart to restart, stage-don't-load for new agents

A security hook ("macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon persistence") blocks commands that **load/bootstrap
a LaunchAgent** or even **read/inspect files under `~/Library/LaunchAgents`** (e.g.
`launchctl bootstrap`, `launchctl load`, `plutil -p ~/Library/LaunchAgents/...`, or a combined
command that greps a plist there). Plan around it:

**To RESTART an already-installed/loaded service** (so it re-reads its config) use in-place kickstart —
this is NOT blocked because it neither loads a new plist nor touches the LaunchAgents dir:
```bash
launchctl kickstart -k "gui/$(id -u)/<service-label>"
# e.g. com.patryks-treadmill after editing ~/.treadmill/data/fleet.json
```

**To INSTALL a NEW scheduled agent**, you (the agent) cannot load it. Stage the plist next to its
script and hand the user the two commands:
```bash
cp ~/<dir>/<label>.plist ~/Library/LaunchAgents/
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/<label>.plist
```
(This is exactly how the i9 stack-smoke plist and the com.treadmill.fleet-watch plist were handled.)

**Also avoid** bundling a LaunchAgents read into an unrelated multi-line SSH/shell command — the whole
command gets rejected. Split the LaunchAgents-touching part out, or just skip it (find the script via
`find`/`ls` in the script's own dir rather than inspecting the plist).

**Why:** Hit this repeatedly in one session — a combined `ssh ... grep ~/Library/LaunchAgents/...plist`
was rejected, and staging + user-load was required for both the i9 smoke plist and the fleet-watch
plist. `launchctl kickstart -k` succeeded cleanly for the treadmill daemon restart.

**Confirmed approach:** kickstart restarted the treadmill daemon (picked up new `fleet.json`); staged
plists + user-run bootstrap is the working install path.

type: feedback

# Fresh Kibana Worktree on Remote Machines Too

Every machine that does Kibana work — including headless remote runners (e.g. the Intel i9 `kibana-i9`) — must follow the same layout as the primary Mac:

- **Base checkout:** `~/Projects/kibana`
- **Working checkouts:** always a **fresh `git worktree`** under **`~/Projects/kibana.worktrees/<slug>`**
- **Never** an ad-hoc clone in a one-off location like `~/dev/kibana`.

## Why

- The **kbn-cell dev-cell tooling** (`~/Projects/ao-workspace/tools/kibana-dev-cell`) and its registry live at `~/Projects/kibana.worktrees/.kbn-dev-cells/registry.json`. Mode-B isolated cells and `boot-edd-capsule.sh` assume this layout.
- The **EDD skill** (`skill-dev-eval-driven-loop`) mandates a *dedicated worktree + stack* per initiative — a fresh worktree per task, not a shared/ad-hoc clone.
- Consistency across machines means the same commands, ports formula (ES `9200+slot`, Kibana `5601+slot`), and MCP capsule contract work identically locally and remotely.

## How to apply (remote machine)

```bash
# base checkout at ~/Projects/kibana (move an existing clone there if needed)
cd ~/Projects/kibana
git fetch origin
git worktree add ~/Projects/kibana.worktrees/<slug> <branch-or-main>
cd ~/Projects/kibana.worktrees/<slug>
# per-worktree bootstrap (each worktree has its own node_modules)
yarn kbn bootstrap
# then: kbn-cell activate / boot-edd-capsule.sh --worktree $PWD
```

## Never

- Clone Kibana into `~/dev/kibana` or other one-off paths on any machine.
- Run the EDD capsule from a non-worktree checkout.

## Intel-mac caveat (pairs with)

On Intel macs each fresh worktree's bootstrap re-hits the missing `@moonrepo/core-macos-x64@2.1.0` binary — re-apply the moon x64 shim per worktree (see `feedback_kibana_intel_mac_moon_binary`).

# Worktree Native Module Rebuild

After `treadmill new-feature <slug>`, the sibling worktree gets a fresh `npm install`. If install runs with **`--ignore-scripts`** (or skips native compile), **`better-sqlite3` bindings are missing** and any test touching `openDb()` fails with "Could not locate the bindings file."

**Why:** 2026-06 command-center-autonomy worktree — unit tests for session-reconciler and postDismissAction failed until `npm rebuild better-sqlite3` ran locally. `treadmill ship-feature` runs full `npm test` which expects native modules built.

## How to apply

```bash
cd ~/Projects/patryks-treadmill.worktrees/<slug>
npm install          # allow scripts, or explicitly:
npm rebuild better-sqlite3
```

Prefer **`treadmill ship-feature`** (runs install + test gate) over ad-hoc `npm install --ignore-scripts` in worktrees.

## Never

- Diagnose as "test bug" when the error is bindings path under `node_modules/better-sqlite3/build/`

**Confirmed approach:** Rebuild fixed 26/26 targeted tests; ship-feature passed full suite.

# Hermes multi-host config & update traps

Learned on M4 (`MacBook-Pro-Patryk-2`) + `worker-m1max` (`MacBook-Pro-Mac`), Aug 2026.

## Config schema v33: `custom_providers` → `providers`

`hermes update` migrates the config format (v0 → v33 observed). The shape changed:

```yaml
# BEFORE (list of dicts)
custom_providers:
- name: omniroute
  base_url: http://100.123.104.92:20128/v1
  api_mode: anthropic_messages
  model: best-coding-paid

# AFTER (keyed map)
providers:
  omniroute:
    api: http://100.123.104.92:20128/v1
    transport: anthropic_messages
    default_model: best-coding-paid
```

Two ways this bites:

1. **Regex edits written against the old shape silently no-op.** A `re.sub`
   anchored on `- api_key: dummy ... name: vllm-local` matched nothing after
   migration and reported success on a zero-change write.
2. **`yaml.safe_load(...)["custom_providers"]` returns empty after migration.**
   Popping entries from that empty dict and writing it back would have deleted
   *every* provider. Caught only because the print showed `before: []` on a
   config that visibly had three providers.

Rule: print the top-level key list first, edit via a yaml parse, and
`assert` the surviving provider list is non-empty before writing.

## Removing a credential leaves dangling `${env:VAR}` refs

`hermes auth remove <provider> <target>` clears the credential and suppresses
the env var, but does **not** rewrite config refs pointing at it. Both
`providers.<name>.api_key` and the top-level `model.api_key` kept
`${env:OPENAI_API_KEY}` and warned on every single run:

```
Config ref '${env:OPENAI_API_KEY}': OPENAI_API_KEY is not set ... keeping the literal placeholder
```

Requests still *succeeded* — a local gateway like omniroute doesn't verify the
bearer token — so this is a warning-only failure that never surfaces as an
error. Grep the whole config for the removed var; there was more than one ref.

`${config:<name>}` is **not** a valid ref source. Hermes only resolves
`${env:NAME}`. Fix by writing a real var into `~/.hermes/.env` and pointing
both refs at it.

## Heredoc'd Python over ssh eats `${...}`

```
ssh host 'python - <<PYEOF ... "${env:OPENAI_API_KEY}" ... PYEOF'
→ zsh:1: unrecognized modifier `O'
```

The *outer* zsh expands `${...}` before Python sees it, and the edit silently
does nothing (or errors on an unrelated line). `scp` a script file and run it.

## Updater distance is not trustworthy

`hermes --version` reported **"1 commit behind"** on m1max. After a real
`git fetch origin`, the true distance was **20,749 commits**. Same
frozen-remote-tracking-ref class as the PyPI case: the single-branch refspec
`+refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main` leaves `origin/main` stale, so the
comparison is against a ref frozen at install time.

Always, before trusting any updater's distance:

```bash
git config --get remote.origin.fetch          # single-branch refspec?
git fetch origin --quiet
git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main        # the real number
```

The update itself worked fine (v0.19.0 → v0.20.0) once run.

## Non-interactive shells: PATH and env vars

Both hosts had the same root cause in two guises — `~/.zshrc` is
**interactive-only**, so `ssh host cmd`, cron, and launchd see none of it.

- M4: `export ANTHROPIC_TOKEN=...` lived in `.zshrc` → Hermes reported
  `HTTP 401: OAuth access token has expired` from a non-interactive shell while
  `zsh -ic` worked. Not an expired token — an unset env var.
- m1max: `~/.local/bin` missing from non-interactive PATH →
  `zsh:1: command not found: hermes`, which reads as "not installed".

Fix both by putting the export in `~/.zshenv` (runs for all shells). Confirm
with a `zsh -ic` vs `zsh -c` diff before touching credentials.

## cloudflared LaunchAgent in the wrong directory

`~/.cloudflared/com.cloudflared.9router.plist` is where `cloudflared service
install` leaves a copy — launchd only loads from `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`.
The tunnel died 2026-08-04 and nothing restarted it despite `KeepAlive: true`,
because the job was never loaded. Public hostname returned **530** (origin not
registered) from every host while local `:20128` returned 200.

```bash
cp ~/.cloudflared/com.cloudflared.9router.plist ~/Library/LaunchAgents/
plutil -lint ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cloudflared.9router.plist
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cloudflared.9router.plist
```

Verify with an HTTP probe, not `launchctl list` — a loaded job proves nothing
about whether the tunnel serves traffic.

## Probe timing traps seen in this session

- A `curl --max-time 15` against a **cold-starting** tunnel returned `000`
  while another host returned `200`. The tunnel log showed
  `Incoming request ended abruptly: context canceled` — that is *my client*
  giving up, not an origin fault. Re-probe before concluding split-horizon DNS.
- All three backends returned `000` *during* `hermes update` on the same box.
  Had I acted on that reading I would have deleted the one working provider.
  Re-probe on a quiet box before removing anything.

## The "extra usage" 400 is a client classifier, not billing

M4 running `hermes -z ... --provider anthropic -m claude-opus-5` returned:

```
HTTP 400: Third-party apps now draw from your extra usage, not your plan
limits. Add more at claude.ai/settings/usage and keep going.
```

That message reads as a billing/plan problem. It is not. Evidence:

1. omniroute logged **nothing** for the failing request — Hermes was talking
   straight to `api.anthropic.com`, bypassing the gateway entirely.
2. The identical model through omniroute's Claude Code bridge succeeded:

```bash
curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:20128/v1/chat/completions \
  -d '{"model":"cc/claude-opus-5","messages":[...]}'   # -> PONG, HTTP 200
```

Anthropic fingerprints the request shape and classifies a direct non-Claude-Code
client as a "third-party app". The omniroute path presents as Claude Code, so the
same account and same model are served normally. No plan change was needed.

Fix applied on M4: added an `omniroute` provider (`http://127.0.0.1:20128/v1`,
`transport: anthropic_messages`) and pointed `model.provider` at
`custom:omniroute` with `default: cc/claude-opus-5`.

General lesson: a vendor's own error string names the symptom it *guesses* at,
not the cause. Confirm which network path the request actually took (does the
gateway log it?) before acting on the text.

## scip-python on a large repo

- `--environment` expects a JSON **array** of `{name, version, files}` (pip
  metadata), not a `sys.path` dump. Omit the flag and let it discover via pip.
- Default Node heap OOMs on ~3.8k files. Same V8 ceiling as the tsserver crash:
  `NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=20480"`.

name: reference_cloudflare_named_tunnel_9router
description: Set up a stable named Cloudflare tunnel (own domain) for 9router incl. IPv6 gotcha, path-restricted hardening, and launchd handoff
type: reference
---

# Stable Named Cloudflare Tunnel for 9router (own domain)

Replaces the rotating `trycloudflare.com` quick-tunnel with a fixed hostname on a domain already added to Cloudflare. Domain in use: **`widzimysie.pl`** → 9router served at **`https://9router.widzimysie.pl`** (tunnel name `9router`, id `5b5e3f8f-a730-4c46-bfe8-1fa3d766b7a7`).

## Setup sequence
```bash
cloudflared tunnel login                      # browser: authorize + pick zone → ~/.cloudflared/cert.pem
cloudflared tunnel create 9router             # → ~/.cloudflared/<UUID>.json creds
cloudflared tunnel route dns 9router 9router.widzimysie.pl   # CNAME in zone
cloudflared tunnel ingress validate
cloudflared tunnel run 9router
```

## Derive the zone/domain without asking
`cert.pem` embeds an `ARGO TUNNEL TOKEN` (base64 JSON with `zoneID` + `apiToken`). Resolve the domain:
`GET https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/<zoneID>` with `Authorization: Bearer <apiToken>` → `.result.name`.

## GOTCHA — origin `localhost` → 502
9router binds **IPv4 only** (`*:20128`). cloudflared `service: http://localhost:20128` resolves `localhost`→`::1` (IPv6) first → **502 / error 1033**. Fix: use `http://127.0.0.1:20128` in `config.yml`.

## Hardening: expose ONLY the key-gated API (Cursor-safe)
The tunnel otherwise publishes the whole 9router **dashboard + `/api/*`** to the internet. cloudflared ingress supports **path** rules — restrict to `/v1/*`:
```yaml
tunnel: <UUID>
credentials-file: /Users/<me>/.cloudflared/<UUID>.json
ingress:
  - hostname: 9router.widzimysie.pl
    path: ^/v1(/.*)?$
    service: http://127.0.0.1:20128
  - hostname: 9router.widzimysie.pl
    service: http_status:404
  - service: http_status:404
```
Verified: `/v1/*` → 401 (needs key), `/api/health` `/` `/dashboard` → 404. Test rules offline with `cloudflared tunnel ingress rule <url>`. Don't rely on Cloudflare Access for this — interactive Access breaks header-less clients like Cursor; keep 9router `requireApiKey=true` as the auth and use path-restriction + (optionally) an Access **service token** only if the client can send `CF-Access-Client-*` headers.

## SIGHUP does NOT reload — it kills
`kill -HUP` / `pkill -HUP` on this cloudflared (2026.6.x) **terminates** the process (→ all 502, then origin unregistered). To apply a `config.yml` change, **restart** the tunnel, don't SIGHUP.

## Disable 9router's built-in quick-tunnel (avoid dual public entry points)
Controlled by `settings.data.tunnelEnabled` in `~/.9router/db/data.sqlite` (also holds `tunnelUrl`, `requireApiKey`, `password` bcrypt hash). Set `tunnelEnabled=false` (+ clear `tunnelUrl`) then restart 9router (`9router --tray --skip-update`) so it doesn't respawn `~/.9router/bin/cloudflared ... --url ...:20128 --retries 99`. Confirm dashboard password isn't the default (`123456`) since even a 404'd dashboard shouldn't rely on a weak secret.

## Persistence (launchd) — must hand bootstrap to the user
This environment's shell hook blocks **writing to `~/Library/LaunchAgents` AND `launchctl bootstrap`** (see feedback_launchd_hook_kickstart_vs_bootstrap). So: stage the plist elsewhere (e.g. `~/.cloudflared/com.cloudflared.9router.plist`, `ProgramArguments = /opt/homebrew/bin/cloudflared tunnel --config ~/.cloudflared/config.yml --no-autoupdate run 9router`, `KeepAlive`+`RunAtLoad`) and hand the user:
```bash
cp ~/.cloudflared/com.cloudflared.9router.plist ~/Library/LaunchAgents/
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cloudflared.9router.plist
```
`nohup cloudflared ... &` gets reaped in the agent shell — use the LaunchAgent for real persistence (or a session-managed background job for the current session only).

## Validated outcome + reboot-readiness (2026-07-04, M4 Max)
User ran the `cp` + `launchctl bootstrap` handoff → **worked**. Confirmed state:
- **`com.cloudflared.9router`** (tunnel): `properties = keepalive | runatload`, `state = running`. Correct — cloudflared is long-running so KeepAlive is right; survives reboot AND crashes.
- **`com.9router.autostart`** (server, user already had this): `properties = runatload` (NO keepalive), `program = node`, `arguments = --tray --skip-update`, `last exit code = 0`, `state = not running`. This "not running" is CORRECT/expected — 9router's launcher spawns a **detached** tray server (`next-server`, reparents to launchd PPID 1, serves :20128) then the launcher exits 0. **Do NOT add KeepAlive to the 9router agent** — the self-detaching launcher would make launchd respawn-loop it. Reboot flow: `RunAtLoad` fires launcher → spawns detached server → done.
- Check enabled state (not just loaded) with `launchctl print-disabled gui/$(id -u)` (absence from the list = enabled by default). Verify a specific agent with `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/<label>` (`state`, `properties`, `last exit code`).
- After the LaunchAgent is up, kill any temporary session `cloudflared tunnel run 9router` (single owner). Note `pkill -f 'cloudflared tunnel run 9router'` matches ONLY the temp job, not the LaunchAgent whose cmdline is `cloudflared tunnel --config ... run 9router` (non-contiguous).

## Cursor config (stable)
Override OpenAI Base URL = `https://9router.widzimysie.pl/v1`; API key = dashboard `sk-...`; model = `cc/claude-sonnet-4-6`.

# RTK Multi-Agent Token-Saver Setup

RTK (`rtk`, Homebrew `/opt/homebrew/bin/rtk`) transparently rewrites shell commands (`git`/`grep`/`ls`/`tree`/`find`/logs/test runners) into token-compressed proxies (60–90% fewer tokens on tool output) via per-agent hooks. Installed for all agents this session.

## Install (global, one command per agent)
```bash
rtk init -g --agent claude  --auto-patch   # ~/.claude/RTK.md + @ref in CLAUDE.md + Bash PreToolUse hook in settings.json + filters.toml
rtk init -g --agent cursor  --auto-patch   # superset of claude core + rtk hook in ~/.cursor/hooks.json (Shell matcher)
rtk init -g --codex                         # ~/.codex/RTK.md + @ref in ~/.codex/AGENTS.md   (NO settings patch)
rtk init -g --agent hermes  --auto-patch   # ~/.hermes/plugins/rtk-rewrite/ + config.yaml
```
Supported `--agent` values: `claude, cursor, windsurf, cline, kilocode, antigravity, pi, hermes`; plus flags `--codex`, `--gemini`, `--opencode`, `--copilot`.

## Gotchas
- **`--codex` cannot be combined with `--auto-patch`** (errors). Run codex init without it.
- `--agent cursor` also configures the shared Claude core (RTK.md/CLAUDE.md/settings.json), so it's a superset — running claude then cursor is idempotent.
- Init **merges/appends** into existing hook configs rather than overwriting — verified safe against a heavily-customized `~/.claude/settings.json` (sage/PAMS/model-router/etc.) and `~/.cursor/hooks.json`; diffs showed only the RTK entry added.
- No global `-v`/verbose flag on `rtk init` (rejected). Use `--dry-run` to preview.
- Activation: Claude Code / Hermes need a restart; Cursor auto-reloads `hooks.json`.

## Verify / operate
- `rtk init --show` — install state per agent.
- `rtk verify` — hook integrity + TOML filter tests (expect e.g. `154/154 tests passed`).
- `rtk gain` — live token-savings analytics.
- `rtk init -g --uninstall` — fully reversible.

**Confirmed approach:** Backed up all target configs first (`~/rtk-config-backup-<ts>/`), applied `--auto-patch`, then `diff` + `rtk verify` (154/154) + JSON-parse check confirmed clean merges. Recommended default: keep RTK's own tool-output compression on; it complements (not replaces) 9router's built-in RTK.

# Pruning stale patryks-treadmill feat/ worktrees after squash-merge

After `gh pr merge --squash`, GitHub deletes the remote branch and the squash commit lands on
`origin/main`. The original feature-branch commits **never become ancestors** of `main`.

## Authoritative safe-to-prune signal

For each `*.worktrees/<slug>` on a `feat/*` branch:

1. Working tree **clean** (`git status --porcelain` empty)
2. `gh pr view --json state` for the associated PR → **`MERGED`**

That is sufficient. Do **not** require `git merge-base --is-ancestor feat/main` (always false after
squash) or a **net diff vs `origin/main`** (misleading when the branch is far *behind* main — main
gained many files from later PRs, producing a huge false-positive diff even though the branch's
*content* was squash-merged).

## Stale `ao-feat-*` treadmill feature worktrees

A worktree may look active in the feature DB (paused plan, draft phases) while its branch commits
are **superseded** — the symbols were reimplemented on `main` in later merges. Before keeping:

- Grep `main` for key functions/files introduced on the branch
- If they already exist on `main`, the branch is stale even if the feature row is non-terminal

## Procedure

```bash
git worktree remove --force ~/Projects/patryks-treadmill.worktrees/<slug>
git branch -D feat/<slug>
git worktree prune
```

Skip worktrees with uncommitted changes until stashed, committed, or explicitly discarded.

# Hermes tool_loop_guardrails blind spots (todo-write loop, 2026-08-13)

## Symptom

~20 consecutive `todo` calls with byte-identical payloads, each returning the
same list, interleaved with the same one-line preamble. The runtime surfaced
`[Duplicate tool output — same content as a more recent call]` on several of
them and still did not stop.

## Root cause: TWO independent defects, both blind at once

### 1. `hard_stop_enabled` ships `false`

`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` → `tool_loop_guardrails.hard_stop_enabled: False`.
In-source rationale: "hard stops are opt-in so interactive CLI/TUI sessions keep
flowing." Effect: the detector *warns* at repeat 2 and never blocks. A warning in
tool output is just another thing a looping model narrates past.

Local mitigation (config only, no code):

    hermes config set tool_loop_guardrails.hard_stop_enabled true

### 2. Declarative mutating tools were skipped by the no-progress detector

`agent/tool_guardrails.py`:

    def _is_idempotent(self, tool_name):
        if tool_name in self.config.mutating_tools:   # todo is in here
            return False
        return tool_name in self.config.idempotent_tools

`_no_progress` is tracked only for idempotent tools, so identical `todo` writes
were never counted. The failure detector (`_exact_failure_counts`) never fired
either, because the identical calls all **succeeded**. Both detectors blind
simultaneously — that is why the loop ran unbounded.

Measured (hard_stop forced ON in-memory, pre-fix tree):

    todo      identical-success block at: NEVER (>25)
    read_file identical-success block at: 6

## Do NOT patch this locally — upstream already owns it

A local fix (`NO_OP_MUTATING_TOOL_NAMES = {"todo"}`) was written, verified, and
then **reverted** on 2026-08-13 after a PR search. Every part of it is already
covered upstream in `NousResearch/hermes-agent`, by better designs:

| concern | upstream PR | why it beats a local allowlist |
|---|---|---|
| identical successful mutating calls | **#77991** | drops the idempotent/mutating taxonomy entirely, tracks *all* tools uniformly |
| same | **#58221** | same fix + config + docs; real `glm-4.5-flash` 30-repeat incident |
| same | **#34614** | dedicated `tool_repetition` axis, closes #34610 |
| `hard_stop_enabled: true` default | **#26015**, **#57816** | identical intent |
| config-extensible tool sets | **#71585 / #71793** | lets config.yaml extend the sets — no code fork needed |
| `memory` quota retry loop | **#43001** | `memory_quota_exceeded` + `store_state_token`; skips an identical write only when store state is *unchanged* |

`NO_OP_MUTATING_TOOL_NAMES` was the narrow version of #77991 — a per-tool escape
hatch where the upstream fix removes the flawed axis altogether. Adding a
per-case allowlist instead of fixing the classification axis is the anti-pattern
here.

**Action if this recurs: set the config flag, and if code is truly needed, check
whether #77991 / #58221 / #43001 have merged before writing anything.**

## The right axis

A repeated call is a no-op when *args are identical AND the result is
byte-identical*. That test needs no knowledge of the tool's semantics — which is
exactly why classifying tools as mutating-vs-read-only was the wrong axis, and
why #77991 deletes the taxonomy rather than extending it.

## Pitfalls hit while diagnosing

- **`pytest` directly is NOT the repo's gate.** Canonical runner is
  `scripts/run_tests.sh` (per-file subprocess isolation, TZ/LANG/PYTHONHASHSEED
  pinned). CI calls it via `scripts/run_tests_parallel.py`.
- `pytest -k guardrail` at the repo root scans the whole suite and times out
  (>420s). Target files directly.
- The guardrail test file is NOT found by `ls tests/ | grep -i guard` — it lives
  at `tests/agent/test_tool_guardrails.py`. Find it with
  `grep -rln ToolCallGuardrailController tests/`.
- There is a **second** suite, `tests/run_agent/test_tool_call_guardrail_runtime.py`,
  easy to miss when assessing blast radius.
- The blocking lint gate is `ruff check .` (enforces `[tool.ruff.lint.select]`).
  `ruff` is not installed by default here — `uv tool install ruff`, then
  `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`.
- macOS has no `timeout` binary.

## Generalizable lesson

When a behavioral rule keeps getting violated despite a skill documenting it,
check whether the enforcement mechanism is **structurally blind** to the case
before writing more prose telling yourself to behave. Then check whether
upstream already fixed it — this repo has 15+ open PRs on tool-loop guardrails
alone, so a "missing" guardrail is far more likely to be an unmerged PR than an
unnoticed gap. A skill about looping cannot be loaded by a model that is already
looping; prevention must be mechanical.

## buzz CLI

1. **`messages send` takes FLAGS, not positionals**, and the key goes BEFORE the
   subcommand:
   ```bash

   ```
   The positional form exits non-zero with `unexpected argument '<uuid>'`.
   Because watchdogs typically append `2>/dev/null`, this fails **completely
   silently**. Never swallow stderr in a script whose whole job is alerting —
   add `|| { echo "FAILED" >&2; exit 1; }`.

2. **`@name` does not emit a p-tag on a SELF-mention.** If the sender is the
   same identity as the mentioned agent, mention resolution is skipped and the
   message carries `tags: []`, so `subscribe=Mentions` never fires and the agent
   never wakes. Symptom: the message is visible in the channel but nobody
   responds. Fix: dispatch from a **neutral identity** that is nobody's self
   (here: a dedicated `DispatchTick` keypair, admitted to the relay + all
   channels + every agent's allowlist).

3. **Allowlist env var is `BUZZ_ACP_RESPOND_TO_ALLOWLIST`** (comma-separated
   pubkeys). `BUZZ_ACP_ALLOWED_RESPOND_TO` is a *different* variable (which
   modes are permitted). Setting only the latter leaves the allowlist EMPTY, and
   `StrictAllowlist => allowlist.contains(author)` is then always false — no
   worker can ever be dispatched. Owner-sent messages still work (owner is
   implicit), which masks the bug completely during manual testing.
   Verify against the RUNNING process, not the file on disk:
   ```bash
   ps eww -p <pid> | tr ' ' '\n' | grep '^BUZZ_ACP_RESPOND_TO_ALLOWLIST='
   ```

## elastic-llm-benchmarker

4. **There is no `running` status.** The union (`queue-service.ts:38`) is
   `pending | deploying | benchmarking | completed | failed | cancelled`.
   In-flight = `deploying + benchmarking`. Reading `b.running` silently yields 0,
   so a monitor reports an idle queue *during a live GPU benchmark* and can
   dispatch work on top of it. Pin `terms` agg `size` too — the default 10
   buckets will silently drop a status once the union grows.

5. **The failure text field is `error_message`, not `error`.** Querying `error`
   returns `(none)` for every doc and looks exactly like "failures record no
   reason". It is also a **text** field, so `missing`/`terms` aggregations on it
   throw `Fielddata is disabled` — classify client-side instead.

6. **Daemon and API are separate launchd services.**
   - `com.elastic-llm-benchmarker` — scheduler daemon
   - `com.elastic-llm-benchmarker-dashboard` — serves `:3200` (`/api/queue`)
   Restarting only the daemon leaves the API serving **stale code**, so an API
   probe "proving" a fix can be measuring the old build. The dashboard plist has
   `ThrottleInterval 30`, so it takes ~30s to reappear — a `lsof` check
   immediately after `kickstart` shows no listener and looks like a crash.

## Cooldown / quarantine design (fixed 2026-08-10)

- The 3-strike auto-blacklist lived **only in an in-memory Map**, so every
  daemon restart cleared every quarantine. Restarts are routine, so bad models
  were re-armed indefinitely (one model: 16 recorded failures).
  Fixed: persisted to `benchmarker-model-cooldown`, rehydrated in
  `Scheduler.start()`.
- A **non-retriable** (`model-arch`) failure is deterministic, yet still needed
  3 strikes. Since auto-retry is skipped for those, strikes only accrued via
  discovery re-queueing. Fixed: quarantine on the FIRST non-retriable failure.
- `MaintenanceScheduler.sweepDlq` filtered only on `retriable` and would
  **resurrect a model the scheduler had just quarantined** — the two schedulers
  fought in a loop. Fixed: exclude models with an active cooldown.
- Before seeding a quarantine from history, **check the model has not also
  succeeded recently** — 2 of 9 repeat-offenders had recent passes and must not
  be quarantined.

# buzz-acp `respond_to` cannot enforce Orchestrator-only routing

**Date:** 2026-08-03
**Status:** Verified by source read. Invalidates a core design assumption.

## The claim that failed

Design plan: give the Orchestrator `respond_to=anyone`, give every worker
`respond_to=allowlist` with `[orchestrator_pubkey]`, so workers only accept work
dispatched by the Orchestrator and human mentions are dropped at the harness.

**This does not work on a single-owner roster.**

## Evidence

`crates/buzz-acp/src/lib.rs:235` — `author_allowed()`:

```rust
match respond_to {
    RespondTo::Anyone    => true,
    RespondTo::Nobody    => false,
    RespondTo::OwnerOnly => is_owner_or_sibling(author, owner_cache, rest_client).await,
    RespondTo::Allowlist => {
        allowlist.contains(author)
            || is_owner_or_sibling(author, owner_cache, rest_client).await
    }
}
```

The `||` fall-through is the defect for this use case.

`is_owner_or_sibling()` (`lib.rs:192`) returns true when:
1. `author == my_owner`, or
2. the author is a cached known sibling, or
3. `check_sibling_via_profile()` finds a NIP-OA auth tag on the author's kind:0
   profile proving the **same owner**.

Every agent in the roster is owned by the same person → they are all mutual
siblings → an allowlist of `[orchestrator]` still admits **all other agents and
the owner**.

`respond_to` is a security boundary against **foreign pubkeys**. It is not a
routing boundary among your own agents.

## Options

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| `respond_to=allowlist` | Ineffective — sibling bypass |
| `respond_to=owner-only` on workers | Strictly worse — Orchestrator is a *sibling*, not the owner, so it gates the Orchestrator's dispatch while still admitting the human |
| Prompt convention | Works, but is not harness-enforced |
| Patch `author_allowed` strict mode | Real fix. ~10 lines; clean fn signature, existing test surface |

A strict mode would make `Allowlist` **not** fall through to the sibling check
(or add a `StrictAllowlist` variant), leaving DM hardening intact.

## CLI vs Desktop surface

`buzz agents draft-update --respond-to` accepts only `owner-only|anyone`, and
this is **two independent deliberate gates**, not an oversight:

- `crates/buzz-cli/src/lib.rs:242-247` — `RespondToArg` clap enum has exactly
  two variants; no `allowlist`.
- `crates/buzz-cli/src/agent_management.rs:153-158` — a redundant string check
  rejects anything else: `"respond-to must be owner-only or anyone"`.
- `grep -rn respond_to_allowlist crates/buzz-cli/src/` → **zero hits**. The CLI
  draft wire has no allowlist field at all.

`allowlist` *is* fully wired on the Desktop/Tauri side:

- `desktop/src/features/agents/ui/personaBehaviorDraft.ts:45`
- `desktop/src/features/agents/ui/PersonaAdvancedFields.tsx:53`
- `desktop/src/features/agents/ui/AgentInstanceEditDialog.tsx:153`
- `desktop/src-tauri/src/nostr_convert.rs:950` (parse + test)

**Do NOT conclude "just set allowlist mode via Desktop."** (An earlier revision
of this file said exactly that — it was wrong.) Desktop *can* set the mode, but
because of the sibling fall-through documented above, allowlist mode **does not
achieve Orchestrator-only routing** on a single-owner roster. Setting it looks
like a fix and silently changes nothing — a false-green in the architecture.

The gap is in `author_allowed`'s semantics, not in the CLI surface.

## DM hardening (separate, working as intended)

When `is_dm` is true, `allowlist` and `anyone` are both ignored — only the owner
and cryptographically verified same-owner siblings may fire a turn. This closes a
transitive access grant: clients auto-p-tag every DM participant, so without it
anyone landing in a DM with the agent could prompt it.

## Related

- Supervisor RSS is ~10-19MB; `parallelism` N pre-forks N idle slots
  (`children == parallelism` exactly). High process counts are config, not leak.
- `parallelism` is editable in Desktop `AgentInstanceEditDialog`, not the CLI.

# Buzz fleet operations (macbook-pro-mac)

Verified 2026-08-07 end to end.

## Topology

5 agents, launchd-managed, `ssh mac@100.67.93.90`:

| agent | role | pubkey (prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| jarvis | dispatcher | `642d40fb` |
| shuri | worker (implementation) | `68c00715` |
| captain-america | worker (review) | `04a31feb` |
| hawkeye | worker | `7c4306b9` |
| heimdall | worker (CI) | `416fe473` |

Nick Fury (fleet ops, this agent): `14f600db`.

## Config is read ONCE at startup

`~/agents/<name>/{agent.env,system-prompt.md}` are read by `run-agent.sh`
at process start. **Editing either file changes nothing until restart.**

```
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/xyz.buzz.fleet.<name>
```

`kickstart -k` is required — the jobs have `KeepAlive` with
`SuccessfulExit=false`, so a plain stop leaves them dead.

Verify against the RUNNING PROCESS, never the file:

```
ps -ww -o command= -p <pid>
```

## Three independent silent-failure layers

An agent that never replies proves nothing on its own. Check all three:

1. **Channel membership.** A non-member's inbound sends are REJECTED at the
   relay with `mentioned pubkeys are not channel members`. The agent looks
   idle but literally cannot receive work.
   Fix: `buzz channels add-member --channel <uuid> --pubkey <pk> --role bot`
2. **Allowlist.** `--respond-to-allowlist` drops non-listed senders
   SILENTLY — no error to the sender, no log line worth finding.
3. **LLM backend.** Turn failures surface as a posted error
   (`llm: (combo) transport: error sending request ... 3 attempts`), i.e.
   loudly. 9router blips are usually transient; re-probe the combo before
   treating it as a fleet defect.

**Non-reply is never evidence of a fault.** It is equally consistent with a
long turn on real work — check for child processes before concluding.

## Two `buzz` binaries, not interchangeable

| path | source | `--mention` |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.local/bin/buzz` | Buzz.app bundle | yes |
| `/opt/homebrew/bin/buzz` | `~/Projects/buzz` dev build | **no** |

`buzz-agent` resolved via `shutil.which`, so the winner depended on the
caller's PATH: an interactive shell found the app bundle, a sanitized tool
environment found the stale build. Same command, different result, failing
far from the cause. `buzz_bin()` now prefers the app bundle explicitly.

## macOS gotchas

- No `timeout(1)`.
- `pgrep -fc` is invalid (that's Linux); use `pgrep -f ... | wc -l`.
- `tailscale status` serves a STALE CACHE — use `tailscale ping` to prove
  reachability.
- launchd never rotates `StandardOutPath`/`StandardErrorPath`; agent logs
  grow unbounded (~25MB/3d across 5 agents).

## Fleet layout & identity traps (merged from MEMORY.md, Aug 2026)

Buzz fleet lives on **worker-m1max** under `~/agents/<name>/`:

| agent | role |
|---|---|
| jarvis | coordinator / dispatcher |
| shuri | implementation |
| captain-america | review |
| hawkeye | evals |
| heimdall | CI gate |

The **benchmarker fleet is SEPARATE**: `~/agents-bench/`, on M4. Do not conflate.

### Auth / identity
- Policy is `strict-allowlist`; specialists accept dispatch from **jarvis ONLY**.
- `BUZZ_ACP_DISPLAY_NAME` is a **LABEL, not identity**.
- Duplicate records in `managed-agents.json` resolve to the *first* match, which is
  often `pubkey: None` -> the agent authenticates as nobody and silently does nothing.
- Use the record matching **YOUR pubkey**, and **ITS `relay` value WITH the port**.
- **Read the CHANNEL as truth**, not local state or config.

### Silent stalls
All-green health (process alive, socket ESTABLISHED, presence online) while nothing
happens = **ACK-without-delivery**. See skill `incident-log-forensics`,
ref `ack-without-delivery-silent-transport-stalls.md`.

Two confirmed instances of this class (both fixed in `buzz-acp`, Aug 12 2026):
1. **Stale steer** - `send_steer` matched a task by channel binding rather than a live
   turn, so a fresh mention returned `ack=Ok(Success)` + `drop_withheld=true` and was
   deleted instead of starting a turn. Fix: select only entries whose steer channel is
   still open (`!steer_tx.is_closed()`).
2. **Unconfirmed subscription** - `send_subscribe` returned true once the REQ frame hit
   the socket, which is not proof the relay serves it. Agent sat silent 6.5h with an
   ESTABLISHED socket. Fix: track written REQs, clear on **EOSE**, requeue anything
   unconfirmed past 30s. Note restart does NOT recover the backlog: resubscribe uses
   `since=now`, putting queued messages behind the cursor.

Root cause shared by both: **a write-side success treated as end-to-end delivery.**

## Allowlist routing (measured 2026-08-12)
`BUZZ_ACP_RESPOND_TO=strict-allowlist` + `BUZZ_ACP_RESPOND_TO_ALLOWLIST`
decide who an agent will answer. Live fleet shape:
- **Jarvis** (coordinator, `642d40fb`) allowlists 6 keys INCLUDING the
  operator key `9d948b61` -> answers operator probes directly.
- **Workers** (shuri/captain-america/hawkeye/heimdall) allowlist ONLY
  `642d40fb` (Jarvis) + `14f600db` -> they silently DROP operator messages.

This is intended architecture: workers answer the dispatcher, Jarvis is the
human-facing gateway. A probe to a worker from the operator key looks
exactly like a dead agent (no reply, no log line) but is a correct refusal.
**Always canary/probe Jarvis, not a worker.**

Agents also wake ONLY on a real `p`-tag mention (`require_mention` gate in
lib.rs). A bare "@Name" in message content is display text and never starts
a turn -- pass `--mention <pubkey>` to `buzz-agent messages send`.

# Causal inference: single-observation traps

Two related failure modes, same root cause — treating one correlated
observation as sufficient evidence of causation or intent.

## 1. "X after Y" is not proof Y caused X

Naming a cause from a single "X happened after Y" observation is a causal
error. Any change that precedes an event is a *candidate*, not a confirmed
cause, if only one data point exists.

**Fix:** before committing to the causal story, restart (or otherwise
perturb) the *other* component alone as a negative control. If X still
happens without Y being touched, Y wasn't the cause. Only decide once the
negative control has run — reasoning from a single before/after pair, no
matter how clean it looks, is exactly the shape of error this catches.

This generalizes the same discipline used elsewhere for verification (see
`false-green-verification` and `error-attribution-and-fix-verification`
skills' "negative control" sections) — applied here specifically to causal
attribution in live incidents, not just test/assertion correctness.

## 2. Never infer a customer's/user's goal from their attempted workaround

The workaround someone tried is evidence of *one path* they considered, not
a statement of what they actually want. Inferring the goal from the
workaround silently substitutes your guess for their stated intent — and
the two frequently diverge (the workaround may be a compromise, a wrong
guess, or a habit from a different tool).

**Fix:** re-read the user's stated goal verbatim before proposing or
implementing a fix. If the goal was never stated, ask, or make the
assumption explicit rather than inferring it from what they attempted.

Both traps share a structure: a single observed data point (one timing
correlation, one attempted workaround) gets promoted straight to "cause" or
"intent" without an independent check. The fix is always the same shape —
introduce a second, independent signal (negative control; the verbatim
stated goal) before committing to the conclusion.

# Cursor `state.vscdb` unbounded growth — diagnosis and safe shrink

## Symptom
`~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/globalStorage/state.vscdb` grows
without bound. Measured here: **108.3 GB**. Upstream report:
https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-state-vscdb-growing-at-1-gb-in-a-day/151747

## Root cause
Cursor never expires rows in `cursorDiskKV`. Every agent tool-call is persisted
forever as a "bubble" (`bubbleId:<chat-uuid>:<bubble-uuid>`). Long autonomous
agent loops therefore cost ~GB/agent-hour. Breakdown at 108 GB:

| key family     | rows      | est. size |
|----------------|-----------|-----------|
| `bubbleId:`    | 6,397,171 | ~86 GB    |
| `agentKv:`     | 2,139,581 | ~13 GB    |
| `checkpointId:`| 13,511    | ~1 GB     |
| `ItemTable`    | 3,655     | <1 MB     |

`ItemTable` is trivial — it is *not* the culprit. One single chat held
1,451,379 bubbles (~19.6 GB).

## Tooling (run all three — a bubble-only prune leaves ~70% behind)
- `~/cursor-db-cleanup/shrink.py --cap 2000` — orphans + per-chat cap + compact
- `~/cursor-db-cleanup/gc-blobs.py` — GC unreferenced `agentKv:blob:` rows
  (self-contained: computes the dead set itself, fails closed if any
  workspaceStorage DB is unreadable)
- `~/cursor-db-cleanup/gc-checkpoints.py` — GC orphaned `checkpointId:` rows
- `~/cursor-db-cleanup/audit2.py` — size by key family, sizes remaining levers

Run order matters: cap → blob GC → checkpoint GC → (blob GC again). Deleting
checkpoints can orphan more blobs, so a second blob pass picks up stragglers.

**No cron job** — Patryk stopped using Cursor (Aug 2026), so the weekly
`cursor-db-prune` job and its wrapper were removed. Re-create only if Cursor
comes back into use; the three scripts still work standalone.

## Where the space actually goes

Bubbles are not the main cost once pruned once. Two content families have
**no garbage collector at all**: when the owning chat is deleted, the rows stay
forever.

| family | what it is | GC'd by Cursor? |
|---|---|---|
| `agentKv:blob:<sha256>` | content-addressed attachments | **NO** |
| `checkpointId:<uuid>` | per-chat checkpoints | **NO** |
| `bubbleId:<chat>:<uuid>` | chat messages | no (unbounded) |

Staged result on this box (**108.3 GB → 12.19 GB, 96.1 GB reclaimed**):

| pass | rows removed | size |
|---|---|---|
| bubble cap 2000 | 3,145,843 | 108.3 → 43.2 GB |
| orphan blob GC | 2,109,544 (**98.6% of all blobs**) | 43.2 → 13.9 GB |
| orphan checkpoint GC | 2,015 | 13.9 → 12.19 GB |

Blobs + checkpoints were ~31 GB of pure garbage.

## Floor — when to stop

After all three passes everything left is live: bubbles 5.93 GB, checkpoints
1.81 GB, misc 2.02 GB (largest prefix `ofsContent` 0.17 GB), referenced blobs
1.52 GB. Tightening the cap pays poorly: cap 1000 → 1.71 GB, cap 500 → 2.97 GB,
cap 200 → 4.23 GB. Destroying nearly all history buys ~4 GB. Stop at the GCs.

## Verifying a GC pass without trusting it

Measure the reference set **before** deleting, then compare after. Referenced
count must be identical (30,031 → 30,031 here) — that proves only zero-reference
rows were removed.

Beware two false alarms that look like data loss but predate the cleanup:
- **Dangling refs**: 39,202 refs vs 30,031 blobs present *before* any delete —
  9,171 were already dangling. Cursor's own bookkeeping drift, not damage.
- **"Listed but empty" chats**: cross-check names against earlier delete logs
  before blaming the current pass.

## Four traps (each cost real time / nearly cost data)

### 1. Cursor must be CLOSED, and `pgrep -f` cannot verify it
If the DB is mutated while Cursor holds it open, Cursor detects the change,
renames it `state.vscdb.corrupted.<ts>` and starts a **fresh empty DB** — i.e.
it silently discards all chat history. This actually happened mid-run; the real
file was recovered intact and counts re-verified.

`pgrep -f "/Applications/Cursor.app/Contents/MacOS/Cursor"` **fails to match
even a real process at that exact path** on macOS (verified twice with a
positive control). A guard built on it silently never fires — worse than none.

Use `lsof` on the DB file itself (tests the actual hazard) and fail closed:

```bash
db_is_held() {
  command -v lsof >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 0
  local out rc; out=$(lsof -- "$DB" 2>/dev/null); rc=$?
  [ -n "$out" ] && return 0     # held
  [ $rc -le 1 ] && return 1     # clean "no holders"
  return 0                      # unknown => assume held
}
```
Always positive-control a guard in BOTH directions (held → HELD, free → FREE).

### 2. Plain `VACUUM` on a WAL-mode DB exhausts the disk
The DB is in WAL mode, so in-place `VACUUM` rewrites through `-wal`: peak usage
is roughly `original + compact + WAL`. On a 78 GB DB that consumed ~95 GB and
had to be killed with 11 GB free remaining. It also leaves a large orphaned WAL
(14 GB) that must be `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`-ed back in.

Use `VACUUM INTO '<copy>'` instead: one compact copy, source never mutated,
safely abortable. Then validate the copy (`ItemTable` count + bubble count)
**before** `os.replace()` swapping it in, and delete stale `-wal`/`-shm`.

Pre-flight: `free >= (page_count - freelist_count) * page_size * 1.10`.

### 3. Liveness scan must read ALL ItemTable rows, everywhere
A chat is reachable if its UUID appears in **any** `ItemTable` row of
globalStorage **or** of any `workspaceStorage/*/state.vscdb` (146 of them here).

Narrowing the query to `key LIKE '%omposer%' OR '%aichat%'` looks reasonable and
is **wrong** — composer UUIDs are referenced from many unrelated keys:

| scan scope                              | live refs | "orphans" |
|-----------------------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| globalStorage, filtered keys            | 894       | 1,564,875 |
| + workspaceStorage, filtered keys       | 1,921     | 817,659   |
| + workspaceStorage, ALL rows (correct)  | 6,515     | 151,182   |

The filtered variants would have deleted ~665k **reachable** bubbles as
"orphans". Reconciling two independent implementations against each other is
what caught this — a 10x disagreement means one is wrong; never delete until
they agree.

### 4. Cap by `rowid`, never by `key`
Bubble keys are `bubbleId:<chat-uuid>:<bubble-uuid>` where the suffix is a
**random** UUID — lexical order is chronologically meaningless. `rowid`
reflects insertion order, so "delete oldest N" is `ORDER BY rowid ASC LIMIT N`.

A scratch-DB test using zero-padded keys passes while hiding this bug; the test
fixture must use random UUIDs like the real data.

## Performance note
Reachability implemented as a Python `set` scanned per-key over 3.5M rows was
CPU-bound for 25+ min with zero output. Loading live UUIDs into a TEMP table and
letting SQLite do the join runs the same check in ~2 s.

## Verification checklist
- `PRAGMA quick_check` → `ok`
- `SELECT count(*) FROM ItemTable` unchanged (3,655)
- bubble count matches the post-delete number
- `PRAGMA freelist_count` → 0 after compaction
- no leftover `state.vscdb.compact` / `-wal` / `-shm`

## ES 9.x seeding + semantic_text traps (from chat-profile MEMORY.md)

- Bulk `create` + explicit `_id` **silently drops** documents on a single node.
  Fix: `replicas=0` and `POST _doc`.
- `semantic_text` requires inference. Mustard threat-reports use **ELSER** for
  `content.*` but **Jina** for `diamond.*` — strip `diamond` when seeding.
- The ELSER endpoint needs `model_id` in settings.
- ES|QL returns results under `values`.
- Kibana status lives at `overall.level`.
- Mapping: `source.name`, `ttps.techniques`, `strict`.

Skill: `kibana-dev-cell-seed-and-verify`.

## Behavioural complaint: audit response SHAPE, not status (from MEMORY.md, Aug 2026)

Complaint pattern ("stops after one message", "loop halts") => audit **response SHAPE**, not HTTP status.

- `200 OK` + `NULL error` + healthy provider can hide dropped-tool-call / truncated-stream defects.
- Error histogram is empty **by construction** in that failure mode — so "no errors" proves nothing.
- Negative-control the shape detector on a known-good target first. A log collector that only maps ONE vendor's tool-call encoding will report the other at a FALSE 100% broken rate.
- Nondeterministic => run probes 10x, move the causal knob. Byte-identical pass/fail means race, not shape.

Skills:
- `false-green-verification` ref `empty-error-histogram-audit-shape-not-status.md`
- OmniRoute cursor `kv_after_text` case => skill `model-gateway-operations` ref `omniroute-cursor-silent-turn-stop.md`

default**: every change gets its own `context/changes/<change-id>/` folder

existing change follows this pattern — `context/changes/endpoint-forensic-analysis/shape-notes.md`,

holds the **foundation/orientation** shape-notes (the project-level
`skill.discover` M1 work), not per-initiative shaping. Running the 10x
chain into `context/foundation/` would collide with the foundation notes
and scatter a single initiative's artifacts across two directories.

**How to apply:**
- Create `context/changes/<change-id>/` before invoking `/10x-shape`
- Pass the per-change path explicitly to each downstream skill (the skills
  accept a path argument; use it)
- For Task subagents running a 10x skill, instruct them in the prompt:

- The collision check in `/10x-prd` Step 4 and `/10x-stack-assess` Step 5

- All five chain artifacts co-located: `shape-notes.md`, `prd.md`,
  `stack-assessment.md`, `health-check.md`, `plan.md`
- Cross-link via shape-notes frontmatter `upstream_artifacts:` and
  `related_changes:` keys

**Never:**
- Write 10x chain outputs to `context/foundation/` for a per-initiative change
- Mix the foundation shape-notes (project-level) with per-change shape-notes
- Let the 10x skill's default collision check fire on the wrong path

**Confirmed approach:** Validated Jun 30 — `context/changes/edd-capsule/`
holds all 5 artifacts; both Task subagents (prd, stack-assess) needed the

name: feedback_9router_cheap_empty_content_under_agentic_load
description: 9router's "cheap" combo-model alias returns empty content ("No reply") on multi-turn/high-input-token Hermes agentic sessions, even though it answers trivial single-turn queries fine — distinct failure mode from the shared-status-file race, needs to be diagnosed by turn count/input tokens, not treated as another "agent exited non-zero"
type: feedback
---

# 9router `cheap` Model: Empty Content Under Real Agentic Load

Observed 2026-07-08 during Daybreak S0 spike on `kibana-i9`, after the
shared-status-file race condition (see
`feedback_treadmill_remote_dispatch_race_and_autopause.md`) was already
fixed and reactivated dispatch was confirmed working end-to-end.

## Symptom

Job `1c8f0c92` (task: "Implement fail-closed readiness gate") failed 3
consecutive attempts, each with a **different** terminal signature than
the earlier race-condition bug:

```
"result": "⚠️ No reply: the model returned empty content after retries
and any fallback providers. Try `continue`, switch model/provider, or
inspect the tool output above."
```

- Attempt 1: 12 turns, 354k input tokens, 87s → empty
- Attempt 2: 6 turns, 51k input tokens, 20s → empty
- Attempt 3: 4 turns, 94k input tokens, 25s → empty

Meanwhile a trivial single-turn smoke test against the exact same
provider/model (`hermes chat --provider m4-9router-tailscale --model
cheap -Q -q "Say OK and nothing else."`) returned correctly in ~13s.
This is the inverse tell of the race-condition bug: there, manual
worked and automated failed instantly; here, **simple manual works and
real multi-turn agentic load fails** — so the fault is in the model's
behavior under load, not in treadmill's plumbing.

## Root cause

The `cheap` alias on the 9router combo-router (`m4-9router-tailscale`
→ `http://100.123.104.92:20128/v1`, model id `cheap`) is a
cost-optimized routing tier. Under Kibana-scale agentic sessions
(large tool-result context accumulating across many turns, 90k-350k
input tokens), it appears to intermittently return empty completions
rather than erroring — Hermes surfaces this as "No reply" after
exhausting its own retry/fallback logic, not as an HTTP error. Grepping
302 historical stream files on `kibana-i9`'s worktree found only 3 with
this "No reply"/"empty content" signature, so it is not universal, but
it repeated 3/3 times on this specific task's context size.

The 9router `/v1/models` endpoint also exposes stronger tiers on the
same provider (`main`, `opus`, `glm/glm-5.2`, `cc/claude-*`) — worth
trying one of those for `task-execution` if `cheap` keeps failing on
larger tasks, since the provider/connectivity path (Tailscale-direct,
bypassing the Cloudflare WAF) is already proven working.

## Diagnostic pattern worth repeating

Two visually similar Hermes terminal-failure strings are NOT the same
bug class — read the `result` field, not just "it failed":

| Signature | Likely cause | Where to look |
|---|---|---|
| `agent exited non-zero` (process-level, ~1s, empty stream) | Plumbing: shared status file, orphan process clobber | `orchestrator-loop.ts` monitor/status-path logic |
| `⚠️ No reply: the model returned empty content after retries...` (agent-level, N turns completed, real duration) | Model/provider reliability under load | Model tier choice, input-token size vs. provider's context/output limits, provider-side rate limiting on large payloads |

If a manual **trivial** single-turn query against the same
provider/model succeeds but the **real task** fails, don't re-chase the
plumbing fix — the plumbing is already proven fine; the model tier is
the variable to change next (try a stronger/less-throttled alias on the
same router before giving up on the router entirely).

name: feedback_absence_claim_after_deeper_search
description: Never claim an artifact "doesn't appear to exist" without exhausting keyword variants and author-ID filtered searches
type: feedback
---

# Don't claim absence before exhausting search variants

When a user says "I'm pretty sure X exists" and the first search returns nothing, do NOT respond with "it doesn't appear to exist." The user's recall usually beats a single-pass keyword search.

**Why:** Jun 30 2026 — user said "search deeper I'm pretty sure James shared agent builder cost estimators." My first response had concluded "if you were looking for a specific estimator artifact that James authored, it doesn't appear to exist." User was correct: James had shared `default-llm-calc.secpms.co`, a Google Sheets EIS calculator, AND an ES|QL token consumption query. My premature absence claim wasted a turn and forced the user to push back.

**How to apply:**
- "I couldn't find it" after one search → reframe as "let me try harder" before reporting
- Exhaust: (a) author-ID filtered search, (b) 3-5 keyword variants in parallel, (c) broader date range, (d) channel-scoped search
- Only claim absence after at least 3 distinct query strategies return empty
- When the user insists something exists, weight their recall higher than a single null result — they have context you don't

**Never:**
- Say "it doesn't appear to exist" based on one or two keyword searches
- Frame first-pass negative result as definitive

**Confirmed approach:** Validated Jun 30 2026 — deeper search after user pushback surfaced 3 distinct calculators James had shared across 4 channels over 18 months.

name: feedback_action_input_name_verification
description: GitHub Actions silently ignore wrong input keys; verify against action.yml before pushing
type: feedback
---

# GitHub Action Input Names Must Be Verified Against action.yml

GitHub Actions silently ignore `with:` keys that don't match the
action's declared inputs. The action falls back to its default value
with no warning, and the failure surfaces only at runtime when the
job behaves differently than expected.

**Why:** Captured Jun 30 during the EDD Capsule Phase 0 hygiene PR.
Used `with: path: scripts` for `ludeeus/action-shellcheck@master`. The
action has no `path` input — the correct key is `scandir`. The action
silently fell back to `scandir: .` (whole repo), scanned outside the
intended scope, and failed on a pre-existing SC2011 in
`skills/parallel-experiments/scripts/run-eval.sh` that was never in
the PR's scope. CI went red on a file the PR didn't touch.

**How to apply:**
- Before pushing a workflow that uses a third-party action for the
  first time, fetch the action's input schema:
  ```bash
  gh api repos/<owner>/<action>/contents/action.yaml --jq '.content' \
    | tr -d '\n' | base64 -d | grep -A2 '^\s\+[a-z_]+:'
  ```
- Match every `with:` key in your yaml against the `inputs:` block
- If the action has a `scandir` / `directory` / `working-directory`
  input, use that exact name — `path` is a common wrong guess
- For first-time action use, prefer a 60-second local dry run or a
  trivial test push to a scratch branch before relying on the input

**Never:**
- Assume `path:` is a universal GitHub Actions input name (it's not)
- Trust that the action will error on an unknown `with:` key (it won't)
- Push a workflow using a third-party action for the first time
  without checking its `action.yaml` input schema
- Guess the input name from the README alone — the README may use
  shorthand or omit defaults that `action.yaml` makes explicit

**Confirmed approach:** Validated Jun 30 — the `action.yaml` fetch
confirmed `scandir` (not `path`), and after the fix the shellcheck job
ran scoped to `scripts/` as intended. The 60-second schema check would
have saved a CI round-trip.

**Pairs with:** `feedback_verify_subagent_deliverables` — same theme
of "verify the contract before trusting the output", applied to CI
action inputs rather than subagent file writes.

name: feedback_additive_oss_lane_soft_fail_scoped
description: Additive open-weights subject models (BOTH litellm-* AND eis-openai-gpt-oss-*) in the weekly evals must be soft_fail so a weak OSS model can't red the weekly, while FRONTIER EIS models stay hard-gating — soft-fail by model class, not serving lane
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-04
source: skill-dev 3686518a — weekly #51 (litellm-deepseek) + #54/#56 (eis-openai-gpt-oss-120b redded streams + agent-builder while every frontier lane passed)
---

# Additive OSS Subject Lane Must Be Non-Gating (Scoped soft_fail)

> **CORRECTION (2026-07-04, evidence-led):** an earlier version of this
> memory said soft_fail was scoped to `litellm-*` only and "EIS subject
> models stay hard-gating." That was too narrow. **Open-weights models
> served on the EIS lane (`eis-openai-gpt-oss-*`) are the SAME exploratory
> class and must ALSO be soft-failed.** The correct axis is **model class
> (open-weights / exploratory), NOT serving lane (litellm gateway vs EIS).**
> Frontier EIS models (Claude, Gemini, GPT-5) stay hard-gating. Proven on
> weekly #56: `d9f91ef` extended the condition to
> `litellm-* || eis-openai-gpt-oss-*` and both prior hard fails
> (`streams / gpt-oss-120b`, `agent-builder / gpt-oss-120b`) flipped to
> SOFT while every frontier lane stayed green.

When an OSS/LiteLLM subject model is added additively to a gating weekly eval
suite (DeepSeek/Kimi mirror of the Obs OSS bake-off), it WILL fail some
examples — that is the point of measuring OSS. Those failures must not red the
weekly, or the weekly can never be green with OSS in the subject lane.

## The mechanism

Per-model fanout steps are generated in
`.buildkite/scripts/steps/evals/run_suite.sh` (one step per resolved
`connector_id`). Set `soft_fail: true` on connectors that are the
**open-weights / exploratory class**: ids starting `litellm-` (the gateway
OSS lane) **OR** `eis-openai-gpt-oss-` (open-weights served on EIS). Frontier
EIS subject connectors (`eis-anthropic-*`, `eis-google-gemini-*`,
`eis-openai-gpt-5*`) stay hard-gating. This keeps two properties simultaneously:

- OSS scores still land in the matrix (the OSS-facing signal we added the lane
  for) — soft_fail runs the step, it just doesn't fail the build.
- Frontier EIS subject models remain a strict merge gate.

```bash
if [[ "$connector_id" == litellm-* || "$connector_id" == eis-openai-gpt-oss-* ]]; then
  # append `soft_fail: true` to the generated fanout step
fi
```

**The trap:** `eis-*` looks like "the hard-gating lane," so the original guard
matched only `litellm-*`. But the serving lane (EIS vs gateway) is orthogonal
to model class — an open-weights model is exploratory no matter how it's
served. Gate by CLASS. This is NOT a blanket soft_fail (which would mask real
frontier regressions) — it is scoped to the exploratory class, so it is the
correct classification, not a workaround. The `LITELLM_OPTIONAL` guard in
`setup_connectors.sh` is a separate layer: it handles connector *generation*
failure; soft_fail handles eval *result* failure.

## Distinguishing the two OSS failure shapes

- **Connector never generated** (LiteLLM 403/401, gateway down) → handled by
  `LITELLM_OPTIONAL` graceful-degradation guard (run continues EIS-only).
- **Connector generated, model underperforms** (e.g. DeepSeek emits a malformed
  tool call → "No tool calls found in the response" / negative-case rule
  generated) → handled by scoped `soft_fail`. This is a real model-quality
  finding worth keeping in the matrix, not a bug to fix in Elastic code.

**Why:** Weekly #51 was redded by
`security-ai-rules / litellm-llm-gateway-deepseek-v4-flash` failing one
negative-case routing example while all `eis-*` security jobs passed. A weak
exploratory OSS model must not gate the weekly.

**Never:**
- Blanket `soft_fail` a whole suite/step to get green — that hides EIS
  regressions.
- Revert the OSS lane to get green — that discards the OSS signal the lane
  exists to produce.

**Confirmed approach:** litellm-* scoped soft_fail added Jul 2 (f80da75);
extended to the `eis-openai-gpt-oss-*` open-weights class Jul 4 (`d9f91ef`),
validated live on weekly #56 — both gpt-oss hard fails flipped to SOFT, zero
non-soft hard fails, all frontier lanes green. Also added `streams` to the
off-default-branch cross-team obs soft_fail list (`b33330c`), same policy as
`significant-events` + `agent-builder-dashboards`.

# Agent Builder Built-in Skill Allowlist

Registering a new `defineSkillType` skill via `agentBuilder.skills.register()` **requires** adding the skill `id` to `AGENT_BUILDER_BUILTIN_SKILLS` in:

`x-pack/platform/packages/shared/agent-builder/agent-builder-server/allow_lists.ts`

1. Add skill id to `AGENT_BUILDER_BUILTIN_SKILLS` (Security Solution section)
2. Restart Scout/source Kibana (hot reload does not re-run failed registration)
3. Verify: `curl …/api/agent_builder/skills | jq '.results[] | select(.id=="<id>")'`
4. Check scout log for `Error registering security skills` if missing

**Related (different trap):** `register*()` snapshot FTR tests — see `feedback_kibana_registry_snapshots.md`. Allowlist is **Agent Builder-specific**, not the attachments framework snapshot.

**Inline tools:** Skill-scoped inline tools (e.g. `endpoint-forensic-analysis.patient_zero`) load via `getInlineTools()` and do **not** need entries in `AGENT_BUILDER_BUILTIN_TOOLS` unless also registered globally.

name: feedback_agent_builder_eval_execution_mode_local
description: Agent Builder eval chat clients must send _execution_mode:'local' or trace-based evaluators read 0 (Task Manager runs the agent in a detached trace)
type: feedback
---

# Agent Builder Eval: `_execution_mode: 'local'` or the Trace Splits

When an `@kbn/evals` suite drives an Agent Builder skill through
`POST /api/agent_builder/converse`, the request body **must** include
`_execution_mode: 'local'`. Without it, the server's auto-detect default
runs the agent via **Task Manager** in a detached background context.
Those `gen_ai` / `load_skill` / tool spans form a **separate root trace**,
so `response.trace_id` (the HTTP-request trace the evaluators query) contains
zero agent spans.

Result: every **trace-based** evaluator — `Skill Invoked`, `Tool Calls`,
`Tokens`, `Latency` — reads `0 / N-A`, while `Criteria` and `Trajectory`
(which read the converse `steps[]`, not the trace — see
`feedback_...steps_authoritative`) still score correctly. That split signal
(Trajectory 1.0 + Skill Invoked 0) is the tell.

**Why:** Fixed on the endpoint-forensic-analysis skill (PR #275840). The
canonical eval client `kbn-evals/src/utils/agent_builder_client.ts` already
passes `_execution_mode: 'local'`; the security endpoint suite's custom
`kbn-evals-suite-endpoint/src/chat_client.ts` had copied the converse call
without it. CI build 463775 confirmed: adding it flipped Skill Invoked
0 → 1.0 on all happy paths, populated tool-calls/tokens, and moved latency
from an implausible 0.5-0.9s (HTTP envelope only) to a realistic 4.7-7.4s.

**Diagnostic tells of a detached/forked trace (in priority order):**
1. Implausibly low happy-path latency (sub-second) — the trace is just the
   HTTP envelope, not the agent run.
2. Zero `gen_ai.tool.name` / `inference.span.kind == TOOL` / `gen_ai.usage`
   spans on `response.trace_id`, but `load_skill` spans **do** exist on
   other trace roots when you query `traces-*` directly.
3. Trajectory/Criteria pass while Skill Invoked / Tool Calls read 0.

**Additional C1:L1 gotchas (security-alert-triage, Jul 12 2026):**
- Evaluator skill name must be **`alert-triage`**, not `alert-analysis` — the
  invoked tool is `security.alert-triage`; specs still said `alert-analysis`
  and scored 0 even with `_execution_mode: 'local'`.
- `skill_invoked` trace evaluator must match **`attributes.gen_ai.tool.name`**
  (substring/LIKE), not deprecated `attributes.gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` —
  the old field is absent in current traces so ES|QL returns zero spans.

**Order of diagnosis for "skill_invoked=0 but the skill clearly ran":**
1. Check the suite's chat client for `_execution_mode: 'local'` (this file).
2. Check the evaluator's **skill name** matches the tool actually invoked
   (`alert-triage` not `alert-analysis` for alert triage).
3. Check `skill_invoked` ES|QL uses **`gen_ai.tool.name`**, not
   `tool.call.arguments`.
4. Check the Scout eval config for a **forked exporter**: do NOT set
   `xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.exporters` / `.send_to_self` — a dedicated
   agent-builder exporter forks agent spans off the HTTP trace. Rely on
   inherited platform `evals_tracing` (`telemetry.tracing` +
   `register_tracing.ts` `ElasticsearchOtlpExporter` + `GlobalBridgeProcessor`),
   which nests agent spans under the incoming HTTP trace. (`send_to_self` is
   also schema-invalid on `main` and crash-loops Kibana boot.)
3. Only THEN consider inference-context baggage / nestUnderCaller
   (`feedback_agent_builder_inference_tracing_vs_telemetry`) — that
   baggage-beacon "Fix A" was tried on this PR and **reverted**; it was
   compensating for the config fork, not the real defect.

**Never:**
- Copy a converse call into a new eval chat client without `_execution_mode: 'local'`.
- Re-add `xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.exporters` to an evals Scout config to
  "make tracing work" — it does the opposite for trace-based evaluators.
- Reach for baggage-propagation platform edits before ruling out execution
  mode + config fork.

**Confirmed approach:** Validated end-to-end on PR #275840, CI builds 463775
and 463800 (Sonnet subject / Opus judge).

name: feedback_agent_builder_inference_tracing_vs_telemetry
description: Agent Builder TOOL/CHAIN spans use xpack.agentBuilder.tracing — not telemetry.tracing.exporters alone
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-25
source: endpoint-forensic-analysis EDD session 3513a207 — rerun8–rerun9c
---

# Agent Builder Inference Tracing ≠ Platform Telemetry OTLP

Kibana has **two independent trace export paths**. Enabling only `telemetry.tracing.exporters` does **not** index inference spans (`load_skill`, `execute_tool`, Converse CHAIN) that `@kbn/evals` trace evaluators query in `traces-*`.

| Pipeline | Config | What it exports |
|----------|--------|-----------------|
| Platform telemetry | `telemetry.tracing.exporters` → EDOT `:4318` | HTTP/root telemetry spans |
| Agent Builder inference | `xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.*` via `registerTracingExporter` → `initInferenceTracerProvider` | TOOL/CHAIN spans with `attributes.elastic.inference.span.kind` |

**Why:** Endpoint forensic EDD (Jun 25): L2 trajectory scored 1.0 from HTTP converse steps while L1 `skill_invoked`, `tool_calls`, and token evaluators stayed 0. ES|QL on the converse `trace_id` returned **zero rows** until `send_to_self` was added — and even then local stack instability blocked confirmation. Scout `evals_tracing` config sets telemetry OTLP only; it does **not** set `xpack.agentBuilder.tracing`.

**How to apply (local eval iteration):**

```yaml
# config/kibana.dev.yml (or CLI flags on yarn start)
xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.send_to_self: true   # direct POST /_otlp/v1/traces to ES
xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.scheduledDelay: 50   # dev default is 1000ms batch delay
xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.exporters:
  - url: 'http://localhost:4318/v1/traces'      # optional EDOT duplicate
```

Also pass CLI belt-and-suspenders on start:

```bash
--xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.send_to_self=true \
--xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.scheduledDelay=50 \
--xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.exporters='[{"url":"http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"}]'
```

Spans only export when `agentBuilder:experimentalFeatures` uiSetting is true (`AgentBuilderSpanProcessor.isEnabled()`).

**Never:**
- Diagnose “evaluator bug” when `total_tool_spans=0` before verifying agentBuilder tracing config
- Assume Scout `evals_tracing` alone satisfies matrix L1 trace evaluators
- Use Elastic APM for eval trace capture (`elastic.apm.active=false`)

**Confirmed approach:** Code path `register_tracing.ts` + main-repo `kibana/config/kibana.dev.yml` pattern; validated diagnosis via ES|QL probe on converse `trace_id` (rerun9c: 0 spans before fix, trajectory still 1.0 from steps).

New Agent Builder tools should be skill-scoped (inline tools), not globally registered.

name: feedback_agent_builder_suite_shares_security_config_set
description: Platform agent-builder eval suite boots with the security evals_security_ai_rules Scout config set — a new dark security skill needs ITS flag added there or its deterministic specs get 0 tool calls on every model
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-02
source: skill-dev 3686518a — weekly build #51 triage; recommend_prebuilt_rules.spec.ts 4/4 red on all 6 EIS models
---

# Agent-Builder Suite Shares the Security Scout Config Set

The platform **agent-builder** eval suite
(`x-pack/platform/packages/shared/agent-builder/kbn-evals-suite-agent-builder`)
does not boot with a platform-only Kibana config. In
`.buildkite/pipelines/evals/evals.suites.json` its entry sets
`"serverConfigSet": "evals_security_ai_rules"` — the SAME Scout config set the
security-ai-rules suite uses. That file
(`src/platform/packages/shared/kbn-scout/.../config_sets/evals_security_ai_rules/stateful/classic.stateful.config.ts`)
is the single `--xpack.securitySolution.enableExperimental=[...]` surface that
decides which dark security Agent Builder skills register for BOTH suites.

**Consequence:** the agent-builder suite's `evals/security/*.spec.ts` files
(find_rules, recommend_prebuilt_rules, …) exercise security skills that are dark
by default. If a skill's experimental flag is not in that config set's
`enableExperimental` array, `register_skills.ts` never registers it, the tool is
never offered to the LLM, and every deterministic spec that asserts a tool call
fails.

## The trap: sibling flag present ≠ your flag present

The config set already enabled `dexAiSkillFindRules` (and
`aiRuleCreationEnabled`, `entityAnalyticsEntityStoreV2`). That made it *look*
wired for security. But the newer `recommend-prebuilt-rules` skill (merged PR
#269559, gated on `dexAiSkillRecommendPrebuiltRules`) was never added to the
