# Alerts Snapshot — Local Scout GCS Restore Failure

Security eval suites that call `restoreAlertsSnapshot` from `@kbn/security-evals-alerts-snapshot` (alerts-rag, multi-step, attack-discovery modes smoke) **often fail on local Scout** with:

```
repository_exception: [snapshot-loader-repo-*] Could not determine repository generation from root blobs
```

Weekly CI and golden-cluster runs may succeed; local Scout + `GCS_CREDENTIALS` from Vault is fragile (repo registration, generation blobs, timing).

## Standalone `.alerts-security.alerts-default` index (Jul 13 2026)

Kibana can create **`.alerts-security.alerts-default`** as a standalone index outside
`.internal.alerts-security.*`. If it exists before `restoreAlertsSnapshot`, GCS restore
fails with alias/index conflicts even when `.internal.*` indices were deleted.

**Fix:** extend `restoreAlertsSnapshot` in `kbn-security-evals-alerts-snapshot/src/restore.ts`
to delete `.alerts-security.alerts-default` in the same pre-restore cleanup pass (landed on
`fix/weekly-evals-matrix`, PR #277737). Manual restore workaround: delete that index by
exact name, then re-run `es_snapshot_loader restore`.

## Spec pattern (validated Jun 28)

Wrap restore **and** post-restore verify in try/catch; log warning and continue against existing cluster alerts:

```typescript
try {
  await restoreAlertsSnapshot({ esClient, log, config: snapshotConfig });
  await verifyAlertsRagSnapshot({ esClient, log }); // alerts-rag only
} catch (err) {
  log.warning(`snapshot restore failed: ${message}; evaluating against existing cluster alerts.`);
}
```

Suites fixed on `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` (uncommitted): `alerts_rag.spec.ts`, `multi_step.spec.ts`, `attack_discovery.spec.ts` (modes smoke).

## Attack Discovery dataset resolution

When `EVALUATIONS_KBN_URL` points at golden (score export) but Scout runs locally, **`shouldResolveFromGoldenCluster()` must return false** if `KIBANA_URL` matches `localhost|127.0.0.1`. Otherwise the suite pulls an empty upstream dataset instead of bundled `data/eval_dataset_attack_discovery_all_scenarios.jsonl`.

Default Playwright grep for local matrix: `bundled alerts` (skips failing `modes smoke` / searchAlerts snapshot path).

## Score interpretation without snapshot

- **Trajectory / Sequence Accuracy** can still be **1.0** (tool routing from HTTP steps).
- **Factuality / Relevance** may be **low** (reference answers assume oh-my-malware snapshot data not present on cluster).
- Matrix L2 can improve from fresh exports; L3 content scores need snapshot on CI or accepted degraded local signal.

**Never:**

- Hard-fail the entire suite on snapshot restore for local matrix iteration.
- Assume golden `EVALUATIONS_KBN_URL` implies golden **dataset** resolution on localhost Scout.

**Confirmed approach:** C1 v1 failed all 4 tests on first category; v2 with try/catch passed 8 examples in ~12m. C6 v2 passed 5 scenarios after bundled-JSONL + grep fix.

name: feedback_api_param_casing_silent_truncation
description: camelCase vs snake_case API param mismatch silently truncates data via Zod default fallback
type: feedback
---

# API Param Casing Mismatch Silently Truncates Data

A camelCase param (`perPage`) sent where a Zod/OpenAPI schema expects
snake_case (`per_page`) is not rejected — the unrecognized key is
dropped and the schema falls back to its small default page size. The
caller sees a normal 200 response with plausible-looking but truncated
data, with no error anywhere in the chain.

**Observed:** Kibana Attack Discovery anonymization-fields API
(`example-mcp-app-security`, GitHub issue #46 / PR #52) — the client
sent `perPage`, the server schema expected `per_page`, so only the
default page of anonymization fields came back and starved the
downstream LLM prompt of most of the actual field set.

**How to apply:**
- Never assume param casing — verify against the actual Zod/OpenAPI
  schema in source before wiring an API call
- Cite the schema file path in a comment on the API call site
- Add a fail-loud guard that warns when a result set looks
  suspiciously small/truncated vs. expected
- Codify "verify casing against source schema, cite the schema file"
  as a `CONTRIBUTING.md` convention so the check isn't ad hoc

**Never:**
- Trust that an unrecognized query param will raise a validation error
  — many schema validators silently ignore unknown keys and apply
  defaults instead
- Ship a param-name fix without also adding a truncation guard —
  the same schema-default fallback can recur with any other param

type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-01
source: session 3686518a — Build #152 chain resume on commit 710a8fdcd0
---

# Babysitter State: Stale KIBANA_BUILD_ID and completedBuilds After New Commit

**The rule:** When resuming `babysit-security-on-demand-evals.sh --continue` after pushing a new commit, the state file (`matrix-output/on-demand-babysit-state.json`) carries forward two stale fields that will make the chain run against the WRONG dist or skip needed suites.

## Two independent staleness issues

### 1. Stale `kibanaBuildId`

The state retains the `kibanaBuildId` from the prior commit's seed build. Subsequent suites reuse it via `KIBANA_BUILD_ID` env, which **skips the Kibana dist rebuild** — so they run against an old dist that does NOT contain the new commit's changes.

**Fix:** Extract the fresh dist UUID from the new seed build's "Build Kibana Distribution" job log (grep for the GCS path `tmp/builds/<UUID>/kibana-default.tar.zst`), then update `state.kibanaBuildId` BEFORE the chain continues past the seed suite:

```python
# Extract fresh UUID from seed build's Kibana dist job log
# Job name: "🧑‍🏭 Build Kibana Distribution"
# Log line: "Copying ... to gs://kibana-ci-artifacts-.../tmp/builds/<UUID>/kibana-default.tar.zst"
bk job log <job-id> -p <pipeline> -b <build> | grep -oE "019[ef][0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}" | sort -u
```

Then `state['kibanaBuildId'] = '<fresh-uuid>'` and reload the launchd job.

### 2. `completedBuilds` tracks suites by name, not by commit

The state marks a suite "complete" when its build passes, without recording which commit it ran against. On resume after a new commit, suites that passed on the OLD commit are treated as satisfying the NEW commit's matrix — so the babysitter won't re-run them.

**Fix:** Filter `completedBuilds` to remove entries for suites you need on the new commit, and add them back to `remainingSuites`:

```python
state['completedBuilds'] = [b for b in state['completedBuilds']
                            if b['suite'] not in ('security-alert-triage', 'security-alerts-rag-regression')]
for s in ['security-alert-triage', 'security-alerts-rag-regression']:
    if s not in state['remainingSuites']:
        state['remainingSuites'].append(s)
```

**Why:** Both issues discovered when resuming the babysitter on commit `710a8fdcd0` — it picked up `kibanaBuildId=019f00d1-...` (June 26 dist) and treated `security-alert-triage` (#134) and `security-alerts-rag-regression` (#133) as complete despite them having run on the old commit `ab38a12f`.

**How to apply:** Whenever you push a new commit to `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` and resume the babysitter, run both fixes above as a pre-flight before letting the chain continue. Or — per `feedback_on_demand_iteration_vs_weekly_matrix.md` — skip the on-demand chain entirely and trigger the weekly pipeline for matrix data.

**Never:**
- Assume `state.kibanaBuildId` is fresh after a commit push.
- Assume `completedBuilds` entries apply to the current commit.

name: feedback_background_shell_does_not_survive_turns
description: Background shells (block_until_ms=0, nohup, &) die when the Cursor conversation advances turns — use a single foreground blocking poll or accept re-dispatch
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-30
source: skill-dev 3686518a — 3 separate background watchers died across turns; poll logs went stale
---

# Background Shells Don't Survive Cursor Turns

When you dispatch a long-running shell with `block_until_ms: 0` (background) and the conversation advances to the next user turn, the backgrounded process is **killed**. This affects:

- `block_until_ms: 0` shells with `notify_on_output` sentinels
- `nohup ... &` background dispatches
- `&`-suffixed backgrounding within a wrapper shell

## Failure mode

```bash
# Turn 1: dispatch watcher
bash babysit-40-ab.sh   # block_until_ms=0, notify_on_output="SENTINEL"
# → Shell ID 981651 started, polling every 2 min

# Turn 2 (user sends a message):
# → Shell 981651 process killed; log stops at last poll; sentinel never fires
```

The `notify_on_output` mechanism relies on the shell process staying alive to emit the sentinel line. Once the process dies, the notification never fires, and the watcher must be manually restarted.

`nohup` does NOT help — Cursor's process management kills the process group on turn advance, not just the foreground process.

## Correct patterns

### Pattern 1: Single foreground blocking poll (preferred for <60 min waits)

```bash
# block_until_ms set high enough to cover expected runtime (e.g. 3600000 = 60 min)
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  # poll logic
  if <terminal_condition>; then echo "SENTINEL"; break; fi
  sleep 120
done
```

The shell stays in the foreground, the user sees progress, and `notify_on_output` fires when the sentinel matches. Cap iterations to avoid infinite loops.

### Pattern 2: Accept re-dispatch across turns

If the wait exceeds ~60 min, the conversation will likely advance. Accept that the watcher dies and re-dispatch a fresh poll on the next turn. Each poll is stateless (queries Buildkite API), so no state is lost.

### Pattern 3: External scheduler (launchd/cron)

For truly long-running watches (hours), use a launchd plist or cron job that writes to a log file. The agent reads the log file on each turn. This decouples the watch from the Cursor session lifecycle.

## Never

- Assume a `block_until_ms: 0` shell with `notify_on_output` will fire across turns
- Use `nohup` or `&` to "keep alive" — Cursor kills the process group
- Dispatch a watcher and tell the user "I'll be notified" without qualifying that the conversation must not advance

## Confirmed approach

Jun 30 session: 3 background watchers (babysit-40, babysit-41, combined poll) all died across turns. Replaced with a single foreground `for` loop with `block_until_ms: 0` and `notify_on_output` — worked until the 30-iteration cap, then re-dispatched a focused poll on the next turn.

# Benchmarker: two daemons on one GPU VM + serial pipeline silently starve each other

## Symptom
The i9 24/7 benchmarker (`kibana-i9`) had a model stuck in `benchmarking` for
~2h. Its log spammed:

```
Buildkite: waiting for pipeline to become idle {"activeBuilds":[{"number":195,"message":"Benchmarker: deepreinforce-ai/Ornith-1.0-35B on-demand eval"}], "elapsedMs":307090}
Scheduler: waiting for deferred Buildkite poll before dequeuing next model {"pending":1}
```

The blocking builds (#191, #195) were **Ornith** on-demand evals that kept
appearing on the shared serial pipeline `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`
(`skip_queued_branch_builds` → one build at a time).

## The tell (non-obvious)
Grepping the i9 log for `triggering on-demand build.*Ornith` **after the
Qwen run started returned NOTHING** — the i9 only ever saw the Ornith builds
in its `waiting for pipeline idle` *poll*, never triggered them. A daemon
that is *waiting on* builds it never *triggered* means **a second producer
exists**.

## Root cause
A **rogue second benchmarker daemon on the M4 host** (started in a prior
session, NOT under launchd so it survived silently):

```
node /tmp/benchmarker-queue start --config .../config/local.json \
  --stage2 --stage3 --ci-evals --poll-interval 10000 \
  --clear-pending --enqueue-after-clear deepreinforce-ai/Ornith-1.0-35B
```

`--enqueue-after-clear Ornith` made it re-process Ornith forever: redeploying
the **same shared GPU VM** and firing Ornith builds onto the **same serial
pipeline** the i9 was trying to use. The `maxConcurrentRuns: 1` invariant is
enforced *inside* one scheduler; nothing enforces it *across* daemon
instances. Two daemons thrash: each redeploys the vLLM container under the
other's in-flight eval, and they queue-block each other on the serial
pipeline.

## Fix (single-owner)
1. `ps aux | grep -iE "benchmarker-queue|dist/cli.js (start|benchmark)"` on
   every host that might run one (M4 + i9). Exclude the `Cursor Helper` and
   `ssh ... tail -f` lines.
2. Kill the rogue one. Graceful `kill -TERM` **hangs** because the shutdown
   handler drains the detached Buildkite poll (up to `pollTimeoutMs` 3h) —
   escalate to `kill -9` for a rogue competitor (its stale poll state is
   worthless). "Never pkill during CI eval polling" protects the daemon you
   *keep*, not a rogue you're removing.
3. `rm -f .benchmarker-queue.lock` (the M4 repo lock still points at the dead
   PID — this lock is per-checkout, does NOT cover cross-host).
4. Cancel the stale in-flight build so the pipeline frees immediately:
   `bk build cancel <n> --pipeline elastic/kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals -y --no-input`
   (note: `bk build cancel` has **no `--org` flag** — use
   `--pipeline <org>/<slug>`; and it 422s if the build already finished).

Within ~1 poll cycle the surviving daemon detects idle and triggers the
correct model's build.

## Durable takeaways
- **Only ONE benchmarker daemon may run against a given GPU VM + on-demand
  pipeline.** The i9 is the designated 24/7 owner — do not leave an M4
  foreground daemon alive.
- The `.benchmarker-queue.lock` file is **per-checkout**, not a cross-host
  lease. A real fix would be an ES-backed lease on the GPU VM keyed by VM
  host, so a second daemon refuses to deploy.
- Diagnosis heuristic: **a daemon waiting on builds it never triggered ⇒
  look for a second producer**, not a wedge in the local daemon.
- `--enqueue-after-clear <model>` is a foot-gun for a long-lived daemon: it
  makes the model immortal (re-queued forever). Use it only for a one-shot
  foreground run, never for a persistent daemon.

# Never parse free-text LLM reasoning as literal CLI arguments

`stage1-worker.ts` used to regex-scrape a model's free-text "reasoning
feedback" (LLM prose explaining suggested deploy overrides) for CLI flags,
e.g. `--chat-template\s+(\S+)` and `--dtype\s+(\w+)`. This is unsafe: prose
like "...passing `--dtype` should be bfloat16..." matches the regex and
captures the stopword `"should"` as the literal flag value, producing a
corrupted `--dtype should` (or `--chat-template with`) argument that breaks
the vLLM container on boot. This is the same class of bug across every
regex-scraped override in that function — audit **all** of them, not just
the one that surfaced, once the pattern is found in one flag.

**Fix pattern**: constrain the capture group to the tool's actual accepted
enum/vocabulary (e.g. `--dtype\s+(auto|half|float16|bfloat16|float|float32)\b`)
instead of a generic `\S+`/`\w+` wildcard. A wildcard capture from
LLM-generated prose will eventually capture a stopword.

## Never

- Regex-capture a CLI flag value from LLM-generated free text using a
  generic wildcard (`\S+`, `\w+`) — constrain to the tool's real accepted
  value set.
- Assume a single flag's parsing bug is isolated — grep the same function
  for sibling flags parsed the same way.

# A locally-committed fix does nothing until it's pushed — verify before assuming a redeploy has it

Found and fixed the chat-template regex bug, committed locally
(`382f57b`), but never pushed. The i9 daemon later redeployed
`Devstral-Small-2-24B` (unrelated trigger) and used `deploy-benchmarker.sh`,
which pulls **`origin/main`** on i9 — not the local dev machine's working
tree. Since the fix commit only existed locally, i9 redeployed with the
exact same broken `--chat-template with` flag the fix was supposed to
prevent, silently, with no error surfaced (deploy scripts don't diff against
"the fix I have but haven't shipped").

**Rule**: after committing a fix intended to change daemon/deploy behavior,
verify `git log --oneline origin/main -5` includes the fix commit (or push
it) **before** trusting the next redeploy to have it — a passing local
typecheck/test/lint run gives zero signal about whether the remote daemon
will actually run the new code. This is a specific instance of "self-verify
everywhere" for distributed daemon/worker architectures: the verification
surface is the remote host's checked-out commit, not just local CI.

## Never

- Assume a locally-committed fix is live on a remote daemon that deploys
  from `origin/main` — check `git log --oneline origin/main` (or push)
  before relying on the fix being active in the next deploy cycle.

# `bk build create` flag semantics — env vs commit

## What happened

Triggered weekly Build #47 (`kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals`) to validate a
skill fix. Passed build parameters like this (WRONG):

```bash
bk build create -i --no-input --yes \
  -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals \
  -c "KIBANA_GIT_BRANCH=fix/weekly-evals-matrix" \
  -c "KIBANA_BUILD_ID=$(cat .last-weekly-seed-id || echo '')"
```

Build #47 failed in ~7 min with **1 job** — the `Upload Pipeline` step —
and never fanned out. Log showed:

```
git fetch -v --prune -- origin KIBANA_BUILD_ID=
fatal: couldn't find remote ref KIBANA_BUILD_ID=
git checkout -f KIBANA_BUILD_ID=
error: pathspec 'KIBANA_BUILD_ID=' did not match any file(s) known to git
```

## Root cause

In `bk build create`, `-c` is **`--commit`**, NOT an env-var setter. The
last `-c` won, so Buildkite treated the literal string `KIBANA_BUILD_ID=`
(empty because the seed file didn't exist) as the commit to check out. The
pipeline-upload step died on the invalid ref before expanding into the
per-suite/per-model eval jobs. The code under test never ran.

## Correct shape (matches proven-good Build #46)

```bash
bk build create -i --no-input --yes \
  -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals \
  -c <ACTUAL_COMMIT_SHA> \
  -b fix/weekly-evals-matrix \
  -e KBN_EVALS=1 \
  -e KBN_EVALS_WEEKLY=1 \
  -e KIBANA_SLACK_NOTIFICATIONS_ENABLED=true
```

- `-c` / `--commit` = the actual commit SHA (get via `git rev-parse upstream/<branch>`).
- `-b` / `--branch` = the branch name.
- `-e` / `--env` = `KEY=VALUE` env vars (this is where KBN_EVALS etc. go).
- **No `KIBANA_BUILD_ID`.** The weekly pipeline does NOT take a
  `KIBANA_BUILD_ID` build param — that was an invention. (KIBANA_BUILD_ID
  for Kibana-dist reuse is an on-demand / babysit concept, and even there
  it must be the seed build's Buildkite UUID, never a human build number
  or an empty string.)

## Second cause of the SAME symptom: abbreviated commit SHA (2026-07-04)

Even when `-c` is used correctly for a commit, passing an **abbreviated**
SHA fails identically — 1 job, `Upload Pipeline` dies, no fanout:

```
[INFO]: Fetching d9f91ef67f5d from origin
fatal: couldn't find remote ref d9f91ef67f5d
[ERROR]: Failed to fetch d9f91ef67f5d from origin
```

**Root cause:** the sparse-checkout plugin runs `git fetch origin <sha>`,
and `git fetch` **cannot resolve an abbreviated SHA** — it needs the full
40-char SHA or a ref name. Weekly #55 died on this; #56 (identical trigger
but full SHA) cleared the upload step immediately.

**Rule:** always pass the FULL 40-char SHA to `-c`. Get it with
`git rev-parse <ref>` (NOT `git rev-parse --short`, NOT copy-pasting a
short SHA from `git log --oneline`).

```bash
FULL=$(git rev-parse d9f91ef67f5d)   # -> d9f91ef67f5ddc341e1baa1e2dedffc6d6a67a46
bk build create -c "$FULL" -b <branch> -i -y -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals
```

Both the env-via-`-c` mistake and the abbreviated-SHA mistake produce the
**same failure signature** (1 job, `Upload Pipeline` failed, "couldn't find
remote ref"). When you see that signature, check BOTH: (1) is `-c` a real
commit and not an env pair, and (2) is it the full 40-char SHA.

## Verification gate before trusting a weekly trigger

A weekly build that shows only **1 job** after a couple of minutes is a
FAILED fanout, not a slow start. Confirm the pipeline expanded:

```bash
bk build view <N> -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys; raw=sys.stdin.read(); d=json.loads(raw[raw.find('{'):]); print(len(d['jobs']),'jobs')"
```

Healthy weekly = ~27 jobs after the `Upload Pipeline` step passes. The
upload step itself legitimately takes 3–5 min because it git-fetches all
branches/tags first, so don't panic at "1 job running" in the first
minutes — but DO panic if it's still 1 job after the upload step is
`passed`/`failed`.

# Buildkite `bk job retry` — Args + Token Scope

Retrying a specific Buildkite job from the CLI has two non-obvious constraints.

**Why:** While babysitting a Kibana PR build (463251) whose only failures were
3 known flakes, I tried to retry just those jobs and hit both traps in sequence.

## 1. It takes ONLY the job UUID

```bash
bk job retry <job-uuid>        # correct
bk job retry -p <pipeline> --build <n> <uuid>   # WRONG: unknown flags -p / --build
```

The pipeline + build context are derived from the job UUID itself — do not pass
`-p`/`--build`/`--pipeline`. (Contrast `bk build create`, which does use
`-c`/`-b`/`-e`.)

## 2. It needs a WRITE-scoped GraphQL token

The default read-only `bk` token returns **403 (insufficient GraphQL scope)** on
`job retry`. Retrying jobs is a mutation.

**How to apply — greening a build blocked only by flakes, without a write token:**
- Click **Retry** on the flaky jobs in the Buildkite UI (fastest), OR
- Re-trigger the whole build with `/ci` (spends a fresh build), OR
- Get a write-scoped `bk` token for programmatic retries.

Read paths (`bk build view`, `list_annotations`, `search_logs` MCP) all work with
the read-only token — only *mutations* (job retry, build create/cancel) need
write scope.

**Never:** conclude a PR is regressing from a red build without first
classifying the failing jobs — a build red purely on pre-existing flakes
(cross-check `gh issue list` for the failing spec) is not your PR's fault, and
its cloud deploy is still valid.

**Confirmed approach:** Verified on elastic/kibana#272111 build 463251 — all 3
hard failures matched open flaky-test issues; none in the PR's file scope.

# Buildkite `limited` Jobs Are Not API-Retriable

On `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`, model fanout child jobs can land in **`limited`** when the suite's shared concurrency group is already full at schedule time (sibling build still holding slots). These jobs **never started** — zero logs, no agent assigned.

## API behavior

Retry endpoints (`retry_job` MCP, Buildkite REST) reject `limited` jobs:

> **"Only failed, timed out, canceled or expired jobs can be retried"**

Also tried and failed:
- `bk job retry` → may 403 without GraphQL scope
- `unblock_job` → **"This job type cannot be unblocked"**

`limited` is **not** the same as `waiting` for an agent under normal load — it is concurrency-group starvation at upload time.

## Unblock pattern

1. Identify which **other build** holds the concurrency group (e.g. stuck `workflows/opus` on build #295 running 2h+).
2. **Cancel the blocking job** (or entire blocking build if safe) to free the group.
3. **`limited` jobs do not auto-resume** — trigger a **full rebuild** of the stuck build (or a fresh on-demand trigger), not per-job retry on the original fanout UUIDs.

## Never

- Recommend `bk build retry` / MCP `retry_job` on `limited` fanout jobs as the unblock path
- Trigger a third full rebuild while diagnosing — duplicates Kibana rebuild cost without fixing group contention
- Interpret `limited` on a second concurrent on-demand build as a wiring failure before checking CI slot / concurrency-group occupancy (see also `feedback_concurrent_weekly_builds_ci_contention.md`)

## Related

- `feedback_concurrent_weekly_builds_ci_contention.md` — why two builds on same branch starve each other
- `reference_security_matrix_on_demand_chain.md` — on-demand worker pipeline + babysitter lock

# Buildkite CI Diagnosis — Use the Read-Only MCP First

When diagnosing a failed Buildkite build/job, reach for the
`user-buildkite-read-only-toolsets` MCP server **before** curl or `bk`.

**Why:** During Ornith eval triage I hunted for a `BUILDKITE_API_TOKEN`
in `.env` files and fell back to `bk build view`, which is slow, needs
auth plumbing, and dumps huge JSON. The user stopped me: "why you cannot
use MCP instead?" The MCP toolset was available the whole time and got
the root cause in one call.

**How to apply:** For failure diagnosis, the canonical path is:
- `tail_logs` — last N entries (recommended first; most failures land in
  the final log lines). Args: `org_slug`, `pipeline_slug`, `build_number`,
  `job_id`, `tail`.
- `search_logs` — regex with `context`/`before_context`/`after_context`,
  `limit`. Use `pattern:"error|failed|exception|ENOTFOUND|..."`.
- Supporting tools in the same server: `list_builds`, `get_build`,
  `list_jobs`, `get_job`, `list_annotations`, `list_artifacts_for_job`.
- Always **read the tool's JSON descriptor** under
  `mcps/user-buildkite-read-only-toolsets/tools/<tool>.json` before the
  first call to get required arg names.

**Gotcha:** `search_logs` over a whole eval job matches a lot of *normal*
boot noise (e.g. `curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 5620`
during Kibana startup is expected retry, not the failure). Prefer
`tail_logs` for the actual terminal error; use `search_logs` only to
locate a specific known string.

**Never:**
- Hunt for a Buildkite API token in `.env` to curl the raw `log.txt`.
- Default to `bk build view <N> --json` for log reading when the MCP is
  connected — reserve `bk` for actions the read-only MCP can't do
  (e.g. `bk build create -y -i` to trigger, per
  `feedback_bk_build_create_env_vs_commit_flag`).

**Confirmed approach:** 2026-07-03 — `tail_logs` on the failed on-demand
eval job returned the `[cause]` line (`ENOTFOUND` on the tunnel host) that
classified the failure as infra, not model quality, in a single call.

name: feedback_buildkite_trigger_needs_full_sha
description: Buildkite weekly/on-demand eval triggers must pass the full 40-char commit SHA — a short SHA makes the sparse-checkout git fetch fail and the build dies at pipeline upload in seconds
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-02
source: skill-dev 3686518a — weekly kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals build #52 died in 5s
---

# Buildkite Eval Triggers Need the Full 40-Char SHA

When triggering a Kibana eval pipeline (`kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals`,
`kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`, matrix chains) by commit, pass the **full
40-char SHA**, never an abbreviated one.

**Why:** the pipelines use the `sparse-checkout-buildkite-plugin`, whose checkout
hook runs `git fetch <origin> <BUILDKITE_COMMIT>`. GitHub's smart-HTTP transport
can fetch a reachable **full** SHA (`allowReachableSHA1InWant`) but rejects an
**abbreviated** SHA — a short SHA isn't a valid ref or want-line. The build then
dies at the very first step:

```
fatal: couldn't find remote ref f80da75c7cd6
[ERROR]: Failed to fetch <sha> from origin
🚨 Error: running "plugin sparse-checkout-buildkite-plugin checkout" shell hook ... exited with status 1
```

Symptom: build `state: failed` with a **~5-second** runtime (created → finished),
failing on `:pipeline::arrow_up: Upload Pipeline` / `terrazzo-initial-pipeline-upload`,
BEFORE any suite fanout. The commit can be perfectly fine and present on
`elastic/kibana` (`git ls-remote upstream <branch>` shows the full SHA as the tip);
the *only* problem is the abbreviated trigger SHA.

**How to apply:**
- `bk build create -c <FULL_40_CHAR_SHA>` — get it with `git rev-parse HEAD`, not
  `git rev-parse --short HEAD` and not the 12-char SHA copied from `git log --oneline`.
- Non-default branches also need `-i` / `--ignore-branch-filters` (the pipeline has
  branch filtering; API/CLI triggers from `fix/*` branches 422 without it).
- Distinct from the fork-vs-upstream trap (`feedback_on_demand_buildkite_upstream_branch`):
  that one is "SHA only on the fork"; this one is "SHA is on upstream but abbreviated".
  A 5-second upload-step death = suspect the SHA form first (short vs fork), not the
  pipeline YAML or `run_suite.sh`.

**Never:**
- Trigger with a 7/12-char SHA and assume "the commit is on upstream, so it'll work."
- Blame the pipeline YAML / `run_suite.sh` edit for an instant upload-step death
  before checking the trigger SHA form.

**Confirmed approach:** #52 (short `f80da75c7cd6`) died in 5s at upload; re-trigger
#53 with full `f80da75c7cd60e0e4739f76cc5a2d1066fb95614` + `-i` ran past upload into
the suite fanout.

source: skill-dev 3686518a — build #40 matrix analysis; converse API + evaluator + registration code traced; flag verified in Scout config
---

# C2 L2 Trajectory = 0 — Skill Loads But Agent Doesn't Call Tools

The security-ai-rules C2 L2 (Trajectory) score has been **0 across all 6 models** on every weekly build. Root cause investigation (Jun 30, build #40) confirmed this is a **genuine model behavior gap**, not a wiring bug, trace export failure, evaluator malfunction, or missing feature flag.

## Investigation chain (what was ruled out)

| Hypothesis | Evidence | Verdict |
|------------|----------|---------|
| Evaluator not wired | `evaluate_routing_dataset.ts:140-188` — `createRuleRoutingTrajectoryEvaluator` is in the eval stack | ❌ Wired correctly |
| Golden sequence missing | `routing_examples` dataset has `tool_sequence: [security.discover_rule_tags, security.find_rules]` | ❌ Goldens present |
| Scores not exported | Matrix shows `Trajectory: median=0, count=3` — evaluator ran and emitted scores | ❌ Scores exist |
| Traces missing on golden cluster | `trace.pull-otlp` returns 0 spans for build #40 and #41 runs | ⚠️ True, but irrelevant — trajectory reads `output.steps`, not traces |
| Converse client doesn't return steps | `chat_client.ts:74-79` — `converseNaturalLanguage` returns `steps: syncResponse.steps ?? []` | ❌ Client is correct |
| Converse API doesn't populate steps for Track B | `chat_converse.yaml` example shows `steps` with `tool_call` type for natural-language calls | ❌ API supports it |
| `getToolCallSteps` can't parse the shape | `evaluation_helpers.ts:52-65` — filters `type === 'tool_call'`, maps `tool_id` | ❌ Parser is correct |
| **Feature flag `dexAiSkillFindRules` off** | `register_skills.ts:72` gates the skill; Scout config `evals_security_ai_rules/stateful/classic.stateful.config.ts:31` sets `dexAiSkillFindRules` in `enableExperimental`; weekly `run_suite.sh:254` runs `--arch stateful` with this config set | ❌ Flag is ON |
| **Inline tools not injected on skill load** | `load_skill_tools.ts:79-86` calls `toolManager.addTools({dynamic:true})` for inline + registry tools; `load_skill_tools_after_read.ts` hook fires on SKILL.md readFile | ❌ Tools ARE available after load |

## Actual root cause

The agent loads the `find-security-rules` skill (confirmed by L1 "Skill Invoked" = 10/10) but **does not call the prescribed tools** (`security.discover_rule_tags`, `security.find_rules`). Instead, it answers the user's question directly from the skill's embedded methodology content. The converse response's `steps` array has no `tool_call` entries → `getToolCallSteps` returns `[]` → trajectory LCS coverage = 0.

This is consistent across all 6 models (Opus, Sonnet, Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, OSS-120b), which indicates a **skill design gap**, not a model-specific failure.

## Why L1 passes but L2 fails

- **L1 (Skill Invoked)**: Checks whether the SKILL.md was loaded (via OTel spans / filestore.read). The skill loads → L1 = 1.
- **L2 (Trajectory)**: Checks whether the agent called the prescribed tool sequence. The agent skips tools → L2 = 0.

This is a **split signal**: the skill is discoverable (good routing) but not actionable (the methodology doesn't enforce tool usage).

## What won't fix it

- Playwright `retries: 1` — the agent consistently skips tools, not a flake
- `validateToolCalls` empty-name filter — unrelated infra fix
- Trace export fixes — trajectory reads `output.steps`, not traces
- More repetitions — deterministic behavior across all models

## What would fix it

1. **Skill content change**: Make the find-security-rules SKILL.md mandate tool usage ("You MUST call `security.discover_rule_tags` before answering any inventory query") rather than describing the workflow as optional methodology.
2. **Routing-level enforcement**: Agent builder could enforce that skills with `tool_sequence` annotations must call those tools before responding (platform feature, not a suite fix).
3. **Accept the gap**: Document C2 L2 = 0 as a known product limitation in the matrix, with the improvement lever pointing to skill content hardening.

## Current status

C2 L2 = 0 is a **real product gap** that blocks the DoD threshold (≥ 8.0). It cannot be resolved by eval infrastructure changes alone. The matrix accurately reflects that current skills load but don't drive tool usage in the routing path.

**Verified end-to-end (Jun 30):** the skill registers (flag on), the inline tools are defined (`security.discover_rule_tags`, `security.find_rules`), and they're injected into the ToolManager via `loadSkillTools` when the agent reads SKILL.md. The tools are physically available to the LLM — the agent simply chooses not to call them. This rules out every setup hypothesis and confirms a model/skill-design gap.

**Accepted as documented gap** per operator decision (Jun 30). Matrix DoD proceeds with this known limitation; improvement lever is skill content hardening or platform-level tool enforcement.

# Check In-Flight / Merged Work Before Starting a Fix

In a multi-session, multi-worktree environment (parallel agents,
self-updating daemon, sibling `feat/*` branches), a fix you're about to
start may already be in flight or merged from another session. Check
BEFORE creating a worktree and writing code, not at ship time.

**Why:** On 2026-07-01 I created
`fix-db-worker-pool-parameter-property` and reimplemented the
parameter-property removal — but PR #134 (from sibling branch
`feat/db-worker-and-snapshot-perf`, an earlier session) had already
merged that exact change. I discovered the overlap only when
`treadmill ship-feature` hit a rebase conflict. The work wasn't fully
wasted (my PR #135 added a WAL guard + smoke test #134 lacked), but I
paid a rebase + conflict-resolution tax that a 30-second check would
have avoided, and I'd have branched from #134's state to add only the
delta.

**How to apply — run before branching for any fix:**
```bash
git fetch origin main
git log --oneline origin/main -5          # did it already land?
gh pr list --repo <owner>/<repo> --state all --limit 10 --search "<keyword>"
git worktree list                          # sibling worktree already on it?
git branch -a | grep -i "<topic>"
```
- If the fix already merged: branch from the new `main` and add only
  the missing delta (tests, edge cases), or close your effort.
- If a sibling branch/PR is open: coordinate — rebase onto it or
  contribute to that PR instead of opening a duplicate.

**Never:**
- Assume the daemon's build SHA reflects your last-known state — the
  self-updater may have advanced `main` several commits since.
- Start coding a fix from stale local `main` without a fresh
  `git fetch origin main` first.

**Confirmed approach:** Aligns with the operator's standing preference —
"multi-project context, always clarify which worktree/branch/PR".

name: Claude Code Plugin & Marketplace Schema (CLI-validated)
description: Current .claude-plugin manifest + marketplace schema per `claude plugin validate` v2.1.197 — corrects earlier root-level guidance
type: feedback
---

# Claude Code Plugin & Marketplace Schema

Verified end-to-end against `claude plugin validate` (CLI **v2.1.197**,
2026-07-01). The authoritative check is the CLI, not memory or spec-reading:
`claude plugin validate <dir>` and `--strict` (warnings→errors).

## Manifest location — `.claude-plugin/` (NOT plugin root)

Claude Code reads **only** `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and
`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`. A `plugin.json`/`marketplace.json` at the
plugin/repo **root is ignored** (no error — silently not read). Validator error
when missing: `No manifest found in directory. Expected
.claude-plugin/marketplace.json or .claude-plugin/plugin.json`.

```
repo/
├── .claude-plugin/marketplace.json     ← marketplace here
└── plugins/<name>/
    ├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json      ← plugin manifest here
    ├── skills/    ← auto-discovered
    ├── commands/  ← auto-discovered
    ├── agents/    ← auto-discovered
    ├── hooks/hooks.json  ← auto-discovered (or inline `hooks` in plugin.json)
    └── .mcp.json  ← auto-discovered (LEADING DOT; `mcp.json` is NOT found)
```

> ⚠️ Correction of prior memory: an earlier version of this file claimed
> manifests live at the root and `skills` is a `[{id,path}]` array. That is the
> **Cursor** convention and/or an obsolete Claude layout. Current Claude Code
> rejects it. See the dual-manifest memory for why a repo may still keep a root
> `plugin.json` around.

## `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` — envelope + auto-discovery

Manifest is **optional**; if present, `name` is the only required field.
Component dirs auto-discover — you usually only need the metadata envelope.

```json
{
  "name": "plugin-name",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "...",
  "author": { "name": "Full Name", "url": "https://github.com/user" },
  "repository": "https://github.com/user/repo",
  "keywords": ["a", "b"],
  "license": "MIT"
}
```

Field-level rejections confirmed by the validator (Cursor-format fails Claude):

| Field | Claude wants | Cursor style that FAILS |
|---|---|---|
| `author` | **object** `{name,url,email?}` | string `"Name"` → `expected object, received string` |
| `repository` | **string** URL | object `{type,url}` → `expected string, received object` |
| `skills` | string or array of **path strings**, else omit (auto-discover) | `[{id,path}]` → `skills: Invalid input` |
| `commands` | array of path strings, else omit | `[{id,path}]` → invalid |

Inline `hooks` **object** IS valid in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (same shape
as `hooks/hooks.json`: `{ "EventName": [ { "matcher"?, "hooks": [ {type,...} ] } ] }`).
`agents` as `"./agents/"` string is valid, but auto-discovery of `agents/` also works.

## `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`

```json
{
  "name": "kebab-case", "owner": { "name": "..." },
  "metadata": { "description": "...", "version": "1.0.0" },
  "plugins": [
    { "name": "local-plugin", "source": "./plugins/local-plugin", ... },
    { "name": "external", "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "owner/repo" } }
  ]
}
```

- Local plugin: `"source": "./plugins/<dir>"` (string, `./`-prefixed).
- **External repo: `"source": { "source": "github", "repo": "owner/repo" }`.**
  A bare URL string (`"https://github.com/owner/repo"`) → `plugins.N.source:
  Invalid input`. `{ "source": "git", "url": "...git" }` **also fails**. Only the
  `github`+`repo` object form validated.

## Confirmed approach

- `claude plugin validate` (plain + `--strict`) is the source of truth.
- `claude plugin details <name>` after install shows what actually LOADED
  (`Hooks (7)` vs `Hooks (0)`) — a plugin with inline hooks in an unread root
  `plugin.json` reports `Hooks (0)` and is silently inert.
- Live smoke test without polluting env: `claude plugin marketplace add ./`
  (needs `./` — bare `.` is rejected) → `claude plugin install <name>@<mkt>` →
  `claude plugin details` → `uninstall -y` + `marketplace remove`.

# Cloud PR-deploy: host-enrollment + credential gotchas

Standing up a real Elastic Defend host on a `ci:cloud-deploy` Kibana PR
deployment (e.g. to demo `endpoint-response-actions`, PR #272111) hit three
concrete breakages. All are reusable for any PR-cloud demo.

## 1. Vault cloud-deploy secret shape (creds only, JSON-quoted)

Path: `secret/kibana-issues/dev/cloud-deploy/kibana-pr-<PR>` — **no `-security`
suffix** (an earlier version of the runner used `-security` and always failed
the read).

- The secret contains **only** `username` + `password`. It does **NOT** carry
  `kibana_url` / `elasticsearch_url`. The URLs live in the PR's Buildkite
  **`cloud` annotation** / the `[Cloud Deployment]` PR comment
  (`https://kibana-pr-<PR>-<alias>.{kb,es}.<region>.gcp.elastic-cloud.com`).
  The `<alias>` (e.g. `774f55`) is stable per deployment but not derivable —
  read it from the annotation.
- The `password` value is **JSON-quoted**: `build_and_deploy.sh` stores it via
  `jq` WITHOUT `-r`, so the vault value is literally `"…"` (with surrounding
  double-quotes). Sending it verbatim to ES/Kibana gives
  `401 unable to authenticate user [elastic]`. **Strip the leading/trailing
  `"`** before use. Symptom that misled me: `/api/status` returns 200 even
  with a bad password (it's anonymous), so auth looks fine until you hit an
  authenticated route.

## 2. Elastic Agent download 404s on unreleased SNAPSHOT stacks

A PR deploy runs an unreleased version (e.g. `9.5.0-SNAPSHOT`). The naive
startup script did `V=${KBN_VER%-SNAPSHOT}` then downloaded from the **release**
artifacts URL:

    https://artifacts.elastic.co/downloads/beats/elastic-agent/elastic-agent-9.5.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz  → HTTP 404

Neither the release URL nor `artifacts.elastic.co/...-SNAPSHOT-...` exists for
unreleased builds. The agent binary is never downloaded, the `install`/enroll
step runs `./elastic-agent: No such file or directory` (exit 127), and the host
never checks in — you only see it after the 5-min check-in wait times out at
`online agents on policy: 0`.

**Fix:** for a `*-SNAPSHOT` version, resolve the snapshot build URL:

    BID=$(curl -sS https://snapshots.elastic.co/latest/9.5.0-SNAPSHOT.json | jq -r .build_id)   # e.g. 9.5.0-b041f099
    URL="https://snapshots.elastic.co/${BID}/downloads/beats/elastic-agent/elastic-agent-9.5.0-SNAPSHOT-linux-x86_64.tar.gz"   # HTTP 200

Keep the full `-SNAPSHOT` suffix (the tarball dir is
`elastic-agent-9.5.0-SNAPSHOT-linux-x86_64`). Preflight the URL with
`curl -sI` on the control host so a 404 fails fast instead of surfacing only in
the VM serial/startup log after the wait loop. Recovery without a new VM: SSH
in, download the correct tarball, `sudo ./elastic-agent install -n --url=<fleet>
--enrollment-token=<token> --insecure` (reuse the existing policy + enroll
token from the failed run).

## 3. Enable the experimental flag via the CI deploy config (NOT Console, NOT the product default)

`xpack.securitySolution.enableExperimental: ['<flag>']` is a kibana.yml **boot**
setting: as `elastic` superuser you cannot change it via any ES/Kibana API
(`/api/security/api_key` 404s and `/internal/security/me` says "not available
with the current configuration" on these ESS PR deploys — auth still works, the
route surface is just limited). Two paths people reach for are both wrong:

- **Flipping the default in `common/experimental_features.ts` (`false → true`)**
  — violates the "new skills ship dark" security-review requirement and would
  ship the skill enabled to everyone if it merges. Don't.
- **Manual Cloud Console "Edit user settings"** — works, but requires the
  operator to have Console access; not headless, not reproducible, and the PR
  author here explicitly had no PR-flag access.

**The working path: inject the flag into the deploy script's `user_settings_yaml`
on the branch, deploy via CI.** `build_and_deploy.sh` is the *only* place Kibana
user settings are set, and it does so in two spots you must both patch:

- **Create path** (new deployment): after `ecctl deployment create`, the script
  *overwrites* user settings with just `user_settings_yaml = "logging.root.level: all"`.
  Editing the `deploy.json` template's user settings is therefore **useless** —
  this line clobbers it.
- **Update path** (existing/persisted deployment — the common case for a
  `ci:cloud-persist-deployment` PR): `ecctl deployment show
  --generate-update-payload | jq '…'` only touches image/version/topology and
  **preserves** the live user settings, so a new flag never appears unless you
  add it here too.

Patch both to include the flag (use `jq --arg us "$YAML"` with an ANSI-C
`$'logging.root.level: all\nxpack.securitySolution.enableExperimental:
["<flag>"]'` string — avoids the single-quote/`\"` escaping trap of inlining
multi-line YAML into a `jq '…'` program):

    DEMO_USER_SETTINGS_YAML=$'logging.root.level: all\nxpack.securitySolution.enableExperimental: ["endpointResponseActionsSkill"]'
    # create path:  … | jq --arg us "$DEMO_USER_SETTINGS_YAML" '.resources.kibana[0].plan.kibana.user_settings_yaml = $us'
    # update path:  add  |  .resources.kibana[0].plan.kibana.user_settings_yaml = $us  to the existing jq

Mark it `DEMO ONLY — revert before merge` in the commit + an inline comment so
it can't silently land on `main` (it's branch-local: each PR runs its own
branch copy of `.buildkite/scripts/steps/cloud/build_and_deploy.sh`).

**Preserve the enrolled host:** take the **update path**, never
`ci:cloud-redeploy` — that label does a `deployment shutdown` + recreate, which
orphans any Defend agent enrolled to the deployment's Fleet. The update path
only restarts Kibana (~2 min); ES + Fleet stay up and the agent stays enrolled.
So: enroll the host first (Fleet/Defend ≠ Agent Builder, independent of the
flag), then land the deploy-config commit and `/ci`.

**Verify after `deploy_cloud` passes** (~40–60 min into the build; watch the
`deploy_cloud` step via `bk build view <n> --pipeline kibana-pull-request | jq
'.jobs[]|select(.step_key=="deploy_cloud").state'`): wait ~90 s for the Kibana
restart, then hit
`GET /api/agent_builder/skills?include_plugins=true` (basic auth `elastic:<pass>`
works even though the api_key route 404s) and assert the skill id is present.
End-to-end gate: `converse-smoke.sh` should show `load_skill` + a real tool call
(`endpoint-response-actions.list_endpoints`) with live data, and stay dark on a
distractor. Mint the smoke's `KIBANA_API_KEY` via **ES** `POST /_security/api_key`
(`.encoded` field) since the Kibana api_key route 404s on these deploys.

## 4. Force internal login page with `/login`

Hitting a Cloud QA PR-deployment Kibana base URL directly can land on
whatever default auth the deployment negotiates (not always the login
form). Append **`/login`** to the URL to force the internal login page so
you can authenticate with the Vault SSO/deploy creds (see section 1)
instead of hitting an ambiguous auth state.

Debugging note: macOS has no `setsid`/`timeout`/GNU coreutils by default — 
`nohup … &` background jobs launched from a tool-call shell can be killed when
the call returns; run long provisioning in the foreground with a large block
window instead.

name: feedback_concurrent_weekly_builds_ci_contention
description: Two weekly kbn-evals builds on same branch steal CI slots — agent-builder fanout stuck in limited for 90+ min; trigger sequentially or wait for first to finish
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-30
source: skill-dev 3686518a — builds #40 + #41 concurrent; #41 agent-builder 5/6 stuck in limited/running for >90 min
---

# Concurrent Weekly Builds — CI Slot Contention

Triggering two `kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals` builds on the **same branch** concurrently causes CI slot contention. The weekly pipeline fans out ~40+ jobs (7 suites × 6 models); two builds double that load, and Buildkite's agent pool cannot satisfy both.

## Failure mode

```
Build #40 (cb5ab937): agent-builder jobs grab CI slots first, run to completion (6/6 in ~60 min)
Build #41 (cddab5a7): agent-builder jobs sit in `limited` / `waiting` for 90+ min
                     → appears stalled; operator suspects wiring failure
```

The `limited` state means the job is queued waiting for an agent. With 40+ jobs from #40 still running, #41's agent-builder fanout cannot get slots.

## Why this is sneaky

- Build #41 is not **broken** — it's **starved**
- The matrix rollup shows `0/6 terminal` for agent-builder, which looks identical to the Playwright `describe is not defined` failure mode (#38–#39)
- The build state shows `failing` (because other suites failed), masking that agent-builder is just slow

## Correct pattern

### Option 1: Sequential (preferred)

Wait for build **N** to finish before triggering **N+1**:

```bash
# Poll until N is terminal
bk build view <N> -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals | python3 -c "..."
# Then trigger N+1
bk build create -y -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals -b <branch> -c <sha> -i ...
```

### Option 2: Accept the delay

If you trigger both (e.g. to compare pre-merge vs post-merge), expect the second build's agent-builder to take 2–3× longer than normal. Set the babysit poll interval to 5 min (not 2 min) to reduce API noise.

### Option 3: Cancel the first build once the second is healthy

If build **N+1** on the post-merge SHA starts passing suites that **N** hasn't reached yet, cancel **N** to free slots:

```bash
bk build cancel <N> -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals
```

## Never

- Trigger two weekly builds on the same branch and expect both to finish in normal time
- Interpret `limited` / `waiting` agent-builder jobs as a wiring failure — check CI slot availability first
- Trigger a third build to "get more signal" — it makes the contention worse
- Retry `limited` fanout jobs via API — they are not retriable; see `feedback_buildkite_limited_jobs_not_retriable.md`

## Confirmed approach

Jun 30 session: #40 (cb5ab937) + #41 (cddab5a7) triggered ~30 min apart. #40 agent-builder finished 6/6 in ~60 min; #41 agent-builder still 0/6 terminal after 90+ min (5 jobs in `limited`/`running`). #40 proved the Playwright fix; #41 is the authoritative post-merge gate but needed 2–3× longer to clear.

name: feedback_continual_learning_shared_state_race
description: continual-learning stop-hook state file is shared globally across all concurrent Cursor windows — unlocked read-modify-write silently loses turn-count increments as parallel-window count grows, causing declining follow-up fire rate
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-07
source: transcript 75027484 — continual-learning setup health audit and fix (Jul 7 2026)
---

# continual-learning stop-hook: global shared state races under concurrency

`~/.cursor/hooks/state/continual-learning.json` is **one file shared across every Cursor window/workspace** the operator has open (measured 8–14 distinct workspace IDs hitting the hook per session). The hook logic does an unguarded `readFileSync` → increment `turnsSinceLastRun` → `writeFileSync`.

## Symptom
Follow-up ("Briefly inform the user...") fire rate dropped steadily over time (4.2% → 0.7% of stop-hook invocations) even as raw activity stayed high or grew. This looked like "the setup is broken" but was actually a scaling ceiling.

## Root cause
Classic lost-update race: two+ concurrent windows read the same `turnsSinceLastRun` value, both increment locally, and whichever writes last wins — the other window's increment is silently discarded. More concurrent windows → more clobbered increments → the counter crawls toward the `minTurns=10` threshold far slower than real completed turns would suggest. The `minMinutes=120` global cooldown is also shared, capping total fires to ~1 per 2 hours system-wide regardless of window count.

## Fix
Wrap the read-modify-write critical section in `ao-workspace/cursor/hooks/continual-learning-stop.ts` with an **atomic `mkdir`-based file lock**, with stale-lock reclamation (~10s) in case a hook process crashes mid-write. Verified: 20 concurrent invocations all counted correctly (no lost updates, no lock-busy errors); a simulated stale lock (dated old) was correctly reclaimed.

## How to apply
- Any shared global counter/state file touched by concurrently-running Cursor windows/hooks needs this same lock-guard pattern — don't assume single-writer just because it's "one hook."
- When diagnosing "X feature fires less often than before" for a hook/automation shared across sessions, check concurrent-invocation count first — it's often a race, not breakage.

**Never:** trust `readFileSync`/`writeFileSync` without a lock for state shared across concurrent Cursor windows — this repo pattern (global hook state under `~/.cursor/hooks/state/`) is used by several hooks, all are candidates for the same class of bug.

name: feedback_convergence_driven_completion
description: After implementation, run audit→fix→improve loops until 2 consecutive clean passes with no MEDIUM+ findings
type: feedback
---

After implementation is complete, do NOT just validate and stop. Run a convergence-driven audit loop:

1. **Audit**: Code review for bugs, security, logic errors, API mismatches, missing error handling, type safety gaps, UX issues
2. **Fix**: Fix all CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM findings
3. **Improve**: Reason about what's missing, what could be better, what would make a user never need to look elsewhere. Add those improvements.
4. **Re-audit**: Run another full pass — new code from fixes/improvements may introduce new issues
5. **Repeat** until 2 consecutive audit passes find only LOW or no findings

**How to apply:**
- After each implementation batch validates (types+lint+tests), immediately dispatch a code review agent
- Fix everything MEDIUM+, then dispatch ANOTHER code review agent on the fixed code
- In parallel with fixes, reason about improvements: missing evaluators, better error messages, additional test coverage, UX polish, performance optimizations
- Add improvements, then re-audit
- Stop condition: 2 consecutive code review passes with 0 MEDIUM+ findings
- This applies to ALL "implement everything" / "do it e2e" / "keep running" requests
- Track convergence: "Pass 1: 23 findings → Pass 2: 6 findings → Pass 3: 1 → Pass 4: 0 → Pass 5: 0 → DONE"

name: feedback_cross_team_eval_failure_fix_ownership
description: On a shared weekly eval pipeline, fix cross-team failures by filing precise bugs plus optional scoped reversible on-branch exclusion — never unilaterally patch another team's suite/adapter on your feature branch
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-02
source: skill-dev 3686518a — weekly #51 triage of streams/gpt-oss + significant-events/sonnet on fix/weekly-evals-matrix
---

# Cross-Team Eval-Failure Fix Ownership

When a shared weekly eval pipeline (e.g. `kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals`) has red
jobs owned by **another team's code** and you are iterating on your own feature
branch (e.g. the security matrix), do NOT reach for the other team's suite,
adapter, or model config to green the build. Triage into two buckets first, then
route by ownership.

**Step 1 — classify the failure:**

- **Harness/schema-shape mismatch** — the model works in one harness but not
  another because of *how* the tool call is demanded, not raw capability. gpt-oss-120b
  is the worked example: it makes fine small native tool calls in the multi-turn
  agent-builder converse loop (security suites score non-zero), but the Obs streams
  suggestion path calls `inferenceClient.prompt()` **once** with a *forced*
  `toolChoice` and a large nested schema, and hard-throws `NoLLMSuggestionsError`
  the instant `toolCalls.length === 0` (`streams/.../common_processing_helpers.ts`).
  Same model, same EIS connector, both native FC (`isNativeFunctionCallingSupported`
  returns true for the Inference connector) — the weaker model just can't emit one
  giant structured tool call in a single shot with no retry. There is **no code bug
  to fix in the model path**; the owning-team fix is graceful degradation on the
  one-shot suggestion path (retry / relaxed schema / fallback), or *exclude/soft_fail*
  that model×suite combo — the owning team's decision. Do NOT mistake this for a raw
  capability gap ("can't produce structured tool calls") — it's harness-specific.
- **Genuine code bug** — real defect, but in the other team's code (e.g. the EIS
  anthropic adapter rejecting `nl_to_esql` assistant-prefill on claude-4.6-sonnet).
  Fixable, but by the owning team, because the fix changes behavior for all of
  that code's callers.

**Step 2 — route by ownership, not by "make my build green":**

1. **File a precise bug** to the owning team with the file:line root cause and a
   suggested fix. This IS the fix path for cross-team code — not a cop-out.
2. **Optionally** apply a *scoped, reversible* on-branch exclusion / soft_fail of
   the specific model×suite combo, documented and linked to the filed bug.
   Legitimate for capability gaps; for a real code bug only pair it with (1) so
   you don't silently mask the defect.
3. If the real fix is small and you want to push it, do it as a **separate PR to
   the owning team**, never folded into your feature branch.

**Why:** "intolerant of workarounds" does not mean "unilaterally patch every red
job on a shared pipeline." Editing another team's suite/adapter on your feature
branch (a) risks broad behavior changes you can't validate, (b) muddies your
branch's diff and review, and (c) steps on their ownership. The disciplined path
keeps your branch scoped while still driving the real fix upstream.

**Never:**
- Patch a platform inference adapter / another team's suite on your matrix/feature
  branch to green a cross-team failure.
- Treat a model-capability gap as a code bug — there's nothing to fix in code.
- Apply an on-branch exclusion for a genuine code bug WITHOUT also filing the bug.

**Confirmed approach:** Validated on weekly #51 — gpt-oss/streams (harness/schema
mismatch on the one-shot `prompt()` path → graceful-degrade or exclude/soft_fail,
Obs's call) and sonnet/significant-events (real adapter bug → file to AI-infra)
were both routed this way instead of editing Obs/inference code on the
security-matrix branch. The gpt-oss framing was corrected from "can't produce
structured tool calls" to "harness-specific single-shot forced-schema throw" after
tracing `common_processing_helpers.ts` + `function_calling_support.ts`.

**Quantitative evidence (weekly #51 job matrix):** gpt-oss-120b PASSED all 10
security-domain suites (security-ai-rules, security-alert-triage,
security-alerts-rag-regression, security-automatic-migrations,
security-esql-generation-regression, siem-readiness, pci-compliance, endpoint,
entity-analytics-v2, attack-discovery) + significant-events + 6 others (17 passed).
It FAILED exactly two: `agent-builder` (recommend-prebuilt-rules flag config gap —
separate root cause) and `streams`. On the streams column, all 5 other models
(opus, sonnet, gemini-3.0-flash, gemini-3.1-pro, gpt-5.4) PASSED — gpt-oss was the
ONLY streams failure, the definitive model-strength × harness-shape signature.
Note significant-events/gpt-oss PASSED despite also using single-shot `prompt()`,
so the streams *pipeline-suggestion* schema specifically is the hard one, not all
single-shot paths.

name: feedback_dark_skill_cloud_demo_prereqs
description: A feature-flagged ("dark") Kibana skill won't appear on a persisted cloud deploy until the flag is enabled; response-action skills also need a live host
type: feedback
---

# Dark-Shipped Skill — Cloud Demo Prerequisites

New Agent Builder skills ship behind a Security Solution experimental flag that
defaults to **false** (so serverless QA is unaffected until explicitly enabled).
A persisted `ci:cloud-deploy` deployment therefore has the skill **OFF** — a
reviewer/PM who just logs in sees an empty Agent Builder and (wrongly) concludes
the skill is broken. Two prerequisites must be in the handoff, not discovered
live.

**Why:** On elastic/kibana#272111 the response-actions skill was gated behind
`endpointResponseActionsSkill: false`. The demo README documented enrollment and
converse examples but omitted flag enablement — the single thing that makes the
skill visible. A handoff without it wastes the reviewer's first session.

## Prereq 1 — enable the experimental flag on the cloud deploy

Cloud Console → deployment → **Kibana → Edit user settings**:

```yaml
xpack.securitySolution.enableExperimental: ['<flagName>']
```

Save → Kibana redeploys (~2 min). Without it the skill never registers and
Agent Builder won't route to it. (Local dev uses `config/kibana.dev.yml`
`xpack.serverless.experimental_features: [...]` instead — different key, same
effect.)

## Prereq 2 — write-action skills need a LIVE enrolled host

Read/RAG/forensics skills can be demoed on **synthetic** `logs-endpoint.events.*`
telemetry (seed and go). **Response-action skills cannot** — `isolate` /
`release` / `scan` / `running_processes` dispatch to a real Elastic Defend agent
via the Response Actions service. So the demo must provision + enroll a real host
(GCP VM via the `recreate-*-env.sh --with-host` runner) before any write action
is meaningful. Read-only actions (list endpoints, status) work without a host but
won't show the interesting part.

**How to apply:** For ANY dark-shipped skill demo handoff, state up front: (1)
the exact flag + where to set it, (2) whether synthetic data suffices or a live
host is required. Verify the flag is actually on (authenticated capabilities
probe) before telling a reviewer to log in.

**Never:**
- Assume a persisted cloud deploy has experimental flags enabled — it doesn't.
- Offer a synthetic-seed path for a skill whose actions dispatch to a live agent.

**Confirmed approach:** Captured while assembling the #272111 Raquel handoff;
flag default-off confirmed in `common/experimental_features.ts`
(`endpointResponseActionsSkill: false`).

# Defend E2E — Local vs Lab Split

Do not boot Fleet + Multipass for every PR. Split Defend validation into two modes:

| Mode | Where | What to validate |
|------|-------|------------------|
| **Local (code profile)** | Worktree + Jest/agents | Rule logic, log-injection emulation, Agent Builder skill wiring, API contracts |
| **Heavy (Defend profile / CI)** | `endpoint-lab up` or Buildkite | Real Elastic Agent enrollment, response actions execution, defend_workflows Cypress |

**Why:** Full local E2E (ES 9220 + Kibana 5620 + Fleet 8220 + Multipass) is expensive and fragile. Commercial autonomous agents (Devin, Jules, etc.) also cannot reliably run full Kibana+Defend locally — pattern is orchestrator + remote VM/CI + dedicated Defend lab.

**How to apply:**
- Default daily work: cheap tier (Jest, skill evals on discover stack :5630/:9230)
- Schedule Defend lab blocks: `profile defend && endpoint-lab up`
- CI (Buildkite) for heavy validation on merge/label — treadmill orchestrates, lab/CI executes

**Never:**
- Block every feature on local Multipass enrollment
- Expect inline copilots or cloud coding agents to replace a Defend lab for endpoint execution tests

**Confirmed approach:** `RESOURCE_PROFILES.md` Defend profile; endpoint-lab as canonical lab wrapper (Jun 25, 2026).

description: Detection emulation HITL stays skill-scoped; avoid Agent Builder platform PRs unless user explicitly wants cross-team dependency
type: feedback
---

# Detection Emulation HITL — Skill-Scoped, No Platform PR

Real-execution HITL for detection emulation must ship **inside `security_solution`**, not via Agent Builder platform changes.

**Why:** A platform `getConfirmation → null` skip for `log_injection` was implemented then **reverted** after the operator said to avoid dependency on other teams. Cross-team platform PRs add review latency and coupling for a spike that can use existing on-demand primitives.

**How to apply:**
- **`validate-rule` + `real_execution`:** on-demand `prompts.askForConfirmation` **after** log-injection preflight passes the confidence floor — `log_injection` never prompts.
- **Run-family + endpoint write tools:** declarative `confirmation: { askUser: 'always' }` on the tool definition.
- **Shared prompt body:** `build_validate_rule_confirmation.ts` (optional preflight line in body).
- **Do not** re-introduce platform `run_tool.ts` null-skip unless the user **explicitly** requests a cross-team Agent Builder PR.

name: feedback_docker_digest_check_robustness
description: Docker digest comparison must use length guards, not string equality against sentinels
type: feedback
---

# Docker Digest Check Robustness

When comparing local vs remote Docker image digests via SSH commands on remote VMs, never trust sentinel-string comparisons (`!== 'NOT_FOUND'`). Use length-based guards instead.

**Why:** SSH commands (`docker inspect`, `docker manifest inspect`) can return empty strings, short error messages like `'true'`, or truncated output when piped through grep/cut on different shell environments. A real sha256 digest is always 64+ characters (`sha256:abc123...`). Testing against sentinels like `'NOT_FOUND'` or `'UNKNOWN'` misses edge cases where the command succeeds but returns unexpected short output.

**How to apply:**
- Guard with `localDigest.length > 10 && remoteDigest.length > 10` before comparing
- Wrap the entire digest check in try/catch — it's best-effort optimization, not a required step
- If either check fails or returns short output, fall through to the full `docker pull`
- In test mocks: `command.includes('docker inspect')` matches BOTH the digest check's `docker inspect --format=...` AND the container health inspection's `docker inspect`. Be aware of ordering.

**Never:**
- Use string equality against sentinel values for SSH command output validation
- Let a digest check failure block the deploy pipeline (it's an optimization, not a gate)
- Assume `docker manifest inspect` is universally available (older Docker versions may not support it)

**Confirmed approach:** Validated with 37/37 vllm-deployment tests passing. The `length > 10` guard correctly handles empty strings, 'true', and other short mock responses.

name: Dual-manifest plugin repos — check consumers before deleting a manifest
description: patryks-treadmill-claude-plugins keeps BOTH root plugin.json (its own validator) and .claude-plugin/plugin.json (Claude); never delete the root one
type: feedback
---

# Dual-Manifest Coexistence & "Check Consumers Before Deleting"

`patryks-treadmill-claude-plugins` intentionally maintains **two manifests per
plugin**, and they serve different consumers:

| Manifest | Consumer | Format |
|---|---|---|
| `plugins/<n>/plugin.json` (root) | the repo's own `scripts/validate-plugins.sh --strict` (run by `.githooks/pre-commit`) — iterates `plugins/*/plugin.json` and checks `skills:[{path}]` refs + SKILL.md frontmatter | Cursor-style: `author` string, `repository` object, `skills:[{id,path}]` |
| `plugins/<n>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` | Claude Code (`claude plugin install`) | Claude-style: envelope + auto-discovery (see `feedback_claude_marketplace_schema.md`) |

Claude ignores the root `plugin.json`; the repo's validator ignores
`.claude-plugin/`. Both must exist and both validators must pass.

## The mistake this prevents

While fixing 6 plugins that had ONLY the root `plugin.json` (so they failed
`claude plugin validate`), I first **deleted** the root files as "redundant."
That would have broken the repo's own pre-commit, which requires
`plugins/*/plugin.json` for every plugin. Caught it by reading
`scripts/validate-plugins.sh` + `.githooks/pre-commit`, then restored all root
manifests. The correct fix was **add** `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, **keep**
the root one.

**Why:** the root files look like leftover duplicates of the Claude envelope,
but they are load-bearing for a different tool in the same repo.

**How to apply:** before deleting any file that "looks redundant," grep for
what reads it (`rg -l "plugin\.json" scripts/ .githooks/`, check install
scripts, CI, sibling tools). A file with no producer you can see may still have
a consumer. Blast-radius check beats intuition.

**Never:**
- Delete `plugins/*/plugin.json` (root) in this repo — breaks pre-commit.
- Assume "one plugin = one manifest" in a dual-platform (Cursor+Claude) repo.

**Confirmed approach:** After the fix, `claude plugin validate` (all 14 + marketplace,
plain and `--strict`) AND `scripts/validate-plugins.sh --strict` (14 plugins /
80 skills / 0 issues) both pass; a live install of the previously-inert
`session-safety-hooks` reported `Hooks (7)`.

**How to apply:**
1. After each implementation + validation cycle, compare delivered features against the FULL task list from the OpenSpec `tasks.md` — not just what the current batch of agents built
2. If there are uncompleted tasks, immediately dispatch the next batch of agents — do NOT summarize and wait
3. The "done" signal is: every task in tasks.md is checked off, OR a task is explicitly blocked by external dependencies — document the blocker and do everything else
4. When dispatching team agents, give them the FULL remaining task list, not just one phase — let them self-organize
5. After code review fixes, don't re-summarize — immediately start the next phase
6. The pattern should be: implement → validate → fix → check remaining gaps → implement next batch → validate → fix → repeat until truly zero gaps

# EDD capsule: EDOT silently drops ALL traces on TLS cert mismatch

## Symptom
Trace-based eval evaluators (Input/Output Tokens, latency, tool-calls, skill-invocation)
score `0`/`null` even though inference works and Kibana is healthy. `traces-*` in the
cell ES is **empty** (`_cat/indices/traces-*` returns nothing).

## Root cause
The EDD capsule runs the EDOT collector as a **Docker container**
(`kibana-edot-collector`, image `elastic-otel-collector`). To reach the host-mapped cell
ES port it rewrites `localhost` → `host.docker.internal` (see
`normalizeElasticsearchHost` in `kbn-edot-collector/src/ensure_edot_collector.ts`).
But the cell ES self-signed cert is only valid for `localhost` and the container id,
**not** `host.docker.internal`. The generated collector config
(`data/edot_collector/otel-collector-config.yml`) has **no `tls` block**, so the
elasticsearch exporter verifies the cert, fails, and drops every batch:

```
error: "failed to execute the request: tls: failed to verify certificate:
 x509: certificate is valid for localhost, <cid>, not host.docker.internal", dropped_items: N
```

## Fix (durable): patch the config generator source
`src/platform/packages/shared/kbn-edot-collector/src/get_edot_collector_configuration.ts`
— add to the `exporters.elasticsearch` object (right after `password,`):

```ts
tls: {
  insecure_skip_verify: true,
},
```

`ensureEdotCollector` regenerates `otel-collector-config.yml` from this on every fresh
`node scripts/edot_collector.js`, so patching the source survives new capsule boots.
(`ELASTICSEARCH_SSL_VERIFY=false` that boot-edd-capsule.sh passes does NOT reach the
collector's ES exporter — it does not translate into the OTel config.)

## Fix (immediate, no re-boot): patch live yml + restart container
The collector container is `restart: unless-stopped` and mounts the yml read-only, so a
live patch + restart survives reboots (only a fresh generator run reverts it):

```bash
# node (worktree has js-yaml); python system interpreter usually lacks pyyaml
node -e 'const fs=require("fs"),y=require("js-yaml");const p=process.argv[1];const d=y.load(fs.readFileSync(p,"utf8"));d.exporters.elasticsearch.tls={insecure_skip_verify:true};fs.writeFileSync(p,y.dump(d,{sortKeys:false}))' \
  data/edot_collector/otel-collector-config.yml
docker --context colima restart kibana-edot-collector
```

## Verify
```bash
curl -sk -u elastic:changeme "https://localhost:<esPort>/_cat/indices/traces-*?h=index,docs.count"
# spans carry attributes.gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / output_tokens; both trace.id and trace_id resolve in ES|QL
```

## Note
This latent bug affects EVERY machine that boots an EDD capsule (M4 too), not just the
i9 — traces are dropped wherever the collector runs in Docker against a self-signed cell ES.

## The TLS fix is necessary but NOT sufficient for trace-based evaluators
Getting trace-retrieval / token / latency evaluators to score requires THREE things
together (see feedback_kbn_evals_run_against_capsule.md for the full recipe):
1. This EDOT TLS fix (so traces actually land in ES).
2. `trace.id` → `trace_id` in the ES|QL evaluator queries (ES|QL can't resolve the
   `trace.id` alias in WHERE on OTel-mapped indices). Fixed upstream in branch
   `ao/kbn-evals-trace-id-esql-fix` (commit fcaa77216514).
3. `TRACING_EXPORTERS` set on the eval `run` (otherwise the worker has no tracer,
   `getCurrentTraceId()` returns all-zeros `000…0`, evaluator logs "Invalid traceId").
With all three, smoke-tests `trace-retrieval` scores 1 (verified on i9, trace id
`2db38ea6…`, Input/Output Tokens mean 1).

name: feedback_endpoint_lab_es_bind_loopback
description: "endpoint-lab start_es() binds ES only to loopback — Fleet output config points at host_ip so Fleet container can't reach ES"
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-30
source: "endpoint-lab Phase 2 demo boot — Fleet Server failed ES version check (dial tcp 192.168.252.1:9180: connection refused)"
---

# Endpoint Lab — ES Bind Mismatch (loopback vs host_ip)

`endpoint-lab`'s `start_es()` runs `yarn es snapshot` without `-E network.host`, so ES binds only to `127.0.0.1`/`[::1]:${ES_PORT}`. But `config/kibana.dev.yml.tmpl` sets the Fleet ES output to `http://__HOST_IP__:__ES_PORT__` (e.g. `http://192.168.252.1:9180`). The Fleet Server container (on Docker's `elastic` network) and the Multipass VM can never reach ES at the host IP — nothing listens there.

**Why:** `network.host` defaults to loopback in ES when unset. The `kibana.dev.yml.tmpl` correctly uses `__HOST_IP__` so VMs can reach ES, but `start_es()` was never updated to bind ES to that interface. Symptom: Fleet Server logs `failed version compatibility check with elasticsearch: dial tcp 192.168.252.1:9180: connect: connection refused`, then enroll times out after 240s × 3 retries.

**How to apply:**
- Patched `start_es()` in `~/.local/bin/endpoint-lab` to accept `host_ip` and add `-E network.host=127.0.0.1,::1,${host_ip} -E discovery.type=single-node`
- Verify before declaring boot success: `lsof -iTCP:${ES_PORT} -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n` should show the host_ip binding, not just loopback
- Reachability check from Docker: `docker run --rm --network elastic curlimages/curl:latest -sk -u elastic:changeme http://<host_ip>:${ES_PORT}/_cluster/health`

**Never:**
- Declare "ES ready" based only on `curl 127.0.0.1:${ES_PORT}` — that passes even when host_ip binding is missing
- Assume `network.host` is inherited from kibana.dev.yml — ES reads its own `elasticsearch.yml`, not Kibana's config

**Confirmed approach:** Patched locally Jun 30, 2026. Boot reached "Lab is up" with ES correctly bound to `127.0.0.1, ::1, 192.168.3.38` and Fleet Server reaching ES successfully. Patch not yet committed to `~/Projects/endpoint-lab`.

name: feedback_endpoint_lab_lab_is_up_not_liveness
description: endpoint-lab "Lab is up" message fires when the script returns, not when services are stable — backgrounded ES/Kibana die with the parent shell via process-group cleanup
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-30
source: endpoint-lab Phase 2 demo — "Lab is up" printed, then ES+Kibana found dead 60s later when parent shell exited
---

# Endpoint Lab — "Lab is up" Is Not a Liveness Signal

`endpoint-lab up` prints "Lab is up" when the script reaches its final `log` statement and returns. ES and Kibana are launched as backgrounded children of the script's shell (`node scripts/kibana ... &`). When the parent shell exits — which happens immediately after "Lab is up" — the process group is cleaned up and ES/Kibana receive SIGTERM and die.

**Why:** macOS process groups: when the session leader exits, children in the group get SIGHUP/SIGTERM. `nohup` and `disown` do not survive Cursor's shell-tool session teardown (separate but compounding issue). Docker containers (Fleet) and Multipass VMs survive because they're managed by their own daemons, not as child processes of the shell.

**How to apply:**
- Treat "Lab is up" as "script thinks it finished" — verify each service independently before relying on it
- For interactive use: run `endpoint-lab up` in a terminal you keep open; do not background it
- For agent/CI use: the lab needs a supervisor (launchd plist, or move ES/Kibana into Docker containers like Fleet already is)
- Suggested `endpoint-lab verify` subcommand: probe ES (`/_cluster/health`), Kibana (`/api/status`), Fleet (`/api/fleet/agents`), and enrolled endpoint count — collapses the liveness question to one command

**Never:**
- Treat "Lab is up" as proof services are running
- Background `endpoint-lab up` from an agent shell and expect ES/Kibana to persist
- Re-run `endpoint-lab up` to "restart Kibana only" — `check_ports_for_up` rejects because Fleet port 8180 is held but only ES/Kibana ports have pid-continue logic

**Confirmed approach:** Observed Jun 30, 2026 — three boots reached "Lab is up", all had ES+Kibana dead within 60s of the parent shell exiting. Fleet container + Multipass VM persisted correctly.

# Eval Cockpit View — CI Typecheck Gotchas

`packages/mcp-server` CI runs **`npm run typecheck`** (`tsc --noEmit`) over the whole package, including `src/views/eval-cockpit/`. Vitest can pass while typecheck fails on the React/MCP App view layer.

**Why:** PR #70 first push failed Test (Node 20/22) at typecheck with four errors in `grepReplay.ts` and `useEvalCockpitPoll.ts` — not caught locally if you only ran `npm test` without `npm run typecheck`.

**How to apply:**

| Error shape | Fix |
|-------------|-----|
| `'McpApp' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'` | Use `import { App as McpApp } from '@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps'` (value import) |
| Unsafe cast to `{ text: string }` on tool result | Use shared `extractToolText()` from `parseToolJson.ts` — MCP results are `content[]`, not top-level `text` |
| `Property 'clipboard' does not exist on type 'Navigator'` | Node tsconfig has no full DOM `Clipboard` type — cast navigator inline: `{ clipboard?: { writeText: (t: string) => Promise<void> } }` |

# `node scripts/evals start` needs `eis-` prefixed model/judge ids

Running `node scripts/evals start --suite <suite> --model <id> --judge <id> --profile dev-vault ...`
with a bare model/connector name (e.g. `--model anthropic-claude-4.6-opus`,
`--judge gemini-2-5-pro`) fails with:

```
Project(s) "anthropic-claude-4.6-opus" not found. Available projects: "litellm-qwen-coding", "gemini-2-5-pro"
```

This looks like a config/connector problem but is just an id-format mismatch:
**both `--model` and `--judge` must use the `eis-` prefixed connector id**
(`eis-anthropic-claude-4-6-opus`, `eis-google-gemini-2-5-pro`), matching the
EIS connector naming convention, not the bare model name. The "Project"
names Playwright reports come from the suite's `playwright.config.ts`
project list, which is keyed off these `eis-*` ids.

**Cost trap:** the error only surfaces after Scout/Kibana have already
booted (which can take minutes, including a first-time bootstrap if
`node_modules` is stale) — so a wrong bare model id burns a full boot
cycle before failing. Get the id right before starting the run:
grep the suite's `playwright.config.ts` for the actual project list, or
check `node scripts/evals env` model output, rather than assuming the
bare model/connector name works.

## Never

- Pass a bare model name (`anthropic-claude-4.6-opus`) to `evals start --model`/`--judge` — always the `eis-` prefixed id.
- Assume a "Project(s) not found" error means the connector isn't configured — it usually means the id format is wrong.
