  - **Isolation is decisive:** direct `curl POST /api/agent_builder/converse` (no @kbn/evals+undici client
    span) returns a response `trace_id` that == the inference self-trace WITH tokens — in ALL 3 variants:
    plain (745ad251, out=153), +`traceparent` (da2b02e3, out=150; note NOT the incoming id), and
    +`traceparent`+`baggage:kibana.inference.tracing=1` (c57c59f1, out=132). So neither traceparent NOR the
    beacon baggage causes the split — it is induced only under the eval runtime, where at round-assembly
    `getCurrentTraceId()` returns the active ROUTE span (joined to the eval client trace) while inference
    forked to its own root. **A `with_converse_span` tap rewriting `round.trace_id` to the Converse span id
    is a NO-OP (roundTraceIdBefore already == Converse span id in isolation) and is OVERRIDDEN downstream in
    the converse/persistence assembly under the eval — so the earlier "quickest fix" is wrong.**
  - **Corrected fixes:** (1) SERVER: make the converse response `trace_id` point at the trace that contains
    the inference/ChatComplete spans regardless of an incoming external distributed trace; (2) EVAL (robust,
    no server change): correlate stats evaluators by a shared attr (`conversation_id`, returned + on inference
    spans) instead of a single `trace_id`, OR issue the converse call under a suppressed/ROOT context so no
    client span is propagated (matches the isolated curl that already returns the right id). Note the SECURITY
    suite already uses `raw.trace_id` and the SIGNIFICANT-EVENTS suite uses client-side `getCurrentTraceId()`
    (`kbn-evals/src/utils/tracing.ts`) — so pattern discipline matters. Posted corrected analysis to #276308.
- **✅ SOLVED (Jul 4 2026) — one-line eval-framework fix, VERIFIED GREEN on the live cell.** The real bug
  is NOT server-side and NOT lag. Chain of custody: server converse RESPONSE body `trace_id` IS correct
  (e.g. `cfc4051d…` → 218 docs, out_tokens=2157, ChatComplete=9, scope=`inference`); `chat_client.ts`
  returns it; `evaluate_dataset.ts` task returns `traceId: response.traceId`. BUT the generic executor
  `x-pack/platform/packages/shared/kbn-evals/src/kibana_evals_executor/client.ts` (~line 236) did
  `output: { ...taskOutput, traceId }` where `traceId = getCurrentTraceId()` is the eval's CLIENT
  task-span trace (scope `@kbn/evals`+undici, 0 tokens, 0 ChatComplete). Spread last, it always
  overrode the task's own correct id → trace-based Token/Latency/ToolCalls evaluators queried the client
  trace → null / "No data found". **Fix:** `traceId: (taskOutput as {traceId?:string})?.traceId ?? traceId`
  — prefer the task's own id, fall back to client id. Backward-compatible: significant-events sets
  `traceId: getCurrentTraceId()` in its own task output (identical value) so it's unchanged; agent-builder
  now uses the inference trace. **Verified:** product-documentation slice went fully green — Latency
  mean 12.56s, Input/Output/Cached Tokens populated, Tool Calls mean 12, ZERO "No data found"/null.
  Latency needed NO lag gate (the "No data found" was the WRONG id, not ingest lag). kbn-evals edits need
  NO Kibana restart. Diagnostic trick that cracked it: Playwright scout-worker SWALLOWS `console.error`
  from the task — write to a file via `fs.appendFileSync('/tmp/…')` instead.
- **Do NOT "just raise the retry budget"** to fix Latency lag: token evaluators fail PERMANENTLY
  (correlation split), so a larger budget makes each one burn the full extended time before failing
  (worse wall-time). Latency lag needs a TARGETED fix — lower EDOT/ES ingest lag, or a pre-eval
  "wait until the converse trace is queryable" gate — not more `pRetry` retries in `factory.ts`.

### Broader suite (streams) via runner + synthtrace self-signed-cert fix (m1max, Jul 3 2026)
Queued the `streams` suite through the runner (there is NO `agent-builder` suite in this worktree;
only smoke-tests, significant-events, streams). Runner recipe worked (node v24, connectors env),
but `global.setup` synthtrace seeding failed with `ConnectionError: self-signed certificate in
certificate chain`. Root cause: `kbn-synthtrace/src/cli/utils/ssl.ts` `getEsClientTlsSettings`
loads Kibana's dev `CA_CERT_PATH` and passes an explicit `ca` + `rejectUnauthorized:true`, so it
validates against the WRONG CA (the cell's ES has its own self-signed CA) and IGNORES both
`NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` and `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` (explicit client `ca` wins). The only
knob is the `--insecure` run flag (→ `rejectUnauthorized:false`). The streams suite's
`evals/synthtrace_helpers.ts` `getSynthtraceArgs` doesn't pass it, so patch that array to add
`'--insecure'` (keep a `.bak-edd`). After the patch, synthtrace seeds data and the suite runs its
50 partitioning + pattern-extraction evals (inference + judge) normally.

description: traces-* indexes the trace id as `trace.id` on some cells but `trace_id` on others; kbn-evals trace_based evaluators hardcode `trace.id` and silently return null on `trace_id` cells
type: feedback
---

# `trace.id` vs `trace_id` ES|QL field drift breaks trace-based evaluators per-cell

The `kbn-evals` trace-based evaluators (`kbn-evals/src/evaluators/trace_based/{tokens,latency,
tool_calls,skill_invocation}.ts`) build ES|QL like `FROM traces-* | WHERE trace.id == "<id>" | ...`.
That field name is **not portable across cells**: some `traces-*` mappings expose the id as the
ECS/nested **`trace.id`**, others as the flattened **`trace_id`**. On a `trace_id` cell the
`WHERE trace.id == …` clause matches nothing → Tokens/Latency/ToolCalls/Skill come back
**null / "No data found"** even when the trace, tokens and spans are all present and the traceId is
correct.

**Why this is sneaky:** it looks identical to the *other* two trace-eval failure modes —
(a) the eval querying the wrong trace id (fixed in `client.ts`, elastic/kibana#276310) and
(b) EDOT dropping spans (TLS, see `feedback_edot_capsule_trace_tls_drop.md`). Same symptom (null),
different cause. It's why one cell (m1max) went fully green with **only** the client.ts traceId fix,
while another (i9) also needed the field rename — i9's index uses `trace_id`.

**How to diagnose:** run the evaluator's own query both ways against the cell and see which returns rows:
```
FROM traces-* | WHERE trace.id  == "<traceId>" | STATS n=COUNT(*)   # ECS/nested
FROM traces-* | WHERE trace_id  == "<traceId>" | STATS n=COUNT(*)   # flattened
```
An `Unknown column [trace.id]` error (vs simply 0 rows) is the loud tell that the mapping is `trace_id`.

**How it's currently worked around (per-cell, uncommitted):** i9's `edd-runner` worktree patches all
four `trace_based/*.ts` `trace.id`→`trace_id` as an uncommitted local mod (preserved by the
stash-guarded `refresh-worktree.sh`). This is a band-aid, not a real fix.

**How to apply / real fix:** before assuming elastic/kibana#276310 fully closes trace-eval nulls
everywhere, confirm what field the **CI / prod** `traces-*` mapping actually indexes. If it's
inconsistent, the durable fix is to make the evaluators field-agnostic (e.g. `COALESCE(trace.id,
trace_id)` or detect the mapping once) rather than hardcode `trace.id` — otherwise the PR is correct
only for `trace.id` cells and `trace_id` cells still need the local patch.

**Confirmed:** Jul 4 2026, comparing m1max (`trace.id` works) vs i9 (`trace_id` required) edd-runner
worktrees; i9 carried the `trace_id` rename across all four evaluators.

name: kdev snapshot image fallback
description: kdev must try pulling SNAPSHOT image then fall back to local cache — never error if image exists locally
type: feedback
confidence: proven
---

When the release ES image isn't available, `kdev` falls back to the SNAPSHOT tag. Always attempt `docker pull` first (to get latest build), but **also accept a locally cached image** if the pull fails — don't error out just because the registry is unreachable.

**Why:** During worktree startup for `skill-eval-platform`, kdev errored even though `9.4.0-SNAPSHOT` was already present locally. The original script only tried to pull, never checked local cache for the fallback path.

**How to apply:** In `_ensure_image`, after `docker pull ... || true`, always follow with `docker image inspect` to accept locally cached images. This pattern applies to any image-resolution logic in dev scripts.

# Kibana Dev — Always `--no-base-path`

When starting Kibana from source in a worktree (skill-dev discover stack, detection emulation, endpoint forensic, etc.), **always** pass `--no-base-path`.

**Why:** Repeated explicit corrections Jun 23–24 across detection-emulation and main kibana chats. Without it, API URLs and Agent Builder tool calls drift from `http://localhost:<server.port>/...` assumptions in eval scripts and demos.

**How to apply:**
- `yarn start --no-base-path` (or the worktree's documented start script must include the flag)
- Before curl/browser validation, read `server.port` from `config/kibana.dev.yml` — never assume `5601`
- Pair with `worktree-dedicated-stack.mdc` port discipline

**Never:**
- Default to base-path URLs when the dev config uses a non-5601 port
- Demo Agent Builder skills against a Kibana instance started without checking start flags

**Confirmed approach:** `project_detection_emulation_autodex_v1_slice.md` demo notes; 3× parent-chat corrections in 7-day window.

# EDD capsule config: tracing schema drift on newer Kibana main

When booting the ao-workspace **EDD capsule** (`tools/kibana-dev-cell/boot-edd-capsule.sh`) against a **newer Kibana `main`** than the one the capsule template was authored on, Kibana crashes at startup on config validation (status 78). The capsule template (`templates/kibana.dev.capsule.yml`) carried two now-invalid tracing shapes. Both were fixed in the template AND the generated `config/kibana.dev.cell.yml`.

## Drift 1 — platform tracing (`telemetry.tracing`)
- Error: `[tracing.scheduledDelay]: Additional properties are not allowed ('scheduledDelay' was unexpected)`
- Old (invalid): a top-level `telemetry.tracing.scheduledDelay: 50`
- New schema (`src/platform/packages/shared/kbn-tracing-config/src/schema.ts`): `scheduled_delay` (snake_case) lives **inside each exporter's OTLP config**, not at the tracing level.
- Fix:
```
telemetry.tracing.exporters:
  - http:
      url: http://localhost:4318/v1/traces
      scheduled_delay: 50
```
(delete the top-level `telemetry.tracing.scheduledDelay` line)

## Drift 2 — Agent Builder self-tracing (`xpack.agentBuilder.tracing`)
- Error: `[config validation of [xpack.agentBuilder].tracing.send_to_self]: Additional properties are not allowed ('send_to_self' was unexpected)`
- `send_to_self` was **removed entirely** from source (grep finds zero hits). The old `otlp: {url}` sub-object is gone too.
- New schema (`x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/agent_builder/server/config.ts`, plugin id `agentBuilder`): `tracing.exporters: [{ url, headers? }]` + `tracing.opik_distributed_tracing: bool` + `tracing.scheduledDelay: number`.
- Fix — map old block to:
```
xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.exporters:
  - url: http://localhost:4318/v1/traces
xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.scheduledDelay: 50
```

## Notes
- The capsule REGENERATES `config/kibana.dev.cell.yml` from the template on every boot, so patch the **template** (`templates/kibana.dev.capsule.yml`), not just the generated file, or the fix is lost next boot. (The `agent_builder` plugin dir replaced the old `onechat` plugin — onechat no longer exists on main.)
- Symptom in the log: Kibana's optimizer builds all bundles fine ("217 bundles compiled successfully") then the **server** crashes at config validation — so a compile-success + immediate crash means config schema, not a build problem.
- Diagnose fast: read `~/.cursor/agent-builder-skill-dev-logs/edd-capsule-kibana.log`, grep for `FATAL|ValidationError|Additional properties`.

- `SERVER_VERSIONED_VERSIONRESOLUTION: "newest"` — enables versioned API routes 
- `SERVER_VERSIONED_STRICTCLIENTVERSIONCHECK: "false"` — relaxes version checking
- `UISETTINGS_OVERRIDES_AGENTBUILDER__NAVENABLED: "true"` — shows Agent Builder in nav
- `UISETTINGS_OVERRIDES_AGENTBUILDER__EXPERIMENTALFEATURES: "true"` — enables SML, skills

**Workflows UI** requires enabling via Kibana Advanced Settings UI (Stack Management > Advanced Settings), not just env vars.

**Agent Builder UI** is at `/app/agent_builder` (underscore), NOT `/app/agent-builder` (hyphen).

**Trial license** must be activated for Agent Builder + Workflows: `POST /_license/start_trial?acknowledge=true`

**Fleet Server** needs explicit policy creation via `POST /api/fleet/setup` + `POST /api/fleet/agent_policies` with `fleet-server-policy`.

**Why:** Production Docker images gate features behind these settings. In dev mode (`yarn start`), they're auto-enabled.

# Kibana getLocalhostRealIp() Returns Docker Bridge IP

`getLocalhostRealIp()` in `x-pack/solutions/security/plugins/security_solution/scripts/endpoint/common/network_services.ts` returns the first non-internal IPv4 it finds by iterating `os.networkInterfaces()` in reverse. On macOS with **OrbStack** or Docker Desktop running, this returns the Docker bridge IP (e.g. `192.168.139.3`), not the Multipass host IP (`192.168.252.1`) or LAN IP. The Fleet Server URL registered with Kibana then becomes `https://192.168.139.3:8180` — unreachable from Multipass VMs on the `192.168.252.x` subnet.

**Why:** Docker/OrbStack creates network interfaces that `getLocalhostRealIp()` prefers (it only excludes `.0`-suffixed addresses and internal interfaces). The function has an env-var escape hatch (`KIBANA_LOCALHOST_REAL_IP`) but `endpoint-lab`'s `start_fleet()` and `enroll_agent()` were not setting it.

**How to apply:**
- When invoking `start_fleet_server.js` or `run_endpoint_agent.js` from any wrapper (endpoint-lab, defend_workflows, manual), set `KIBANA_LOCALHOST_REAL_IP=<multipass_host_ip>` (e.g. `192.168.252.1`)
- Patched `start_fleet()` and `enroll_agent()` in `~/.local/bin/endpoint-lab` to prefix `KIBANA_LOCALHOST_REAL_IP="$host_ip"` to the node invocations
- Verify the registered Fleet URL: grep `startFleetServer` log for `Server URL: https://...` — should be the host IP, not a Docker bridge

**Never:**
- Assume `getLocalhostRealIp()` returns the host's primary LAN interface when Docker/OrbStack is running
- File this as a Kibana bug without first setting the env override — the script documents this exact escape hatch

**Boundary diagnosis (per verify-before-blaming):**
```
- Boundary: endpoint-lab wrapper ↔ Kibana startFleetServer script
- Canonical interface: scripts/endpoint/common/network_services.ts:10
- Documented shape: returns first non-internal IPv4, OR override via KIBANA_LOCALHOST_REAL_IP
- Observed shape: returns Docker bridge 192.168.139.3 (unreachable from VM)
- Conclusion: contract_missing → env override is the supported escape hatch
```

**Confirmed approach:** Patched locally Jun 30, 2026. Boot reached `Server URL: https://192.168.3.38:8180` (host IP) and VM enrolled successfully.

name: feedback_kibana_intel_mac_moon_binary
description: Kibana bootstrap fails on Intel macOS because pinned @moonrepo/cli@2.1.0 has no x64-darwin binary published; fix by shimming @moonrepo/core-macos-x64@2.3.5 into node_modules
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-01
source: i9 (Intel Core i9, MacBookPro15,1, macOS 15.7) EDD runner setup — yarn kbn bootstrap failed with "Cannot find module @moonrepo/core-macos-x64/package.json"
---

# Kibana Bootstrap on Intel macOS — moon Binary Gap

Stock Kibana dev is effectively **Apple-Silicon-only on macOS**. On an Intel (x86_64) Mac, `yarn kbn bootstrap` fails:

```
Error: Cannot find module '@moonrepo/core-macos-x64/package.json'
  at findMoonExe (node_modules/@moonrepo/cli/utils.js)
```

## Root cause

Kibana pins `@moonrepo/cli@2.1.0`, and its committed `yarn.lock` only lists the **arm64** binary (`@moonrepo/core-macos-arm64@2.1.0`). moonrepo **never published `@moonrepo/core-macos-x64@2.1.0`** (npm 404) — Intel-mac binaries only exist for 2.3.x+. So on Intel there is no moon binary to run.

## Fix (validated)

Shim the closest published Intel binary into the location the 2.1.0 CLI shim resolves. The `@moonrepo/cli` wrapper only `require.resolve`s the package dir and execs its binary — it does not assert the version, so a 2.3.5 binary drives the 2.1.0 workspace fine:

```bash
cd <worktree>/node_modules/@moonrepo
npm pack @moonrepo/core-macos-x64@2.3.5
tar -xzf moonrepo-core-macos-x64-2.3.5.tgz && rm -rf core-macos-x64 && mv package core-macos-x64
rm -f moonrepo-core-macos-x64-2.3.5.tgz
# verify: ./node_modules/.bin/moon --version  -> "moon 2.3.5"
# then re-run: yarn kbn bootstrap   (succeeds; moon drives the 2.1.0 workspace)
```

## How to apply

- Must be re-applied **per worktree** (each Kibana worktree has its own `node_modules`); see `feedback_remote_kibana_fresh_worktree`.
- `brew install moon` (2.3.5) is an alternative source of the binary, but the npm-pack shim keeps Kibana's invocation path (`node_modules/.bin/moon`) intact.

## Takeaway

Intel Macs are usable as Kibana runners but are *not* a supported/first-class path — expect to patch platform-binary gaps like this. Prefer Apple Silicon for heavy Kibana work (see `reference_dev_machine_fleet`).

# EDD cell trace-based evaluators fail (`traces-*` empty) — ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED: dual Docker runtime port hijack

**CONFIRMED (Jul 3 2026, m1max).** After a long detour through wrong Kibana-side theories, the real
cause was infrastructure, not Kibana: **two Docker runtimes (colima + OrbStack) were both running a
`kibana-edot-collector` container, each publishing `0.0.0.0:4318`. OrbStack started first and won the
host port bind, so every OTLP export (Kibana server, eval worker, and even a raw OTLP probe) hit
OrbStack's collector — which had no path to the colima `es-edd-runner` the eval reads. Colima's EDOT
collector never received a single span.** `traces-*` therefore stayed empty and all trace-based
evaluators (token / latency / trace-retrieval / skill-invocation) failed on null scores.

## The fix (verified end-to-end)
1. `docker --context orbstack rm -f kibana-edot-collector`  (remove the rogue duplicate; it had
   `restart=unless-stopped`, so it kept coming back across restarts).
2. `docker --context colima restart kibana-edot-collector`  (so colima's Lima SSH mux re-binds the
   now-free host `:4317/:4318` → colima EDOT).
3. Verify: real OTLP probe → `traces-*` went `0 → 501`; then smoke-tests `trace-retrieval` eval
   **passed** (`1 passed (34.4s)`, rc=0) with `traces-*` growing `562 → 889` during the run.

After the fix, host `:4318` is owned by `ssh <pid>` = `/Users/mac/.colima/_lima/colima/ssh.sock [mux]`
(colima's own port-forwarder). That is CORRECT — it forwards host `:4318` into the colima EDOT
container. (Colima's `:13133` health is unpublished, so a host curl to `:13133` returns `000`; that is
expected and NOT a fault.)

## The decisive diagnostic that cracked it (use this, not synthetic JSON)
1. Emit ONE **real** OTLP span with the worktree's own exporter (NOT hand-rolled curl JSON, which
   returns 200 + `partialSuccess` but parses 0 spans and proves nothing). Minimal Node script run
   from inside the worktree so `node_modules` resolves:
   ```js
   const { NodeTracerProvider } = require('@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-node');
   const { SimpleSpanProcessor } = require('@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base');
   const { OTLPTraceExporter } = require('@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http');
   const { trace } = require('@opentelemetry/api');
   (async () => {
     const p = new NodeTracerProvider({ spanProcessors: [new SimpleSpanProcessor(
       new OTLPTraceExporter({ url: 'http://localhost:4318/v1/traces' }))] });
     p.register();
     trace.getTracer('probe').startSpan('otlp-probe-' + Date.now()).end();
     await p.forceFlush(); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1500)); await p.shutdown();
   })();
   ```
2. Check `traces-*/_count`. If the probe flushes "successfully" but `traces-*` stays 0 → the span is
   going somewhere other than the EDOT you're inspecting. THEN:
3. `lsof -nP -iTCP:4318 -sTCP:LISTEN` on the host and see WHICH process owns `:4318`. This is what
   exposed OrbStack (PID of `OrbStack Helper`) instead of colima's Lima mux.
4. `docker context ls` + `docker --context colima ps` + `docker --context orbstack ps` to find
   duplicate containers across runtimes. Compare host-port ownership per port with `lsof`.

## Generalized trap (the real lesson)
**When multiple Docker runtimes are installed (colima AND OrbStack/Docker Desktop), a container in the
"wrong" runtime can silently steal a published host port from the runtime you think you're using.**
The stack `DOCKER_CONTEXT`/default context can point at colima while OrbStack quietly owns the host
port. Symptoms are maximally confusing: exporter reports success (200), the inspected collector logs
nothing and shows no errors, and the data sink stays empty — because traffic never reaches the
collector you're watching. Always confirm host-port ownership with `lsof` and enumerate containers in
ALL docker contexts before blaming the application.

## Retracted hypotheses (all WRONG — recorded so we don't repeat them)
- ❌ "Multi-version `@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base` SDK realm mismatch in Kibana." Circumstantial; the
  spans were fine — they just went to the wrong collector.
- ❌ "Missing `xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.send_to_self: true` config." Added + valid
  (`config.ts: send_to_self: schema.boolean`), Kibana restarted clean, but `traces-*` still `0` — so
  NOT the fix for trace-retrieval. (Note: `trace-retrieval` uses `inferenceClient.chatComplete()` =
  PLAIN inference spans, which are NOT `isAgentBuilderSpan`, so the `send_to_self` direct-to-ES path —
  gated by `AgentBuilderSpanProcessor`/`isAgentBuilderSpan` — would not carry them anyway. They travel
  the global OTLP→EDOT→`traces-*` path, which was the blocked one.) `send_to_self:true` is still set on
  the cell (harmless, and correct for genuine agent-builder/skill evals per the config's own comment).
- ❌ "Kibana `recordException Failed ... [object Object]` warnings are the export blocker." A red
  herring; spans were still created and exported, just to the hijacked port.
- ❌ "EDOT traces→ES routing/mapping is broken." Ruled out — once traffic reached the RIGHT (colima)
  EDOT, `traces-generic.otel-default` populated immediately.

## Prevention on m1max
- OrbStack now has ZERO EDD containers (rogue one removed, no stopped duplicates). Because it was
  removed (not just stopped), `restart=unless-stopped` won't resurrect it; nothing recreates it unless
  a setup step is re-run against the OrbStack context. Colima's EDOT (`restart=unless-stopped` + the
  supervisor's explicit `docker start`) binds `:4318` on reboot.
- Ideally run only ONE Docker runtime on a headless cell. If OrbStack must stay for other work, ensure
  no EDD/`kibana-edot-collector`/`es-edd-runner` containers are ever created in it.

## UPDATE (Jul 4 2026) — pipeline is fixed, but the trace-STATS evaluators still fail (different bug)
Once the port hijack was fixed, `traces-*` populates and the smoke `trace-retrieval` evaluator passes.
But a real **agent-builder** run exposes that the trace-STATS evaluator family is still broken, for two
reasons UNRELATED to the OTLP delivery fix above (do not conflate them):
1. **Latency = indexing lag.** `trace_based/factory.ts` retries only 5× (~1 min). The converse trace
   lands in `traces-*` but after that budget → "No data found for trace" during the run; the same
   traceId shows all spans + `MAX(duration)` minutes later.
2. **Tokens = trace-context correlation split.** The token evaluators
   `SUM(attributes.gen_ai.usage.*_tokens)` filtered by the converse `trace.id`. The inference
   `ChatComplete` spans DO carry those token attrs and ARE produced during the run, but under DIFFERENT
   trace.ids than the agent-builder converse trace → SUM over the converse id is null. `send_to_self:true`
   does NOT fix this and flipping it would REGRESS skill-invocation (that's what it was added for). Root
   cause is upstream: agent-builder converse doesn't propagate trace context into its inference calls.
Full analysis + decisive ES|QL diagnostics: `feedback_kbn_evals_run_against_capsule.md`.

# Kibana Pre-Push — Jest Hook on Large Branches

Hook: `~/.cursor/hooks/kibana-git-hooks/kibana-precommit.sh` runs after eslint + scoped `type_check` per changed project, then:

```bash
node scripts/jest.js --ci --no-cache --changedSince=upstream/main
```

## Failure mode

On wide feature branches (many packages touched), jest exits:

```
ERROR we no longer ship a root config file so you either need to pass a path to a test file...
❌ jest failed
error: failed to push some refs
```

All scoped `type_check` projects may have **already passed** (30–60 min sunk).

## Workaround (validated)

1. Run scoped type_check on affected projects locally (pre-push does this anyway)
2. Run scoped jest with **per-package config**:

```bash
node scripts/jest.js --config x-pack/solutions/security/packages/kbn-evals-suite-security-ai-rules/jest.config.js \
  --testPathPattern=evaluate_routing_dataset.test
```

3. Push with `--no-verify` when typecheck + targeted jest are green:

```bash
git push --no-verify upstream fix/weekly-evals-matrix
```

## Also fix typecheck blockers on branch

Large weekly-matrix branches accumulate TS errors across packages (entity-analytics `types: [node]` blocking jest globals, agent-builder `selectEvaluators` generics, security-ai-rules `RuleRoutingDatasetExample` in tests). Pre-push runs **every** changed package — fix all before push or upstream sync stalls.

**Never:**
- Retry full pre-push hoping jest passes without scoped runs
- Push to fork only and skip upstream when Buildkite needs `elastic/kibana`

**Confirmed approach:** `18b6e7ce` pushed upstream with `--no-verify` after 22-project typecheck + scoped jest green (65 skill + 13 routing dataset tests, Jun 28 2026). Same failure mode as Jun 26 `ab38a12`.

name: feedback_kibana_registry_snapshots
description: Kibana plugin register*() calls have downstream CODEOWNERS-gated snapshot tests that drift silently
type: feedback
---

# Kibana Plugin Registry Snapshots

Many Kibana plugin `setup()` registrations have a corresponding **CODEOWNERS-gated snapshot test** that asserts the exact set of registered ids and their SHA-1 hashes. Changing a `register*()` call site without updating the matching test costs a full ~60 min CI cycle.

**Why:** Discovered the trap on PR #260544 (endpoint attachment migration). My fix re-registered the legacy `endpoint` external-reference id for back-compat. The test at `x-pack/platform/test/cases_api_integration/security_and_spaces/tests/common/attachments_framework/external_references.ts:497` had been updated in the same PR to expect `endpoint` to be *removed* from the registry — and the comment on it (`endpoint was migrated from externalReference registry to unified registry`) literally described the diff I was making. Pre-push validation (eslint + scoped jest + scoped type_check) cannot see the mismatch because the assertion is purely a runtime registry snapshot in an FTR config. CI surfaced it ~45 min in. Cost: one wasted build + one extra commit + one extra build.

**How to apply:**

1. **Whenever a diff touches a `register*()` call site** (`registerExternalReference`, `registerPersistableState`, `registerUnified`, `registerType` for alerting/actions, `registerIntegration` for fleet, savedObject `registerType`, etc.), grep for downstream snapshot assertions before pushing:

   ```bash
   rg -nl 'registered_(external_reference|persistable_state|unified)_attachments|registered_rule_types|registered_action_types|check changes on all registered' \
     x-pack/platform/test x-pack/solutions/*/test src/platform/test
   ```

2. **The snapshot's literal hashes are deterministic** SHA-1 over the serialized type definition. You cannot recompute them locally without running the FTR test (~6 min including ES boot). Either run the specific config locally:

   ```bash
   node scripts/functional_tests --config <test-config-path> \
     --grep 'check changes on all registered'
   ```

   …or push and let CI compute the hash, then `ci-babysitter` will auto-update the snapshot from the failure log (see its `Registry Snapshot Drift (Auto-Fix)` section).

3. **The snapshot's *purpose* is to surface the change to CODEOWNERS** (Response Ops, Detection Engine, Fleet, etc.) — not to block it. Updating the assertion to match is the correct action; you are not "silencing" a test, you are completing the change the snapshot was designed to surface.

**Known registry-snapshot test locations:**

- `x-pack/platform/test/cases_api_integration/security_and_spaces/tests/common/attachments_framework/external_references.ts` (cases external-reference registry)
- `x-pack/platform/test/cases_api_integration/security_and_spaces/tests/{basic,trial}/attachments_framework/registered_unified_*.ts` (cases unified attachment registry)
- Alerting rule type / action type registries have similar `to.eql({...sha1})` assertions in their respective `*_api_integration` suites.

**Pre-push automation:**

The `kibana-precommit-checks` skill (Step 5: "Registry blast-radius check") performs this scan automatically when it sees a `register*()` line in the diff and surfaces every matching assertion file before push. If you skip pre-push validation, the `ci-babysitter` skill will catch the failure post-push and auto-fix it — but pre-push is one CI cycle cheaper.

**Never:**

- Drop the registration to "avoid having to update the snapshot" — that's the reverse: a deliberate breaking change masquerading as a snapshot fix.
- Edit the snapshot to look "close enough" without rerunning the test — if the hashes don't match exactly, the next CI cycle will fail again.
- Assume `register*()` changes only need unit-test coverage — they almost always have a downstream FTR snapshot.

**Confirmed approach:** Validated on PR #260544 — added `endpoint: 'e13fe41b5c330dd923da91992ed0cedb7e30960f'` to the assertion and CI went green on the next cycle (build #437809, 428/428 jobs).

# Kibana Shared Branch — Never Force-Push, Merge Remote Tip

When pulling `upstream/main` into a shared Kibana feature branch (e.g. `fix/weekly-evals-matrix`) and pushing back to `elastic/kibana`:

## The rejection

```bash
git push --no-verify upstream fix/weekly-evals-matrix
! [rejected]  fix/weekly-evals-matrix -> fix/weekly-evals-matrix (fetch first)
```

This happens because the remote branch has commits you don't have locally — typically:
- Auto-generated commits from `node scripts/regenerate_moon_projects.js --update`
- Auto-generated commits from `node scripts/lint_ts_projects --fix`
- Another dev or bot pushed to the same branch

## Correct response — fetch + merge

```bash
git fetch upstream fix/weekly-evals-matrix
git log --oneline upstream/fix/weekly-evals-matrix ^HEAD  # see what's there
git merge --no-edit upstream/fix/weekly-evals-matrix       # merge, don't rebase
git push --no-verify upstream fix/weekly-evals-matrix
```

The merge commit is fine — Kibana's PR workflow accepts merge commits on feature branches. The 2 trivial auto-commits (moon regen + lint fix) merge cleanly.

## Why NOT force-push

- `elastic/kibana` `fix/*` branches are **shared** — other devs, CI, and bots may have commits
- Force-push rewrites history → anyone with a local clone has a broken ref
- Buildkite branch builds pinned to a SHA can become unreachable
- The PR (#274606) shows force-push events in the timeline, which reviewers dislike

## Conflict resolution priorities

When merging `upstream/main` into a feature branch with conflicts:

| File | Priority |
|------|----------|
| `.github/CODEOWNERS` | Keep your additions + take upstream team renames |
| Refactored files (`start.ts` → `run_helpers.ts`) | Take upstream refactor; re-apply your changes on top |
| Evaluator stacks (`evaluate_dataset.ts`) | Keep your evaluator additions (skill invocation, trace metrics) |
| Auto-generated (`moon.yml`, `tsconfig.json`) | Take upstream |

## Never

- `git push --force` to `elastic/kibana` on a shared branch
- `git rebase` a branch with 300+ commits onto `upstream/main` — merge instead
- Assume the rejection is an error — it's a safety check; fetch first

## Confirmed approach

Jun 30 session: `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` push rejected after `upstream/main` merge. Fetched remote tip (2 auto-commits: moon regen + lint-ts-fix), merged cleanly, pushed. PR #274606 updated without force-push. Final commit `cddab5a7011c`.

# launchd daemon: wrapper exec-bit + `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false`

Two non-obvious details when supervising a Node daemon with launchd via a **wrapper script** (instead of hardcoding the nvm node path in `ProgramArguments`):

## 1. The wrapper must be executable — and the exec bit must be committed
launchd `exec`s the `ProgramArguments` directly. A wrapper written by a tool/editor lands `100644`, so launchd crash-loops with:

```
scripts/run-daemon.sh: Permission denied
```

Fix and make it durable in git:
```bash
chmod +x scripts/run-daemon.sh
git update-index --chmod=+x scripts/run-daemon.sh   # tracks the mode, survives clone
```
The daemon self-healed on its next `KeepAlive` respawn (30s throttle) once the bit was set — no manual reload needed.

**Why a wrapper at all:** launchd starts with a bare environment and no login shell, so a `#!/usr/bin/env node` shebang can't resolve the nvm-managed node. The wrapper sources nvm to put `node` on PATH, then `exec`s the CLI. (The alternative — hardcoding `/Users/.../.nvm/versions/node/vX/bin/node` in `ProgramArguments`, per `feedback_persistent_daemons_via_launchd_runatload.md` — also works but pins the node version in the plist.)

## 2. `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false`, not blanket `KeepAlive=false`
For a daemon that should **self-heal on crash** but **not respawn-loop on an intentional refusal**, use:
```xml
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<dict><key>SuccessfulExit</key><false/></dict>
```
This respawns on a non-zero/crashed exit (SIGKILL, uncaught throw) but stays down on a clean `exit(0)` — e.g. a graceful `benchmarker-queue stop`, or a deliberate GPU-VM lease refusal when another daemon owns the VM. This **refines** the older advice ("`KeepAlive=false` is deliberate so a crash doesn't loop") — with `SuccessfulExit=false` you get crash self-healing AND no lease-refusal loop, which is strictly better for an unattended 24/7 daemon.

**Never:**
- Write a launchd wrapper and forget the exec bit — it crash-loops with Permission denied and looks like a config bug.
- Use blanket `KeepAlive=false` for a daemon meant to run 24/7 — it won't come back after a genuine crash.

**Confirmed approach:** `deploy/com.elastic-llm-benchmarker.plist.template` routes through `scripts/run-daemon.sh`; SIGKILL → launchd respawned a fresh PID within ~30s (validated live, Jul 4 2026).

name: feedback_lease_reclaim_after_crash_ttl_wait
description: After SIGKILLing a lease-holding daemon, the launchd-respawned instance correctly REFUSES to start until the dead holder's heartbeat TTL (~2min) expires, then reclaims — don't read the initial refusals as broken supervision
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-04
source: Crash-restart test of the ES-lease-fenced benchmarker daemon (Jul 4 2026)
---

# Lease reclaim after crash requires waiting out the heartbeat TTL

When you crash-test a daemon that holds an **ES-backed GPU-VM lease** (fenced by `lease_token` + heartbeat), the recovery sequence is:

1. `kill -9 <pid>` — the holder dies **without releasing** the lease (no graceful shutdown).
2. launchd respawns a new instance (`KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false`, ~30s throttle).
3. The new instance **refuses to start** for as long as the dead holder's lease looks live:
   ```
   error: GPU VM lease held by another benchmarker daemon — refusing to start
     {"heldBy":"host (pid 8675, heartbeat 2026-07-04T19:36:29Z)"}
   ```
   It keeps refusing (once per respawn) until the heartbeat is older than the lease TTL.
4. After the TTL (~2 min here), the next respawn **reclaims** the stale lease and boots fully (lease acquired → schedulers start).

**Why it matters (the trap):** the initial refusals look like "supervision is broken / the daemon can't start." They are the **correct** fencing behavior — the lease exists precisely so a second process can't grab the shared GPU VM while a (possibly still-alive) holder might be using it. A crash can't be distinguished from a network partition instantly, so the survivor waits out the TTL rather than racing.

**How to apply:**
- When validating crash-recovery on a lease-fenced daemon, **wait at least one full heartbeat-TTL** (~2 min) before judging. Watch the log for the `Acquired ... lease` line, not just the first `refusing to start`.
- Distinguish the two "refusing to start" causes: a *clean* refusal (another **live** daemon truly owns the VM) should stay down; a *stale* refusal (dead holder) self-resolves after the TTL. The heartbeat timestamp in the log tells you which.

**Never:**
- Conclude the supervisor/plist is misconfigured from the first post-crash refusal — check whether the cited `heartbeat` is stale and give it the TTL.
- `kill -9` a daemon expecting the lease to free instantly — SIGKILL skips the release path by design; reclamation is TTL-driven.

**Confirmed approach:** SIGKILL of PID 8675 → two refusals (holder heartbeat still within TTL) → third respawn reclaimed at +~2min and booted all schedulers. Validated live Jul 4 2026. Pairs with `feedback_benchmarker_cross_host_daemon_contention.md` (the lease is the fix for that memory's cross-host thrash).

name: feedback_local_docker_prune_safety
description: "Never docker image prune -a across the many parallel stacks on this box — unused-image heuristics false-flag live images; real disk = images + build cache, not checkout dirs"
type: feedback
---

# Local Docker prune safety (many parallel stacks)

This box runs many parallel Docker stacks (Kibana ES, benchmarker ES,
caldera/soc-simulation, automaker, phoenix, CRW, litellm, etc.). Reclaiming
Docker disk needs care because a blunt prune destroys expensive images.

## Never run `docker image prune -a`

`prune -a` removes every image not referenced by an existing container. On this
box that would nuke multi-GB images that cost hours to re-pull/rebuild:
`docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/*`, `benchmarker-elasticsearch:*`,
`soc-simulation-caldera:*`, `automaker-*`, etc. The RAM/disk saving is not worth
the re-pull tax.

## "Unused image" heuristics are unreliable

Comparing `docker ps -a --format {{.Image}}` names against `docker images` to
decide "unused" **false-flags live images** — it flagged the running CRW image
(`ghcr.io/us/crw:latest`) as unused because the container referenced it by a
different resolved name. Docker itself protects images with any container, so
`prune -a` wouldn't actually delete a live image, but the heuristic is not
trustworthy for a curated delete list. Verify per-image before removing.

## What's actually safe / where the disk really is

- **Real disk hogs are images + build cache**, not source checkouts. Retiring
  Firecrawl: the checkout dir was 78MB; the images were ~3.1GB and the build
  cache was 20.45GB.
- Safe reclaim: `docker builder prune -f` (rebuildable cache) + `docker image
  prune -f` (dangling/untagged only) + **manual cherry-pick** of clearly
  disposable re-pullable base/utility images (`alpine`, `curlimages/curl`,
  `debian:*`, `golang`, `redis:alpine`, `rabbitmq`, `rhysd/actionlint`).
- Volumes: `docker volume prune` is dangerous here — dangling volumes include
  real stack data (`docker_es-data`, `docker_es-snapshots`, `kbn-evals-data`,
  `litellm_postgres_data`, `qdrant_data`, ...). List and cherry-pick; never
  batch-prune.

**Confirmed approach:** 2026-07-01 Firecrawl retirement reclaimed ~3.1GB images
+ 20.45GB build cache via targeted removal; `prune -a` deliberately avoided.

name: feedback_macos_bash32_ifs_and_heredoc_quirks
description: macOS bash 3.2 — whitespace IFS collapses empty middle fields on tab-split; an apostrophe in a comment inside a quoted heredoc trips `bash -n`. Line-per-field + apostrophe-free comments.
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-02
source: skill-dev scripts/recreate-demo-env.sh (demo-env dispatcher); anti-pattern #57
---

# macOS bash 3.2: IFS Empty-Field Collapse + Heredoc Apostrophe Trip

Two distinct bash 3.2 (the macOS system bash) gotchas hit while building a
manifest-reading shell dispatcher.

## 1. Whitespace IFS collapses empty middle fields

`IFS=$'\t' read -r A B C D <<<"$row"` — when IFS contains a whitespace char
(tab counts), `read` **collapses consecutive delimiters and drops empty
fields**. A candidate row `status\t\tscenario\ttarget` (empty `runner`)
parses as three fields, not four; every field after the empty one shifts
left, and the script acts on the wrong value. bash 3.2 also lacks
`mapfile`/`readarray`, so the usual array workaround isn't available.

**Fix:** emit one field per LINE from the reader (Python/jq), then extract by
line number — an empty line stays empty:
```bash
STATUS="$(printf '%s\n' "$resolved" | sed -n 1p)"
RUNNER="$(printf '%s\n' "$resolved" | sed -n 2p)"   # empty stays empty
SCENARIO="$(printf '%s\n' "$resolved" | sed -n 3p)"
```

## 2. Apostrophe in a comment inside a quoted heredoc trips `bash -n`

An apostrophe (`what's`, `isn't`) inside a comment within a `<<'PY' … PY`
quoted heredoc — or even a plain shell comment near one — makes bash 3.2's
`-n` (no-exec syntax check) report `unexpected EOF while looking for
matching quote`. The quote scanner counts the apostrophe even though it's in
a comment/heredoc body.

**Fix:** keep comments apostrophe-free in scripts that embed quoted heredocs
("what is" not "what's").

**How to apply:**
- Smoke every dispatcher path INCLUDING a row with an empty middle column,
  not just the happy path — the happy path hides the IFS collapse.
- Run `bash -n script.sh` after edits; if it reports a bogus EOF/quote error,
  grep the script for apostrophes in comments near heredocs.

**Never:**
- Assume `IFS=$'\t' read` preserves empty fields — it doesn't when IFS is
  whitespace. Use a non-whitespace sentinel or line-per-field.
- Trust that a comment is inert to `bash -n`'s quote scanner.

**Confirmed approach:** line-per-field + apostrophe-free comments made
`recreate-demo-env.sh --list` / `--env` and `bash -n` pass; shellcheck CI green.

**Pairs with:** `feedback_heredoc_stdin_collision` (a different heredoc trap:
`python3 - <<'PY'` swallows piped stdin — clean `bash -n`, wrong semantics).

# Matrix Score Filters — git_commit Prefix Match

When filtering eval scores by commit SHA in the golden cluster (plugin `evaluations_kbn_client.ts` / Kibana `evaluations_kbn_client.ts`):

- **Short SHA (12 chars)** passed as `--commit f13b82c8` → must use **prefix match**, not exact term match
- **Full SHA (40 chars)** → exact match works, but callers usually pass short SHAs

## Failure mode

```bash
node scripts/generate-matrix --build-url weekly-llm-evals/builds/37 --commit f13b82c8
# Returns 0 score docs with exact term match
# Returns 17,388 score docs with prefix match
```

The ES query in `evaluations_es_client.ts` was using `term` (exact) on `git_commit` — short SHAs don't match the full 40-char stored value.

## Fix shape

```ts
// evaluations_es_client.ts
{
  term: {
    git_commit: { value: commit } // WRONG for short SHA
  }
}
// →
{
  prefix: { git_commit: commit } // RIGHT for short SHA
}
```

Or in `evaluations_kbn_client.ts`, pass `git_commit` as a prefix query when length < 40.

## Related filter gotchas

- **`build_url`** is empty until Buildkite scores export to the golden cluster — interim branch rollups use `git_branch` + 14d window
- **`git_commit` prefix match** works for short SHAs but is slower than term match on full SHAs
- **`run_id`** is legacy pre-revamp; revamp uses `execution_id` / `suite_id` (with `_norm` runtime fields)
- **`metadata.ci.build_id`** is the numeric Buildkite build number; `build_url` is the full URL

## Never

- Pass a short SHA to a `term` query expecting exact match
- Assume empty matrix = no scores exported — check the filter shape first
- Use `run_id` for revamp (post-CI-build-18) score reads

Plugin commit (uncommitted in `agent-builder-skill-dev-cursor-plugin`): `evaluations_kbn_client.ts` `gitCommitMatchesFilter` + `evaluations_es_client.ts` prefix vs term. Build #37 matrix regenerated with 17,388 docs after fix.

name: feedback_mcp_recipe_hint_schema_drift
description: MCP recipe/nextStep payloadHints drift from the referenced action's Zod schema — action-id parity tests don't catch it; dogfood the journey + lock with a hint-grep test
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-02
source: skill-dev PR #87 shipped wrong runtime-smoke hint (response/tool_substring); caught dogfooding validate-on-pr-cloud, fixed PR #88; anti-pattern #56
---

# MCP Recipe `payloadHint` Names Drift From the Action's Schema

A `nextSteps[]` / recipe entry references a real action id (so drift tests
pass) but its `payloadHint` string names parameters the target action's Zod
schema does not accept. An agent copies the hint verbatim → the call fails
schema validation, or worse silently drops the unknown fields.

**Why:** skill-dev PR #87's `local.propose-demo-env` emitted a gate hint
`{ response: "...", tool_substring: "..." }`, but `evaluation.runtime-smoke`
actually wants `{ converse_response, skill_id, expect, tool_substrings[] }`.
Action-id parity tests (`pm_e2e`) only verify that `action` resolves to a
*registered* action — they never cross-check the `payloadHint` against that
action's schema, so the wrong contract sailed through CI. Found only by
dogfooding the `validate-on-pr-cloud` journey and reading step 4's hint
side-by-side with the schema in `evaluation.ts`.

**How to apply:**
- Dogfood the stitched path (`system.guide { journey }`) or the proposer
  output and read each step's `payloadHint` against the target action's Zod
  schema — the divergence is obvious side-by-side.
- Lock load-bearing hints with a test that greps the emitted hint for the
  real param names (`demo_envs.test.ts` "gate step uses the real
  runtime-smoke param names") — assert the correct names present AND the old
  wrong names absent.
- Better: a generic `pm_e2e` check that every hint's keys are a subset of the
  referenced action's schema keys, killing the whole class at once.

**Never:**
- Treat "the action id resolves" as proof the recipe is correct — the id and
  the params are two separate contracts.
- Hand-author a payloadHint without opening the target action's `z.object({…})`.

**Confirmed approach:** #88 fixed the hint + added the drift-lock test; the
live proposer render then showed `converse_response`/`skill_id`/`tool_substrings`.

**Pairs with:** `feedback_action_input_name_verification` (GitHub Actions
silently drop wrong `with:` keys — same "verify input names against the
declared schema, silent failure on mismatch" family, different surface).

name: feedback_memory_export_per_category_cap
description: Memory export cap must be applied per-category after grouping, not globally before; dominant category otherwise starves smaller ones
type: feedback
confidence: proven
updated: 2026-06-30
source: loop-first-approach skill distribution session, PR #128
---

# Memory Export — Cap Per Category, Not Globally Before Grouping

When an exporter fetches a ranked list and groups by category **after** applying a global cap, a dominant category consumes the entire budget and smaller categories vanish from the output entirely. The cap must be applied **per category** after grouping, with unused headroom reclaimed across the remaining categories.

**Why:** Jun 30 2026 — the treadmill `exportMemoryToCursorRule` had `LIMIT maxEntries` in `listMemoryEntries` followed by a group-by-category loop. With 181 active entries (133 feedback, 36 reference, 9 project, 3 user) and cap=40, the global limit returned 40 feedback entries — reference, project, and user sections never appeared. The cap looked like it was working (40 in, 40 out) but was structurally hiding 4 entire categories. Bumping the cap to 80 didn't help: feedback still ate all 80 because it had 133 candidates ranked higher. Fix landed in PR #128 (`d3d190d`).

**How to apply:**
- Any `topN` + `groupBy` pipeline must compute the cap **after** grouping, not before.
- Fair-share formula: `perCategory = max(1, floor(cap / numCategories))`; unused headroom reclaimed from small categories to larger ones, largest first, so the overall cap is still honoured.
- The same anti-pattern applies to any "ranked export with categories": dashboards, leaderboards, RSS feeds, search facets.
- Audit existing `LIMIT ?` calls that feed into grouping logic — they're the smoking gun.

**Never:**
- Apply `LIMIT` to a query whose result will be grouped downstream — the limit is structurally incompatible with fair category representation.
- Assume a cap is "working" because the count matches — it may be silently dropping entire categories.
- Bump the cap as a fix without checking whether the ranking itself is the problem (see `feedback_ranking_tiebreak_recency`).

**Tiebreak companion:** the global-cap fix shipped alongside a recency tiebreak fix (`ORDER BY weight DESC, first_seen DESC, entry_id ASC` instead of `entry_id ASC`). Both are needed: per-category cap gives small categories a slot, recency tiebreak ensures newly confirmed entries win that slot. Either alone is insufficient.

**Confirmed approach:** 2026-06-30 — PR #128 merged, 3176/3176 tests green (added 2 regression tests), all three newly captured memories now appear in `~/.cursor/rules/treadmill-memory.mdc` (previously 0/3).

name: feedback_memory_sync_daemon_unreachable_fallback
description: memory-sync degrades to local SQLite + queued (not confirmed) ES backfill when the treadmill daemon (:3100) is down — report ES sync as deferred, not done
type: feedback
---

# memory-sync Daemon-Unreachable Fallback

`~/.cursor/hooks/memory-sync.sh` (and `treadmill memory-sync`) **succeed with
exit 0 even when the treadmill daemon on `:3100` is unreachable** — they fall
back to local SQLite for import + reindex and **enqueue** the ES backfill
without confirming it landed. Do not report "propagated to ES" on the strength
of exit 0 alone.

**Why:** Observed 2026-07-04 (Project Daybreak) across **two consecutive runs**
with the daemon down:
```
run 1: Imported 0, updated 294 ... enqueued 295 ... esDocs=n/a   (total 295)
run 2: Imported 3, updated 294 ... enqueued 298 ... esDocs=n/a   (total 298)
```
A new `knowledge/*.md` file written **just before run 1** did NOT appear in
SQLite that run (`Imported 0`); it was only picked up in run 2 (`Imported 3`,
which included it + 2 more). So the local-fallback importer can **lag a
just-written new file by a run** — the `Imported` counter is real signal, and a
`0` there does mean nothing new landed *that run*. Exit was 0 both times, and ES
only ever got a **queue entry** (`esDocs=n/a`), never a confirmed write.

**How to apply:**
- The **durable source of truth** is always safe: the `knowledge/*.md` files +
  `MEMORY.md` index on disk (git-tracked via ao-workspace auto-sync). Those are
  updated by the write itself, independent of sync/daemon state — they are the
  safety net if SQLite/ES lag.
- Read the sync tail before declaring success. `esDocs=n/a` /
  `mappingRepaired=false` / "Daemon unreachable" ⇒ **ES propagation is
  deferred**, not done. Say so honestly; offer to re-run once the daemon is up.
- **If `Imported N` is lower than the number of new files you just wrote,
  re-run the sync** (or run it with the daemon up) — the local fallback may
  need a second pass to import a freshly-written file. Confirm the expected
  `Imported`/`total` delta rather than assuming "updated N" covered it.
- Local-fallback **export cap = 40** entries to `treadmill-memory.mdc`
  ("(local)", capped at 40); daemon-backed export caps at **80**. Fewer active
  memories reach the exported rule when the daemon is down.

**Never:**
- Claim "synced to SQLite + ES" when the log says the daemon was unreachable.
- Assume a new file reached SQLite when `Imported` is 0 / below the count of
  files you added — re-run and check the delta.

**Confirmed approach:** Verified across two live runs — durable md + MEMORY.md
always updated; SQLite import of a new file lagged one run; ES write only
queued throughout.

description: Gemini/EIS judge streams empty toolCallId — merge_chunks index fallback fixes C4/C6 weekly 500s
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-29
source: skill-dev 3686518a — builds #36 vs #37; merge_chunks.ts f13b82c8
---

# merge_chunks Index Fallback — Security Matrix Judge Gate

## Symptom (pre-fix)

Weekly evals fail on **siem-readiness (C4)** and **attack-discovery (C6)** for models that use **Gemini 3.x as LLM judge** (via EIS):

```
POST /internal/inference/prompt → 500
Tool call key is missing for index 0 in chunk …
```

Scout worker logs also show `Correctness analysis returned an invalid or missing tool call` and trace evaluators retrying (`Cached Tokens`, `Latency` N/A after 6 attempts).

**Throw site:** `x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/inference/server/chat_complete/utils/merge_chunks.ts` (mergeToolCalls).

## Root cause

Some EIS/Gemini judge streams emit a tool-call chunk with **empty `toolCallId`** but a populated **`index`**. Legacy merge logic required `toolCallId` or a prior index→id map entry — first chunk at index 0 failed.

## Fix (Kibana f13b82c8)

When `toolCallId` is empty but `index` is defined, use stable merge key `__index_${index}`:

```typescript
if (!key && toolCall.index !== undefined) {
  key = `__index_${toolCall.index}`;
  indexToToolCallId.set(toolCall.index, key);
}
```

## Validated on weekly build #37 (f13b82c8)

| Suite | #36 (a4733ccd) | #37 (f13b82c8) |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| attack-discovery C6 | 5/6 (Opus fail) | **6/6** |
| siem-readiness C4 | 3/6 (Opus/Sonnet/Gemini-flash fail) | **4/6+** (Opus + Sonnet pass; Gemini-flash still model-specific) |

**How to apply:**
- Any eval suite using Gemini-as-judge with tool-call streaming — verify merge_chunks handles index-only first chunks
- Distinguish this from **subject-model** failures (multi-turn find_rules, routing) — judge 500s hit trace/token/correctness evaluators uniformly

**Never:**
- Patch eval specs to swallow judge 500 when the platform merge contract is wrong
- Attribute C4/C6 Opus-only failures to skill content before checking inference prompt 500 in job log

**Confirmed approach:** Build #37 attack-discovery 6/6 all models; C4 Opus/Sonnet flipped fail→pass vs #36 on same weekly pipeline.

name: feedback_no_data_smoke_eval_criteria_calibration
description: No-data smoke eval criteria must assert attempt/method (attempts/cites/references), not populated output — a strict "produces ordered list" criterion is unsatisfiable without seeded data; don't weaken to game the score
type: feedback
---

# No-Data Smoke Eval: Calibrate Criteria to the Tier, Don't Game the Score

A **smoke-tier** eval that runs against a stack with **no seeded domain data**
can only prove routing + tool trajectory + scoping. It cannot prove
data-dependent output quality. So happy-path `criteria` for a no-data smoke
must be phrased around what the agent *attempts*, not what it *produces*.

**Why:** On the endpoint-forensic-analysis smoke suite (PR #275840), three
happy-path datasets ran against a stack with **no seeded `SRV-DC01`
telemetry** (so `execute_esql` returned empty):

- `patient-zero` (Criteria 1.0) — criteria phrased *"Attempts forensic
  reconstruction... rather than refusing"*, *"Uses or references ES|QL..."*.
- `lateral` (Criteria 1.0) — *"Cites query approach or data source"*.
- `timeline` (Criteria **0.67**) — one criterion was *"Produces a
  chronological narrative or **ordered event list** for the named host"*.
  With empty query results there are no events to order, so the Opus judge
  failed that sub-criterion — even though Skill Invoked and Trajectory were
  both 1.0 (the skill routed and ran the right ES|QL calls).

The 0.67 is a **data-availability bound**, not a skill defect. The two
siblings pass on the same empty data purely because their wording tolerates a
methodology answer.

**How to apply:**
- For a no-data smoke tier, write criteria like *"attempts / references /
  cites / is scoped to X"* — parallel across all datasets in the suite so
  one isn't stricter than the rest by accident.
- If you genuinely need to assert populated, data-dependent output
  (an actual ordered timeline, a real patient-zero host), that belongs in a
  **seeded eval tier** — seed the telemetry (`evaluation.seed-endpoint-fixture`

name: No fetch() between Kibana plugins
description: Never use fetch() or HTTP calls to call Kibana APIs from server-side plugin code — always use the plugin's exported contract/client
type: feedback
---

Never use `fetch()` or HTTP requests to call Kibana APIs from server-side plugin code. Always use the plugin's exported setup/start contract instead.

**Why:** Fetch bypasses Kibana's plugin dependency system, auth scoping, space isolation, and request context. It creates fragile couplings to HTTP routes that may change, requires manually forwarding auth headers, and breaks in production deployments behind proxies. Plugin contracts are the designed integration surface.

**How to apply:** When a plugin needs to interact with another plugin (e.g., Agent Builder, Actions, Saved Objects), declare it as a dependency in `kibana.jsonc` and use the start/setup contract. For example, use `agentBuilder.skills.getRegistry({ request })` instead of `fetch('/api/agent_builder/skills')`. This applies to all inter-plugin server-side communication, including background tasks and fire-and-forget workflows.

name: feedback_npm_audit_transitive_via_sdk
description: npm audit HIGHs transitive via @modelcontextprotocol/sdk can't be fixed locally; document and defer
type: feedback
---

# npm Audit HIGHs Transitive via MCP SDK — Document and Defer

When `npm audit` reports HIGH vulnerabilities in packages like `hono`
or `ip-address` and `npm ls` shows them as transitive dependencies of
`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, they **cannot be fixed locally**. The
fix requires the SDK to bump its own dependency ranges. Document them
as deferred with explicit rationale rather than attempting `npm audit
fix --force` (which breaks the SDK) or pinning overrides (which masks
the issue and may cause runtime mismatches).

**Why:** Captured Jun 30 during the EDD Capsule Phase 0 hygiene PR.
The health-check's `/10x-health-check` estimated "15-30 min" to close
all three HIGH findings via version bumps. In practice:

- `vitest@2.x` CRITICAL — direct devDep, fixed by `vitest@4.x` ✓
- `vite@6.x` HIGH — direct devDep, fixed by `vite@8.x` ✓
- `hono` HIGH (CSS injection, JWT, cache leakage) — **transitive via
  `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.29.0`** which declares `hono: ^4.11.4`.
  `npm audit fix` cannot bump this without the SDK's range moving.
- `ip-address` HIGH (XSS) — transitive via `express-rate-limit` ←
  `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.29.0`. Same blocker.

The health-check's "all three have `fixAvailable: true`" was accurate
for the direct deps but misleading for the transitives — `npm audit
fix` reports "fix available" even when the fix requires a major bump
of an upstream you don't control.

**How to apply:**
- Before estimating "audit fix time", run `npm ls <vulnerable-pkg>`
  to trace the dependency chain
- If the vulnerable package is a **direct dep** (dev or prod): bump it
- If it's **transitive via a package you control**: bump the parent's
  range and republish
- If it's **transitive via a third-party SDK** (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`,
  `express`, etc.): document as deferred with:
  - The full chain (`hono ← @hono/node-server ← @modelcontextprotocol/sdk`)
  - The SDK version that introduced / still carries the range
  - Whether the advisory is dev-only or prod-affecting
  - The upstream issue/PR tracking the fix (if any)
- Add an `npm audit` CI step with `continue-on-error: true` so the
  advisory surfaces on every run without blocking merges
- When the SDK ships a version with the bumped range, remove the
  `continue-on-error` and close the deferred item

**Never:**
- Run `npm audit fix --force` to "close" transitive findings — it
  major-bumps the SDK and breaks the runtime contract
- Use npm `overrides` to force a hono version outside the SDK's tested
  range — runtime mismatches are harder to debug than the advisory
- Estimate "15 min to close all audit findings" without tracing each
  chain to direct vs transitive
- Omit the dependency chain from the PR body — reviewers need to see
  WHY this finding is deferred, not just that it is

**Confirmed approach:** Validated Jun 30 — PR #77 documented hono +
ip-address as transitive-via-SDK with the full chain, set the audit
CI step to advisory (`continue-on-error: true`), and closed the two
direct-dep findings (vitest, vite). Audit went from 11 vulnerabilities
(1 crit, 2 high, 8 mod) to 1 low (esbuild Windows-only).

**Pairs with:** `feedback_action_input_name_verification` — both
captured from the same hygiene PR; both are "verify the real shape
before estimating the fix" lessons applied to different surfaces.

name: feedback_npm_min_release_age_cooldown_blocks_updates
description: npm min-release-age/before cooldown silently pins global installs to an older version with a confusing "no matching version" error
type: feedback
---

# npm `min-release-age` Cooldown Silently Blocks Updates

When `npm install -g <pkg>@latest` refuses to move off an old version and errors with:

```
npm error notarget No matching version found for <pkg>@<newver> with a date before <DATE>
```

…the cause is npm's supply-chain **cooldown**: `min-release-age` (npm internally converts it to a `before=<now − age>` date). Any version published *after* that cutoff is invisible to the resolver, so `@latest` silently falls back to the newest version published *before* the cutoff. You end up "unable to update" with no obvious reason.

**Why:** Observed updating 9router — stuck at 0.5.12 while `npm view <pkg> dist-tags` clearly showed `latest: 0.5.18`. `npm config get before` returned a date that was ~7 days ago and whose seconds *recomputed on every run* (the tell that it's derived from `min-release-age`, not a static config). `npm install ... --before=<date>` then failed with `--min-release-age cannot be provided when using --before`, which named the real setting.

**How to apply:**
- Diagnose: `npm view <pkg> dist-tags` (real latest) vs installed `package.json` version. If they differ and installs won't advance, run `npm config get before` / `npm config get min-release-age`.
- Update anyway, scoped to one command (leaves the global safety policy intact):
  ```bash
  npm install -g <pkg>@<version> --min-release-age=0
  ```
- `--before` and `--min-release-age` are mutually exclusive — override the one that's actually set (usually `min-release-age`).

**Gotcha — source may be invisible:** `npm config get min-release-age` can return `null` and there may be **no line in `~/.npmrc` / global npmrc / env**, yet the cooldown still applies. That strongly suggests it's injected by the **Cursor agent shell sandbox** (protecting agent-run installs), not the user's own config. Verify in a *real interactive terminal*: if `npm config get before` returns `null` there, the cooldown is agent-only and the user can update normally without the flag.

**Never:**
- Assume `@latest` installs the dist-tag `latest` — the cooldown overrides it silently.
- Rip out a global `min-release-age`/`before` policy to force an install (it's real supply-chain protection). Prefer the per-command `--min-release-age=0` override.

**Confirmed approach:** `--min-release-age=0` unblocked the 9router 0.5.12 → 0.5.18 global upgrade in one shot.

name: feedback_npm_workspace_tsx_root_hoisting
description: tsx must be in root devDependencies for node --import tsx to work across workspaces
type: feedback
---

# npm Workspace tsx Root Hoisting

When using `node --test --import tsx` in npm workspaces, `tsx` must be declared in the **root** `package.json` devDependencies, not just in individual workspace packages.

**Why:** Node's `--import` flag resolves modules from the process's working directory (the repo root when running `npm test --workspace=X`), not from the workspace package's own `node_modules/`. Even when all 4 workspace packages declared `tsx: "^4.19.2"`, the supervisor tests failed with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` because `tsx` wasn't hoisted to `<root>/node_modules/tsx/`.

**How to apply:**
- When adding `--import <pkg>` to any workspace's test/build script, also add `<pkg>` to root devDependencies
- When debugging `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` in workspace test scripts, check root `node_modules/` first
- The `node_modules/.bin/tsc` symlink can also be dangling for the same reason — a symlink exists but points to a missing `node_modules/typescript/`

**Never:**
- Assume workspace-level devDependencies are sufficient for Node's `--import` resolution
- Assume a dangling symlink in `node_modules/.bin/` means the package was never installed — it may have been evicted by a later `npm install`

**Confirmed approach:** Adding `"tsx": "^4.19.2"` to root devDependencies fixed all 82 supervisor tests.

name: feedback_on_demand_buildkite_upstream_branch
description: On-demand kbn-evals Buildkite clones elastic/kibana — fork-only pushes fail checkout with pathspec error
type: feedback

updated: 2026-06-26
source: skill-dev 3686518a — C2 routing fix on-demand chain builds #130–#131

# On-Demand Evals — Push to `elastic/kibana`, Not Fork Only

The Buildkite pipeline `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals` is configured with `repository: elastic/kibana` (see `.buildkite/pipeline-resource-definitions/evals/kibana-evals-on-demand.yml`). Agents clone **upstream**, not the PR fork.

## Failure mode

Triggering with `-b fix/weekly-evals-matrix -c <sha>` when `<sha>` exists only on `patrykkopycinski/kibana`:

```
git checkout -f ab38a12fcf97
error: pathspec 'ab38a12fcf97' did not match any file(s) known to git
```

Build fails at pipeline upload / checkout — **before** Kibana build or eval runs.

## Verify before trigger

```bash
gh api repos/elastic/kibana/git/ref/heads/<branch> --jq '.object.sha[:12]'
gh api repos/patrykkopycinski/kibana/git/ref/heads/<branch> --jq '.object.sha[:12]'
# Must match the COMMIT you pass to bk build create
```

## Fix

After pushing to fork `origin`:

```bash
git push --no-verify upstream fix/weekly-evals-matrix
# upstream = git@github.com:elastic/kibana.git
```

Then trigger on-demand. Pre-push on upstream can take 30–60 min (scoped type_check); `--no-verify` is acceptable when scoped checks already passed locally.

**Why:** Builds #130–#131 failed Jun 25 2026; #132 passed only after upstream sync to `ab38a12`.

**Never:**
- Assume `git push origin` updates the ref Buildkite sees
- Retry the same `-c` SHA without checking `elastic/kibana` branch HEAD

**Confirmed approach:** Build #132 passed at `ab38a12` on upstream `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` ([build 132](https://buildkite.com/elastic/kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals/builds/132)).

name: feedback_on_demand_iteration_vs_weekly_matrix
description: On-demand is for validation iteration (1-2 suites); weekly is authoritative for generating a complete matrix — never babysit N serial on-demand suites to produce matrix data
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-01
source: session 3686518a — Build #152 on-demand chain vs Build #45 weekly
---

# On-Demand vs Weekly — Pick by Goal, Not by Default

**The rule:** Match the pipeline to the goal, not to the trigger script's default.

| Goal | Pipeline | Why |
|------|----------|-----|
| Validate a fix didn't regress (1-2 suites) | on-demand (`kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`) | Fast, single suite, no Slack noise |
| Generate a complete matrix for the merge gate | **weekly** (`kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals`) | Parallel fanout (all categories at once), exports scores to golden cluster that `generate-matrix` reads |
| Iterate on evaluator wiring before scores emit | on-demand | Serial is fine when you're fixing wiring, not collecting data |

**Why:** On-demand is **serial-only** (`skip_queued_branch_builds`) — 6 suites × ~30 min = 3+ hours of wall-clock, and its scores are NOT the authoritative source the merge gate reads. Weekly runs all ~25 jobs in parallel (dist build + ~30 min evals) and exports to the golden cluster.

**The mistake this prevents:** Defaulting to on-demand because the trigger script (`trigger-security-on-demand-evals.sh`) is the path of least resistance, then babysitting 5-6 serial suites for hours to "get a complete matrix" — when the weekly pipeline would have produced the authoritative data in ~50 min total.

**How to apply:**

1. After landing a hardening fix, trigger ONE on-demand run of the seed suite (e.g. `security-ai-rules`, which includes agent-builder) to confirm no regression. That's the iteration step.
2. If the goal is a matrix, immediately trigger the weekly pipeline: `bk build create -y -i -p elastic/kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals -b <branch> -c <SHA> -e KBN_EVALS=1 -e KBN_EVALS_WEEKLY=1`. The `-i` is required (weekly has branch filters).
3. Never babysit N>2 serial on-demand suites for matrix data.

**Confirmed approach:** Validated on Build #152 (on-demand, `security-ai-rules` passed — confirmed hardening fixes sound) immediately followed by Build #45 (weekly, 9/10 matrix jobs passed in ~50 min parallel). The on-demand run served its purpose; the weekly run produced the matrix.

name: feedback_on_demand_skip_queued_branch_builds
description: On-demand kbn-evals `skip_queued_branch_builds` skips parallel triggers on same branch — only the first build runs, rest are canceled
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-30
source: skill-dev 3686518a — 6 parallel on-demand triggers on fix/weekly-evals-matrix → 5 skipped, 1 passed
---

# On-Demand Evals — Serial Only on Same Branch

The Buildkite pipeline `elastic/kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals` is configured with `skip_queued_branch_builds: true`. Triggering multiple on-demand builds on the **same branch** in parallel does NOT fan out — only the **first** trigger runs; subsequent triggers are skipped/canceled.

## Failure mode (Jun 30 session)

Fired 6 on-demand triggers in parallel for the 6 matrix-critical security suites on `fix/weekly-evals-matrix`:

```
builds/130  skipped  (skip_queued_branch_builds)
builds/131  skipped  (skip_queued_branch_builds)
builds/132  skipped  (skip_queued_branch_builds)
builds/133  passed   (the one that ran)
builds/134  skipped
builds/135  skipped
```

Result: only 1 of 6 suites actually executed. The matrix remained sparse and looked like a wiring failure when it was a trigger-shape failure.

## Correct pattern — serial chain

Use `scripts/trigger-matrix-critical-on-demand.sh` (or `scripts/babysit-security-on-demand-evals.sh`) which:

1. Triggers one suite
2. Polls until terminal
3. Triggers the next suite
4. Single-instance lock at `matrix-output/.babysit.lock`

```bash
scripts/trigger-matrix-critical-on-demand.sh --commit <sha> --branch fix/weekly-evals-matrix
```

## When parallel IS safe

- **Different branches** — each branch has its own queue
- **Different pipelines** — `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals` vs `kibana-evals-weekly-llm-evals`
- **Sequential triggers with `skip_queued_branch_builds: false`** — not the default

## Why local iteration is faster

For matrix iteration, **local Scout** (`scripts/run-local-matrix-suite.sh`) is faster wall-clock than serial on-demand CI:

- Local: ~5 min per suite on Scout `:5620` with EDOT
- On-demand: ~20–40 min per suite (Kibana boot + seed + converse + judge + export)

Use on-demand only for the **final Opus-judge validation** on a known-good SHA, not for iterative wiring fixes.

## Never

- Fire N parallel `bk build create` calls against `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals` on the same branch
- Treat "5 skipped, 1 passed" as a wiring bug — it's the trigger shape
- Assume `skip_queued_branch_builds` is false because the docs don't mention it

## Confirmed approach

Jun 30 session: replaced parallel fanout with `trigger-matrix-critical-on-demand.sh` (serial). User preference: **prefer local Scout iteration** over sequential on-demand CI for wiring fixes.

name: opencode ask_question infinite loop
description: Opencode headless jobs loop on unavailable ask_question tool until upstream fixes no-op handling
type: feedback
---

# Opencode `ask_question` loop (headless treadmill jobs)

## Symptom

Opencode agent repeats the same turn: prints intent text, calls `ask_question` (mapped to `invalid` tool), receives *"Model tried to call unavailable tool 'ask_question'"*, then retries indefinitely. Jobs never complete and occupy fleet slots.

## Root cause

1. **Model reflex** — models in the `main` cascade reflexively call `ask_question`/`AskUserQuestion` for clarification despite the treadmill prompt constitution explicitly forbidding it.
2. **Opencode behavior** — as of 1.17.15, unavailable-tool errors are not treated as a graceful no-op; the session continues and the model retries the same tool (upstream: [anomalyco/opencode#28989](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/28989)).

## Mitigation

- Prefer `AO_AGENT_TYPE=claude-code` for headless treadmill dispatch until opencode upstream fixes the loop.
- `claude-code` may still attempt `ask_question` once but recovers and completes (verified Jul 12 2026).
- Prompt guardrail in treadmill constitution reduces frequency but does not fully prevent opencode loops.

name: feedback_openspec_usage
description: When to use OpenSpec workflow vs just implementing directly
type: feedback
---

# OpenSpec Usage Decision Framework

Use OpenSpec for complex, multi-file changes. For simple fixes, just implement directly.

## Decision Tree

```
Single file / trivial (typo, rename, docstring)?  → Implement directly
Multiple files but obvious, no arch decision?      → Implement directly
Architectural decision, new package, API change?   → Use OpenSpec
Cross-package (3+ packages) or coordination?       → Use OpenSpec
Requirements unclear or multiple approaches?       → Use OpenSpec
Complex feature with unknowns or iteration risk?   → Use OpenSpec
```

## Use OpenSpec When
- Adding new packages/modules or changing public APIs
- Changes span 3+ packages or involve breaking changes with migration path
- Requirements are vague or multiple approaches need evaluation
- Multi-step implementation with high risk of rework

## Skip OpenSpec When
- Typos, docstring updates, formatting, simple variable renames
- Obvious bug fix or adding a unit test for existing code
- Single-file changes with no architectural impact
- Mechanical/repetitive refactors with a clear pattern

## Commands
- `/openspec-new-change` — create change artifact
- `/openspec-ff-change` — fast-forward (change → plan → spec at once, when requirements are clear)
- `/openspec-apply-change` — implement from plan
- `/openspec-verify-change` — verify completeness

When the user asks to **stop** a host/task and explicitly says **don't recommend anything** (or equivalent: "just stop", "no next steps"), the response must:

1. Execute the stop action
2. Confirm result briefly
3. **Omit the next-steps list entirely** — no `(Recommended)` bait for auto-continue hooks

- **Normal completion:** still end with actionable next steps (draft-only for outbound comms)
- **Explicit stop + no recommendations:** terminal response only — do not append recovery/enrollment/RDP follow-ups the user already rejected

## Trigger phrases

- "stop … and don't recommend anything"
- "just stop it" / "stop, no next steps"
- User abort + explicit "don't recommend"

# Branding Leak + Live-Validation Workflow Discipline

Two related recurring patterns from debugging sessions in unrelated
project repos.

## Branding leak

Copy-pasted scaffolding (dot-dirs, env-var prefixes, doc/comment
mentions naming a personal orchestrator tool) can leak into an
unrelated project's committed files — docs, `.gitignore` comments,
env-var names — even though the repo has nothing to do with that
tool.

**Observed:** `example-mcp-app-security` (issue #46 session) had
orchestrator-branded paths/env-vars leak into
`docs/testing-shared-instance.md`, `scripts/e2e/env.ts`, and
`.gitignore` comments.

**How to apply:** before committing or opening a PR, scrub any
orchestrator-specific dot-dirs/env-var prefixes/doc mentions to
project-neutral names (e.g. rename orchestrator-prefixed env vars,
retarget orchestrator-branded home-dot-dirs to a project-scoped dir
like `~/.mcp-e2e/`). Local operator scaffolding directories belong in
`.gitignore`, not renamed into the tracked tree.

## Live-validation workflow

When validating a fix against a real cluster via a local git-ignored
credentials file (a `clusters.json`-style file):

- Sanity-check the file for copy-paste artifacts (e.g. a duplicated
  `https://https://` URL prefix) before assuming credentials are bad
- Keep the PR diff minimal: revert/don't commit scratch E2E harness
  code and debug-only env-flag instrumentation (e.g. a `*_DEBUG` flag)
  once the fix itself is proven live — only the durable prevention
  (fail-loud guards, schema-citation comments, CONTRIBUTING
  conventions) ships
- A "mismatch" observed during live validation can itself be a bug in
  the throwaway validation script (e.g. misreading a UI-resource-tool
  response wrapped in an envelope like `mcp_app_bootstrap` as flat
  JSON) rather than a product bug — verify the response-envelope shape
  before concluding the mismatch is real

# Pipeline Optimization Patterns (Benchmarker)

Three structural patterns that reliably speed up multi-stage pipelines without deep refactoring.

**Why:** Discovered while optimizing the elastic-llm-benchmarker pipeline. Each pattern saved 15-75% wall-clock time on its stage with minimal code complexity.

**How to apply:**

1. **Early termination gates** — compute eligibility once in the cheapest stage, carry the boolean downstream, gate expensive stages on it. Example: `stage2Eligible` computed in Stage 1 (5 min), gates Stage 2 CI evals (3h). Never re-derive the same decision in a later stage.

2. **Reduced sampling for gating vs. production** — when the first iteration of a benchmark loop is just a pass/fail gate, use a smaller sample (50 vs 200 prompts). The statistical signal for "clearly fails" needs far fewer datapoints than "measure precisely". Wire as `gatingSampleSize` option, only for `concurrency === 1 && levels.length > 1`.

3. **Pre-warm parallel resources during blocking operations** — if Stage N blocks for 10+ min (health check, benchmark loop), start Stage N+1 infrastructure in parallel (tunnel, SSH forward, ngrok auth). The key insight: check whether the pre-warmed resource actually needs Stage N's output, or only needs config-derived values (ports, hosts).

**Never:**
- Re-pull Docker images without digest comparison (10 min wasted per identical pull)
- Run expensive CI suites for models that fail basic performance thresholds
- Make sequential API calls for the same modelId within a single session (cache in-memory)
- Enqueue models that are already pending/running (add dedup guard)

**Confirmed approach:** All patterns validated — 899/899 tests passing, tsc clean. Combined estimated savings: ~60% reduction in wall-clock time for the happy path (from ~5h to ~2h per model).
