name: feedback_plugin_dist_rebuild_scoped_commit
description: npm run build --workspace mcp-server also rebuilds eval-cockpit MCP App HTML — restore it before staging to keep commits scoped
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-06-30
source: skill-dev 3686518a — commit 5ce6d14 staging caught unrelated mcp-app.html modification
---

# Plugin dist Rebuild — Scope to Changed Code

In `agent-builder-skill-dev-cursor-plugin`, `npm run build --workspace packages/mcp-server` runs **two** build pipelines:

1. `tsup` — compiles `src/` → `dist/*.js` (the MCP server bundle)
2. `vite` — compiles `dist/views/eval-cockpit/mcp-app.html` (the MCP App view)

When you only changed server source (e.g. `evaluations_kbn_client.ts`), the vite step still rewrites `mcp-app.html` with a new content hash in the inlined JS/CSS, producing an unrelated modification in `git status`.

## Failure mode

```bash
npm run build --workspace packages/mcp-server
git status --short packages/mcp-server/dist
# M packages/mcp-server/dist/views/eval-cockpit/mcp-app.html   ← unrelated noise
# M packages/mcp-server/dist/index.js
# ... real changes
```

If staged blindly with `git add packages/mcp-server/dist/`, the commit includes a spurious `mcp-app.html` diff that inflates the PR and confuses reviewers.

## Fix — restore before staging

```bash
# After build, before staging:
git checkout -- packages/mcp-server/dist/views/eval-cockpit/mcp-app.html
# Then stage the server bundle changes:
git add packages/mcp-server/dist/
```

Only restore the view when you **didn't** change view source. If you did change `src/views/eval-cockpit/*`, the HTML rebuild is legitimate and should be staged.

## How to apply

- After any `npm run build --workspace packages/mcp-server`, run `git status` and check whether `mcp-app.html` is modified
- If your change is server-only (utils, tools, routes), restore the HTML
- If your change touches the view, stage everything
- The CI bundle-verify check compares `dist/` against a fresh build, so a spurious HTML diff won't break CI — but it muddies the PR

## Never

- `git add packages/mcp-server/dist/` blindly after a workspace build without checking what changed
- Assume the HTML rebuild is always legitimate — it fires on every build regardless of what you touched

## Confirmed approach

Commit `5ce6d14` (gitCommit prefix fix) — restored `mcp-app.html` before staging; commit stayed scoped to the 4 src + dist bundle files. PR diff clean.

name: feedback_post_rebase_typecheck_stale_deps
description: Post-rebase Kibana type_check errors in unrelated plugins = stale node_modules (bootstrap needed); `| tail` masks the pipeline exit code
type: feedback
---

# Post-Rebase type_check Errors in Unrelated Plugins = Stale node_modules

After rebasing a Kibana branch onto a far-ahead `main` (hundreds of commits),
`node scripts/type_check` can report dozens of errors in plugins you never
touched. Before assuming your change broke something, check whether it's just
**stale `node_modules`** vs. main's dependency manifest.

**Why:** A forensics-skill demo branch (rebased ~900 commits) type-checked with
54 errors — all in `agent_builder` (`Cannot find module 'just-bash'`) and
`fleet` (`HttpsProxyAgent is not generic`, `Expected 1 arguments, but got 2`).
Zero errors touched the changed files. Root cause at the manifest boundary:
`package.json` declared `just-bash@3.0.1` (missing from `node_modules`) and
`http-proxy-agent@7.0.2` (installed `5.0.0` — v5 types aren't generic). CI
bootstraps fresh so it never sees these.

**How to apply:**
- Errors clustered in *unrelated* plugins + "Cannot find module X" / "type is
  not generic" / wrong-arg-count on a library type → suspect stale deps.
- Confirm: `rg '"<dep>"' package.json` (declared version) vs.
  `node -e "require('./node_modules/<dep>/package.json').version"` (installed)
  and `ls node_modules/<dep>` (present?).
- Fix locally with `yarn kbn bootstrap`; it's not blocking for CI (CI bootstraps).
- Don't file a "type error" against another team's plugin on this evidence.

**Gotcha — `| tail` hides the failure:** `node scripts/type_check … | tail -60`
in a backgrounded shell (a) buffers all output until EOF (no incremental
progress) and (b) reports `tail`'s exit code (0), not the pipeline's, when
`pipefail` is off — so a 54-error failure looked like `exit_code: 0`. Read the
body for `Found N errors` / `exited with code 2`, or set `set -o pipefail`.

**CRITICAL — "not in the error list" ≠ "clean":** When the stale-deps errors
end with `ERROR [tsc] exited with code 2 / Unable to build TS project refs`,
the project-ref build **bailed** — tsc never reached your package, so the
absence of *your* file from the reported errors proves nothing. In this session
I mis-read that as "forensics type-checks clean" and shipped a commit that CI's
Check Types then failed on with 1 real error (`Boolean(id)` doesn't narrow
`string | undefined`, so `Set<string>.has(id)` saw `undefined` — fix:
`typeof id === 'string' && …`). The only trustworthy local signal is:
**`yarn kbn bootstrap` first to clear the wall, THEN re-run the scoped
`node scripts/type_check --project <pkg>/tsconfig.json`** and require
`[tsc] exited with 0`. Never infer clean from a code-2 ref-build bail.

**Confirmed approach:** After bootstrap, scoped type_check exited 0 and eslint
on the changed file was clean — that is the real green.

name: feedback_pr_scope_audit_two_dot_vs_gh_files
description: To audit real PR scope, trust `gh pr view --json files` and two-dot `git diff base HEAD` — not three-dot `base...HEAD`, which shows stale-merge scope-creep when a branch merged an ahead-of-main integration branch
type: feedback
---

# PR Scope Audit: `gh pr view --json files` Is the Source of Truth

When pre-ship auditing a branch that has **merged an integration branch ahead
of `main`** (common on demo/feature branches), local `git diff` can wildly
misrepresent the PR's real scope. Use the right diff for the right question.

**Why:** Auditing PR #275840, `git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD` reported
**9880 files / +467k / -503k** (thousands of unrelated kbn-scout / cypress
churn). The actual PR was **12 files / +611 / -11**. The three-dot noise came
from the branch merging a main-ahead integration branch, so the merge-base is
old and the three-dot diff attributes everything since the fork point to HEAD.

**The three diffs and what each answers:**

| Command | Answers | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| `gh pr view <n> --json files --jq '.files[].path'` | **What GitHub will actually show/merge** | none — this is the source of truth |
| `git diff <base> HEAD -- <file>` (two-dot) | **Net change that lands on `<base>` on merge** | reveals stale-merge scope-creep that collapses to no-ops once base catches up |
| `git diff <base>...HEAD` (three-dot) | Everything on HEAD since the merge-base | **misleading** when merge-base is stale; do NOT use for scope audits |

**How to apply:**
1. `gh pr view <n> --json changedFiles,additions,deletions,files,mergeable`
   first — get the authoritative file set + `mergeable` state.
2. For each file GitHub lists, run **two-dot** `git diff <base> HEAD -- <file>`
   to see the real net change. Entries owned by *other* in-flight features
   (that both HEAD and eventual-base will carry) are scope-creep from the
   merge; flag them as "rebase to drop", but they are no-ops on merge and
   don't block `mergeable`.
3. Ignore three-dot totals for scope — they conflate main's own progress.

**Never:**
- Report a PR as "touches thousands of files / massively destructive" based
  on three-dot `base...HEAD` without checking `gh pr view --json files`.
- Try to "clean up" the two-dot scope-creep by reverting other teams' entries
  on a branch — the fix is a rebase onto current base, not manual reverts.

**Confirmed approach:** Used in the PR #275840 pre-ship audit — three-dot said
9880 files, GitHub said 12; the scope-creep (allow_lists / experimental_features
entries owned by streams/YARA/entity-analytics) was documented as a rebase
follow-up, not hand-reverted.

# Pre-Code Primitive-Verification Pass

Before writing the first line of a feature on a mature platform (Kibana,
Elastic stack, any large in-house framework), run an explicit pass that
takes **each "we will build X" claim in the plan** and greps for whether
the platform already ships X. Budget it as a real step, not an
afterthought — and expect the outcome to be *scope removed*, not just
"plan confirmed."

**Why:** On the Project Daybreak spike prep (2026-07-04) this pass fired
three times in a row, each time collapsing planned build work into "the
platform already does this":

1. **Persistence:** plan said "Proposal persists as an Agent Builder
   investigation conversation" (original D9). Reading the code: AB's store
   is chat-shaped `dynamic:false`, no such primitive → but the grep also
   surfaced the **platform Inbox + Workflows HITL rails**, turning the
   whole Proposal Queue from a *build* into an *integration*.
2. **Store + concurrency:** plan implied hand-rolled index creation + a
   custom CAS. `@kbn/storage-adapter` `StorageIndexAdapter` already gives
   `dynamic:'strict'` mappings, serverless-aware settings, additive schema
   versioning, and **OCC via `if_seq_no`/`if_primary_term`** — the exact
   "409 on stale" the plan wanted. Zero custom concurrency code.
3. **RBAC:** plan implied Daybreak read/decide privileges. The Inbox
   already splits `inbox_read`/`inbox_respond` by design, so the first
   three slices need **zero new privileges**; the Daybreak feature-privilege
   pair defers to the slice that has a Daybreak-owned route.

Net: commit 1 shrank from "plugin + index infra + CAS + feature/privileges"
to "plugin + flag + types + adapter store + space field + status gate."

**How to apply:**
- Make a checklist of every noun/verb in the plan that implies new code
  ("store", "queue", "audit log", "CAS", "privilege", "form renderer",
  "retry"). For each, grep the platform for an existing primitive BEFORE
  designing it. This is `anti-overengineering.mdc` gate 1 run pre-code, and
  `prose-vs-primitive.mdc` applied to your own plan.
- Read ONE full canonical consumer end-to-end (not just the abstraction) —
  it doubles as the copy-template for commit 1 (e.g. the AB conversation
  client gave both the OCC pattern and the 4-file module shape).
- Treat a plan decision that says "build/reuse X" as a **hypothesis until
  grepped.** The plan's own confidence is not evidence.
- Re-encode the shrink back into the plan artifacts (epic skeletons, ACs,
  spike POR) so the reduced scope is what actually dispatches.

**Never:**
- Start commit 1 with unverified "we'll build a store/queue/audit/CAS"
  language still in the plan.
- Assume a pre-code verification pass will only confirm scope — its
  highest-value outcome is deleting scope.

**Confirmed approach:** Three consecutive scope collapses in one Daybreak
pre-code session. Pairs with `anti-overengineering.mdc`,
`prose-vs-primitive.mdc`, `feedback_orchestrator_analysis_preflight`, and
`reference_agent_builder_conversation_persistence`.

name: Pre-PR Review Checklist — Viduni's Review Patterns
description: Before opening any Kibana PR, proactively fix issues that viduni94 consistently flags in code reviews to pass her review on first pass
type: feedback
---

Before opening any Kibana PR, run this checklist against all changes to preempt viduni94's review findings. She is thorough, detail-oriented, and focuses on code quality, consistency, type safety, testability, and architectural boundaries.

## 1. Naming & Consistency
- **Consistent casing everywhere**: No mixed snake_case/camelCase in the same interface or schema. Pick one and stick to it.
- **Consistent `data-test-subj` patterns**: All test subjects in the same plugin must follow one convention (camelCase or kebab-case, not both).
- **i18n key consistency**: All i18n translation keys in the same plugin must follow the same prefix pattern (e.g., `xpack.pluginName.featureName.componentName.label`).
- **Accurate function/variable names**: If a function does more than its name says (e.g., `logReindexFailures` but always throws), rename it to match behavior (`throwOnReindexFailures`).
- **File names match contents**: If a file contains more than just "feedback" schemas, rename it to something broader (e.g., `ai_insight_events.ts`).

## 2. Type Safety — No Shortcuts
- **Never use `any`**: Use `FlagsReader`, `ResponseError`, or the correct type from the library. She calls out every `any`.
- **No unnecessary type assertions (`as`)**: If you need `as`, you likely need a proper type instead.
- **No non-null assertions (`!`) without justification**: If a value can't be undefined at that point, restructure the code so TypeScript knows it (early return, guard, narrowing).
- **Schema types must match the actual data**: If an ES schema field should be `text`, don't put `keyword`. If `embedding` is in the TS type, it must be in the ES mapping.
- **Generic interfaces over `Record<string, any>`**: Especially for rule configs, payloads, and API params.

## 3. DRY — Eliminate Duplication
- **Extract shared constants**: If the same value appears in 2+ files, move it to a shared constants file.
- **Extract shared types**: If the same interface is duplicated across client/server/schemas, move to `common/types.ts`.
- **Extract shared helper functions**: If `reportTelemetryEvent` with try-catch appears in multiple places, extract to a reusable helper in an `analytics/index.ts` or similar.
- **Deduplicate logic**: Same connector resolution logic on server and client? Return it from the API response instead.
- **Shared profile/config code**: If the same parsing logic appears in `run.ts` and `start.ts`, extract to `profiles.ts`.

## 4. Error Handling — Be Explicit
- **Telemetry/analytics calls must be wrapped in try-catch**: Never let telemetry errors break the UI.
- **Don't swallow all errors**: When catching, filter by status code (404) — don't catch everything silently.
- **No `console.log` in error handlers**: Either use the logger properly (`logger.debug`, not `logger.info` for debug-level detail) or remove the log entirely.
- **Log level matters**: `info` = operator should act on it. `debug` = developer detail. She corrects misused log levels.

## 5. Test Coverage — She Expects Tests
- **New components need unit tests**: She explicitly asks "Can you add unit tests for this component?" for every non-trivial component.
- **Tests must cover the actual behavior**: Not just that something renders — test clicks, callbacks, error states, disabled states.
- **Test telemetry events fire correctly**: `reportEvent` called with correct type and payload.
- **Test error paths**: Not just happy paths.
- **Use existing test helpers**: Don't reinvent — use `invokeChatCompleteWithFunctionRequest` and similar helpers that already exist.
- **Move tests to correct locations**: Tests should live alongside the code they test, in the expected test directory.

## 6. Architectural Boundaries — Generic Packages Stay Generic
- **Domain-specific logic does NOT belong in generic packages**: If `kbn-es-snapshot-loader` is generic, don't add Streams-specific parent-stream fallback logic. Let the caller own domain-specific behavior.
- **No side effects in utility functions**: A generic `reindex` function should not create data streams or cluster resources. The caller should ensure prerequisites.
- **Prefer callbacks/hooks for extensibility**: Instead of hardcoding domain logic, accept `beforeReindex` hooks or `shouldUseInlineScript` predicates.
- **Respect package boundaries**: Don't create tight coupling via 4-level deep relative imports across feature domains.

## 7. Edge Cases & Robustness
- **Guard against empty/missing optional data**: If `connectorInfo` can be undefined, handle that explicitly — don't just add `?.` everywhere.
- **Widening queries is risky**: Removing a `type` filter from a query "widens the query and could match unintended documents." Always justify.
- **Race conditions**: Concurrent operations on shared resources (write indices, temp indices) — at minimum document the limitation.
- **Pagination**: If fetching with `perPage: 1000`, what happens when there are 1001+ items?
- **Stale TODOs**: Convert TODOs to tracked GitHub issues, not inline comments.

## 8. Documentation & Readability
- **README must match the code**: If the code has 4 steps, don't say "three-step" in the README.
- **Default values in docs must match code**: If the help text says default is X but code uses Y, fix the discrepancy.
- **Add comments for non-obvious decisions**: Why one version uses `ctx._id = null` and another doesn't.
- **Describe blocks should be descriptive**: `describe('Alert AI Insights')` for every scenario → use `describe(\`Alert AI Insights — ${scenario.id}\`)`.

## 9. Feature Completeness
- **Track ALL relevant events**: If tracking feedback and conversations, also track the initial generation/usage event.
- **Track failures too**: Not just success — report error events with available context.
- **Return useful data from APIs**: If the client needs connector info for telemetry, return it from the server response instead of duplicating resolution logic.

**Why:** Viduni (viduni94) is a thorough reviewer who catches consistency issues, type safety gaps, missing tests, architectural boundary violations, and DRY violations. She provides concrete code suggestions. By running this checklist before opening the PR, we avoid 2-3 review round-trips.

**How to apply:** After Garrett's deep review pass, run this checklist specifically. Focus on: (1) grep for `any` types, (2) check all names/casing for consistency, (3) verify test coverage for all new components/functions, (4) ensure no domain-specific logic leaked into generic packages, (5) check all error handlers are specific not broad, (6) verify no duplicated types/constants/helpers.

# Proactive Memory Capture (Don't Wait to Be Asked)

`capture-learnings` is the agent's responsibility, not a user command. Run it autonomously after the first successful end-to-end verification of a hard-won pattern — do not wait for the user to say "capture".

**Why:** During the endpoint-response-actions demo setup, the launchd persistence pattern was discovered through multi-turn debugging (nohup fails → tmux works briefly → tmux dies → launchd is the answer). This took ~2 hours of real debugging across sessions. When the pattern finally worked, I declared victory and stopped. The user had to explicitly say "capture, but you should be capturing it automatically" — meaning I made them spend a turn asking for something I should have done unprompted.

The cost of not capturing: next session, I'd re-derive the same launchd vs tmux distinction from scratch. Multi-turn debugging insights are the highest-value things to persist — they're precisely what can't be re-derived quickly.

**How to apply:**

1. **Trigger**: after a non-trivial task reaches its first working end-to-end state (smoke test passes, demo flow runs, API returns expected result).
2. **Threshold**: if the task took >2 hours of debugging, involved >3 failed approaches, or surfaced a non-obvious environmental constraint — capture immediately.
3. **Don't ask**: just do it. The user can always say "skip" if they disagree.
4. **Categorize yourself**: skip the skill's reflection questions; you know what was surprising/mistaken/validated. Write the memory directly.
5. **Write 2-4 memories per hard task**: the solution pattern, the gotcha that blocked you, the reference setup. One memory rarely captures everything.

**Never:**
- Wait for "capture" / "save this" / "remember" — those prompts are fallbacks, not the primary trigger.
- Declare a hard task "done" without either capturing or explicitly noting "skipping capture because <reason>".
- Capture trivia (one-line fixes, single-file edits) — the bar is "would future-me spend >10 min rediscovering this?"
- Ask the reflection questions when the user has already implied urgency ("keep going", "do it automatically") — just write.

**The rule of thumb:** if I spent >30 minutes debugging something and finally got it working, that's a capture event. Full stop.

**Pairs with:**
- `capture-learnings` skill — this memory is the meta-instruction on when to invoke it.
- The stop-hook automation (`CAPTURE_LEARNING_MIN_TURNS=8`, `CAPTURE_LEARNING_MIN_MINUTES=60`) — that fires the *followup* prompt; this memory is about firing *before* the followup is needed.
- `self-verify-everywhere.mdc` rule — verification completes the task; capture completes the learning.

**Confirmed approach:** User explicitly said "you should be capturing it automatically" after I declared the demo done without capturing. The correction is the rule.

name: feedback_readonly_dryrun_for_date_gated_sweeps
description: Validate a date-gated or side-effectful sweep (e.g. DLQ auto-re-queue) by mirroring its exact selection logic read-only — proves behavior today without waiting for the window or triggering real side effects
type: feedback

source: Validating the benchmarker DLQ auto-re-queue sweep without waiting for 07-06 or triggering GPU benchmarks (Jul 4 2026)

# Read-only dry-run to validate date-gated / side-effectful sweeps

When asked to "confirm X auto-happens on <future date>" for a sweep whose real run **writes state with side effects** (a DLQ re-queue flips `failed → pending`, which the live daemon then picks up and starts a real GPU benchmark), don't wait for the date and don't trigger the live write. Instead write a **read-only script that mirrors the production selection logic exactly** and forecasts.

**Pattern:**
1. Import the *same* query + classifier the production sweep uses (`findFailedEntries` → `classifyFailure` → `.slice(cap)`), never a reimplementation — a divergent copy would validate the wrong thing.
2. Run it with the real "now" (shows 0 today, confirming the date-gate) AND with a simulated future timestamp (`now(future) - windowDays`) to forecast exactly which entries the future tick will select, capped.
3. Write **nothing** to ES. Print the classification breakdown + the forecast list. Label output `READ-ONLY`.

**Why:** The user's `#3` was "confirm the aging failures auto-re-queue on 07-06." Running the live sweep with a shortened window WOULD have re-queued them today and triggered surprise GPU benchmarks (real cost, `maxConcurrentRuns=1` contention). The dry-run proved the mechanism on the real 58 failed entries — 38 retriable / 20 quarantined, 0 eligible today, exactly 5 aging `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` transient failures eligible on the 07-06 tick — with zero side effects.

**Classifier nuance worth remembering:** in `failure-classifier.ts`, `"smoke test failed at tier health|inference"` → `transient-infra` (retriable), but `"...at tier tool-calling"` → `unknown` (quarantined). Tool-calling is a **model-capability** signal, not transient infra, so it's deliberately NOT auto-retried. "Kibana CI eval failed" → `model-arch` (quarantined). First matching rule wins; model-arch/eval patterns are checked before broad transient patterns.

**Never:**
- "Validate" a side-effectful sweep by actually running it with a tweaked window on the live cluster — you trigger the side effect you were only trying to preview.
- Reimplement the selection logic in the dry-run — import the production functions so the forecast can't drift from reality.

**Confirmed approach:** `scripts/dryrun-dlq-sweep.ts` imports `QueueService.findFailedEntries` + `classifyFailure` and forecasts read-only; matched the sweep's `sweepDlq` selection 1:1.

# Feedback — Reconcile Drift After a Decision Revision (sweep ALL docs, not just the one in hand)

**Type:** feedback
**Created:** 2026-07-04
**Context:** Project Daybreak planning workspace (`~/Projects/daybreak-planning`)

## The pattern

When a settled decision is **revised** (not newly created), the revision
almost never lands in every doc that references the old decision on the
first pass. The doc you happen to be editing gets updated; sibling PRDs,
capability specs, and object-model tables that cite the *same* decision
keep the stale framing — and the inconsistency can survive across
multiple sessions because nothing forces a doc-wide sweep.

## Concrete instance

**D9** was revised from "Proposal persists as an Agent Builder
*investigation conversation* (container)" → "Proposal persists in a
**Daybreak-owned `StorageIndexAdapter` store**, reviewed via the platform
**Inbox**; the AB conversation is only the linked chat thread."

The revision was applied to `slice-acceptance-criteria.md` and the
`alignment-board.html` data arrays **two sessions before** anyone noticed
that `prd-capabilities/platform-primitives.md` still described the *old*
D9 in **7 places** (Current-System table, Scope-of-Change, Object Model,
Investigation section, Dependencies table). The board rendered both the
new D9 (in `DECISIONS`) and the old D9 (in the embedded PRD) at the same
time — internally contradictory.

## The rule

When you revise a decision (D-record, ADR, settled shape):

1. **Grep the whole doc set for the decision id AND its old framing**
   before declaring the revision done — not just the id (`D9`) but the
   *concept* it replaced (`investigation conversation`, `container`,
   `as container`). The id often survives correctly while the prose
   around it stays stale.
2. **Sweep every doc that cites it**, not only the one you opened.
   Capability PRDs, object-model tables, dependency tables, and
   rendered dashboards each hold their own copy of the framing.
3. **Reconcile rendered/derived artifacts too** — a build-time board
   that embeds N markdown docs can show the new decision (hand-authored
   data array) and the old decision (embedded PRD) simultaneously.
   Rebuild after the sweep.
4. **Bump any "settled per D1–DN" legends** so the new id is in-range.

## Why it matters

A revised decision that only half-lands is worse than an un-revised one:
the reader can't tell which framing is authoritative, and a downstream
consumer (an epic, a treadmill plan, a reviewer) may anchor on the stale
copy. The cost of the sweep is one grep + a handful of edits; the cost of
skipping it is a contradiction that ships.

## Pairs with

- `feedback_verify_next_step_claims.md` — verify before asserting a gap
  still exists; same "grep first" discipline, applied to next-steps.
- `feedback_pre_code_primitive_verification.md` — grep plan claims
  against real platform code before building; the pre-code analogue.
- `prose-vs-primitive.mdc` / `apply-pr-feedback.mdc` pre-flight — both
  encode "scan the whole artifact set, don't trust the input scope."

name: feedback_response_actions_authz_reassert_gap
description: Agent Builder response-action tools (isolate/scan/etc) must re-assert per-action authz checks — isAutomated:true on the internal client only checks license, not action-level permissions like canIsolateHost
type: feedback
confidence: strong

source: kibana#272111 (endpoint-response-actions skill, Slice 1) — github-actions bot review + live Cloud QA regression caught by Raquel's demo handoff verification
---

# Response-action skills must re-assert authz, not trust `isAutomated: true`

Agent Builder response-action tools (`isolate`, `unisolate`, `scan`, `get_running_processes`, etc.) call into `getInternalResponseActionsClient` with `isAutomated: true`. That flag **only checks license entitlement** — it does **not** check per-action authorization (`canIsolateHost`, `canWriteScanOperations`, etc.) that a normal user-driven request would go through.

## Verified gap (kibana#272111)
Without an explicit re-assertion of the per-action authz checks inside the agent-dispatched tool handler, **any chat user could isolate/scan arbitrary hosts** regardless of their actual RBAC permissions — caught via github-actions bot review, not by existing tests.

## Related live regression (same PR)
`getInternalResponseActionsClient` was later found hardcoding `isAutomated: true` for **every** caller, including AI-Agent calls. This silently made `isolate`/`unisolate`/`scan`/`get_running_processes` **no-op** ("action not supported") on the deployed Cloud QA environment. CI didn't catch it — it was only caught because the operator (Raquel) re-verified the demo end-to-end on the actual deployment before signing off on the handoff.

## How to apply
- Any new Agent Builder tool that wraps an "internal"/"automated" client bypass **must independently re-check the specific action-level RBAC permission** the equivalent human-driven UI path would enforce — don't rely on the internal client's own gating.
- For response-action / write-capable skills, **always re-verify live on the actual deployed environment** (not just CI green) before declaring a PM/stakeholder demo handoff ready — CI green does not guarantee the deployed behavior matches, especially for internal-client bypass paths.

**Never:** treat `isAutomated: true` (or similar internal-bypass flags) as sufficient authorization for a write/high-risk action dispatched by an agent — it is a license gate, not a permission gate.

## Addendum: the gap can hide inside a shared service, not just the tool handler

A variant of this same anti-pattern (documented as anti-pattern #59 in
`agent-builder-skill-dev-cursor-plugin`'s `knowledge/anti-patterns.md`, lesson
landed via PR #123, branch `lesson/generate-insight-authz-gap-59`) was found in
`automatic_troubleshooting`'s `generateInsightTool`: the tool handler itself
looked fine, but it called a **shared service constructed with
`asInternalUser`**, and that shared service was missing the
`canWriteWorkflowInsights` check a human-driven request would go through. The
authz check was never in the tool handler at all — it needed to live in the
shared service, or be re-asserted at the tool boundary before delegating.

A follow-up audit swept `osquery`, `cases` (`manage_cases.ts`), and
`alerting_v2` for the same pattern and found no further violations: `cases`
and `alerting_v2` only mutate request-scoped/in-conversation state, and
`osquery` has no Agent Builder tools registered yet.

**Lesson generalized:** when auditing for this anti-pattern, don't stop at the
tool handler — trace every call into a shared service built with an internal/
automated user context and verify the per-action RBAC check exists somewhere
on that path, not just "somewhere in the tool file".

# SCS Docker Indexer Environment Variable Conventions

The SCS Docker image (`ghcr.io/elastic/semantic-code-search:main`) uses different env var names than treadmill. Three attempts failed before finding the right combination.

**Why:** Three distinct naming conventions coexist:
- **Treadmill:** `TREADMILL_ES_URL`, `TREADMILL_ES_API_KEY`
- **SCS Docker:** `ELASTICSEARCH_ENDPOINT`, `ELASTICSEARCH_API_KEY`, `SCS_ELASTICSEARCH_INFERENCE_ID`
- **Treadmill semantic:** `TREADMILL_ES_SEMANTIC_INFERENCE_ID` (for jina-v5 migration)

**Working invocation:**
```bash
docker run --rm \
  -e ELASTICSEARCH_ENDPOINT="$TREADMILL_ES_URL" \
  -e ELASTICSEARCH_API_KEY="$TREADMILL_ES_API_KEY" \
  -e SCS_ELASTICSEARCH_INFERENCE_ID=".elser-2-elastic" \
  -v "/path/to/repo:/repos/reponame:ro" \
  "$SCS_DOCKER_IMAGE" \
  index /repos/reponame:index-name --repository owner/repo
```

**How to apply:**
- Always check `docker run <image> index --help` before invoking a Docker CLI tool for the first time
- Map `TREADMILL_ES_URL` → `ELASTICSEARCH_ENDPOINT` (not `ELASTICSEARCH_URL`)
- For Elastic Cloud, use `.elser-2-elastic` as the inference ID
- The treadmill doctor's SCS index check hint has the correct remediation steps

**Never:**
- Use `ELASTICSEARCH_URL` with SCS Docker (it requires `ELASTICSEARCH_ENDPOINT` or `ELASTICSEARCH_CLOUD_ID`)
- Omit `SCS_ELASTICSEARCH_INFERENCE_ID` when semantic_text is enabled (the indexer errors immediately)

**Confirmed approach:** Fourth attempt succeeded after correcting all three env vars. Full Kibana index (106k files) completed successfully.

name: feedback_serverless_es_index_settings_rejected
description: Elastic Serverless rejects number_of_shards/number_of_replicas on index create with illegal_argument_exception — ensureIndices must retry mappings-only
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-04
source: Adding benchmarker-vm-cost index to elastic-llm-benchmarker on serverless ES (Jul 4 2026)
---

# Serverless ES rejects index `settings` — create mappings-only

On **Elastic Serverless**, `indices.create({ index, settings: { number_of_shards, number_of_replicas }, mappings })` fails with:

```
illegal_argument_exception: Settings [index.number_of_replicas,index.number_of_shards]
are not available when running in serverless mode
```

Serverless manages sharding/replication itself and forbids these settings at create time. A mapping that carries a `settings` block works on a self-managed cluster but breaks the moment the same code runs against serverless.

**Why:** Adding the `benchmarker-vm-cost` index worked in unit tests (mocked) and would have worked on a local ES, but `scripts/smoke-maintenance.ts` against the live serverless cluster threw `illegal_argument_exception` on first create. Unit tests do not catch this — the mock accepts any create payload.

**How to apply:**
- Make `ensureIndices` **serverless-safe**: attempt create with `settings` first; on `illegal_argument_exception` (the serverless tell), retry the same create with **mappings only** (drop the `settings` key). Propagate any *other* error (e.g. `resource_already_exists_exception`).
- Add a unit test that asserts the mappings-only retry fires on `illegal_argument_exception` AND that non-settings errors propagate — mocks otherwise hide the whole failure mode.

**Never:**
- Assume an `indices.create` payload that passes locally will work on serverless — shard/replica settings are the common landmine.
- Rely on unit tests alone for index creation — run a live smoke against the actual (serverless) cluster.

**Confirmed approach:** `es-index-mappings.ts` `ensureIndices` now try/catches and retries mappings-only; validated end-to-end by `scripts/smoke-maintenance.ts` writing a real `benchmarker-vm-cost` snapshot to the serverless cluster.

name: feedback_shared_kbn_evals_change_validation
description: How to author + validate a change to the shared @kbn/evals scorer/evaluators (draft PR, on-demand-from-commit eval gate, no local stack needed)

# Validating a Shared @kbn/evals Change (scorer / evaluator)

A change to the shared `@kbn/evals` correctness scorer or evaluators touches
EVERY suite's scores, so it must ship as a **draft PR pending the runtime eval
gate** — never rushed into a wide feature branch (e.g. the matrix branch).
Author + validate it like this.

**Authoring (worktree + push):**
- Cut a dedicated worktree off `upstream/main` (`git worktree add -b <branch> <path> upstream/main`) — don't pollute an unrelated feature branch, don't switch a live dev-cell worktree's branch.
- A fresh worktree is NOT bootstrapped, so the pre-push `type_check` hook fails ("failed to push … type_check failed: …/tsconfig.json") because it can't resolve `@kbn/*` types. Push with `--no-verify` — CI runs the authoritative type_check/jest. This matches the documented wide-branch practice.
- Verify pure-function scorer changes with a standalone `node -e` script (geometric-mean math etc.) AND add a jest test — you can't run jest locally in an unbootstrapped worktree, but the standalone check + unit test are the proportionate local proof; CI runs jest.
- Open the PR from the FORK (`origin`), marked **draft**, body stating exactly which gate is incomplete (verify-bug-fix rule allows draft-when-gate-pending).

**The empirical eval gate = on-demand CI from the SAME commit (no local stack):**
- The `@kbn/evals` runner (Playwright) runs from the **checked-out source at the COMMIT**, not from the Kibana server dist. So an on-demand build from your commit exercises your scorer change even though the change isn't in the server dist — no local Scout stack, bootstrap, or connectors needed.
- **on-demand clones `elastic/kibana` upstream** → the commit must be pushed to `upstream` (not just the fork) before triggering.
- Trigger: `BRANCH=<b> COMMIT=<sha> bash scripts/trigger-security-on-demand-evals.sh --suite <suite-id>` (plugin repo). `--suite` mode triggers one build and exits (no blocking wait); default subject = Sonnet via `matrix-eval-config.sh`; pipeline `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`, serial (`skip_queued_branch_builds`).
- Compare the new build's per-evaluator failing counts + the affected cell median against the baseline build the artifact was diagnosed on (apples-to-apples: same suite + same subject model).

**Cheaper first check (prefer when possible):** re-score EXISTING golden verdicts
offline — the `Factuality` score docs persist `metadata.correctnessAnalysis`
(see `feedback_factuality_groundedness_split_scoring_artifact.md`). Zero new runs.

**Why:** shared-scorer changes are high-blast-radius; unit tests prove the
function but not the empirical distribution on real judge verdicts. The
on-demand-from-commit run is the sanctioned, tooled gate and needs no local
runtime — a common misconception is that eval validation requires a booted
local stack.

**Never:**
- Merge a shared `@kbn/evals` scorer change on unit tests alone (needs the eval gate).
- Trigger on-demand with the commit only on the fork (on-demand clones upstream → "commit not found").
- Assume you must boot a local Scout stack to exercise an eval-runner change — on-demand from the commit does it.
- Land the change on a wide/unrelated branch (e.g. the 90+-commit matrix branch).

**Confirmed approach:** used for `elastic/kibana#276331` (soften Factuality
`NOT_IN_GROUND_TRUTH`), 2026-07-05 — draft PR from fork, branch pushed to
upstream, on-demand alerts-rag build #248 (Sonnet) triggered from the fix commit
`bf202829` as the live gate.

name: feedback_shared_tool_description_boundary_self_defeat
description: A "do not use this tool if skill X is available" boundary clause added to a default/global agent tool's description is self-defeating for any skill that itself legitimately calls that same tool internally — audit the full skill catalog for self-referencing dependents before shipping a global tool-description edit as a misrouting fix
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-11
source: kibana-worktrees-weekly-evals-matrix transcript 39a259da — RFC #18054 Option C (generate_esql tool-description boundary) blast-radius audit
---

# Global tool-description boundary clauses can be self-defeating

## The pattern

Kibana's Agent Builder `find-security-rules` skill was getting misrouted to
the generic `generateEsql`/`executeEsql` default tools (in
`defaultAgentToolIds`, spliced into every conversation regardless of skill)
instead of loading the dedicated skill. The cheapest fix (Option C, 5 lines)
added a boundary clause to `generate_esql`'s own description:

> "Do NOT use this tool if a more specific skill is available for the
> request — prefer loading that skill first."

This fixed the tested case (`find-security-rules`, 0.83 distractor score,
matching the more invasive Option B at 1/30th the diff). But it was **never
tested against the other ~39 registered skills** until the user explicitly
asked "make sure to check non-security skills as well... full evidence
before opening a PR."

## Why the fix is self-defeating for some skills

A full-catalog audit (security + platform-core + observability, 3 parallel
subagent sweeps) found that several skills — `streams-investigation-management`,
`observability.rca`, `visualization-creation`, `discover-data-analysis` —
**intentionally grant themselves `generate_esql`/`execute_esql` and call it
as a documented step in their own workflow** (e.g. as a fallback for data
the skill's dedicated tools don't cover).

The boundary clause has no runtime concept of "before vs. after this skill
was loaded" — a tool description is static, global text the model reads on
every turn. Once one of these skills IS loaded and its own instructions say
"now call `generate_esql`," the tool's own description is simultaneously
telling the model not to use it. The fix that solves misrouting-into-the-tool
can silently break routing-through-the-tool for its own legitimate dependents.

## The generalizable rule

Before editing the description of any **shared/default tool** (one spliced
into every skill's candidate list, not scoped to a single skill) as a
misrouting fix:

1. **Enumerate every skill that can reach the tool** — grep the full skill
   catalog (`defineSkillType(`/`getRegistryTools()`) across every solution
   area (security, platform-core, observability, etc.), not just the one
   where the bug was reported. A single-area audit undercounts blast radius.
2. **Flag self-referencing dependents** — any skill whose OWN documented
   workflow calls the tool you're about to restrict. These are the
   highest-risk candidates for the fix backfiring, distinct from skills that
   are merely at risk of losing routing TO them.
3. **Word the boundary clause to be turn/state-scoped, not domain-scoped**
   if possible (e.g. "...if a more specific skill has not yet been loaded
   for this request" rather than "if a more specific skill is available") —
   though even this only partially helps since the model still can't
   verify "has been loaded" from a static description alone; empirical
   verification (regression evals for the self-referencing skills) is
   still required.
4. **Add regression eval cases for self-referencing skills** asserting they
   still successfully call the shared tool internally after loading —
   this is the test that would have caught the conflict before it shipped.

## Never

- Ship a global default-tool-description edit as a misrouting fix based on
  evidence from only the one skill/area where the bug was reported.
- Assume a fix that clears one skill's distractor eval is done — a
  tool shared across skills needs the full-catalog audit before it's
  considered evidence-complete for a PR.

name: feedback_silent_data_drop_debugging
description: When an exporter "succeeds" but data never lands and the sink logs nothing, positive-control the receiver and verify host port ownership BEFORE blaming the application
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-03
source: EDD-cell OTLP trace drop — days of wrong Kibana-side theories, real cause was a dual-runtime port hijack (Jul 3 2026)
---

# Debugging silent data drops (exporter says OK, sink stays empty, no errors anywhere)

When client-side telemetry/data "exports successfully" but never appears at the destination, AND the
destination service logs nothing and shows no errors, STOP theorizing about the application. This
symptom triad — success on send, silence at the sink, zero errors — almost always means the traffic
is **not reaching the service you're inspecting** (wrong endpoint, shadowed port, wrong runtime),
not that the app failed to send.

**Why:** On the m1max EDD cell, `traces-*` stayed empty for a long investigation. I chased app-side
theories in order — EDOT processor dropping spans, a multi-version `@opentelemetry` SDK realm
mismatch, a missing `xpack.agentBuilder.tracing.send_to_self` config — and each was plausible and
each was WRONG. The real cause: a rogue `kibana-edot-collector` container in the **OrbStack** docker
runtime had grabbed host `:4318` before the intended **colima** collector, so every OTLP export
(Kibana, eval worker, and a raw probe) hit the wrong collector and never reached the colima ES the
eval read. Every "smoking gun" I found was circumstantial noise.

**How to apply — do these FIRST, before reading app source:**
1. **Positive-control the receiver with a REAL client.** Emit one datum with the real
   exporter/SDK (NOT hand-rolled curl JSON — a fake OTLP JSON POST returns HTTP 200 `partialSuccess`
   yet parses 0 spans and proves nothing). If the real emit still doesn't land, the sink/receiver
   or the path is at fault, not the app.
2. **Verify host port ownership**: `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`. Confirm the OWNING process
   is the one you think (e.g. colima's Lima mux `...colima/ssh.sock`, not `OrbStack Helper`).
3. **Enumerate ALL container runtimes**: `docker context ls`, then `docker --context <each> ps` for
   duplicate/rogue containers publishing the same host port. A container in the "other" runtime can
   silently steal a published port from the one your `DOCKER_CONTEXT`/default points at.
4. Only after 1–3 come back clean should you dive into app dependency/version/config theories.

**Never:**
- Trust a 2xx / "flushed successfully" from an exporter as proof of delivery.
- Trust hand-crafted OTLP/JSON POSTs to prove a receiver works — use the real client SDK.
- Conclude "the app's SDK/telemetry is broken" while the collector logs show it never received data.
- Assume one docker runtime when two are installed (colima + OrbStack / Docker Desktop).

**Confirmed approach:** The real-OTLP-probe + `lsof` port-ownership check localized the fault in
minutes after days of wrong app-side theories; removing the rogue OrbStack collector fixed it and
`traces-*` populated immediately. Incident detail: `feedback_kibana_otlp_trace_export_not_delivering`.

name: feedback_skill_dev_pr_admin_merge

# skill-dev Plugin PR Merge — Use `--admin`

The `elastic/agent-builder-skill-dev-cursor-plugin` repository has **branch protection** on `main` that blocks PR merges even when all required CI checks pass, unless:

1. A review approval is on the PR (none required for solo operator), OR
2. The merger uses administrator privileges (`--admin` flag)

## Failure mode

```bash
gh pr merge 76 --squash --delete-branch
# X Pull request ... is not mergeable: the base branch policy prohibits the merge.
# To have the pull request merged after all requirements have been met, add the `--auto` flag.
# To use administrator privileges to immediately merge the pull request, add the `--admin` flag.

gh pr merge 76 --squash --delete-branch --auto
# GraphQL: Auto merge is not allowed for this repository (enablePullRequestAutoMerge)
```

Auto-merge is disabled at the repo level. The only path for a solo operator with all CI green is admin merge.

## Fix

```bash
gh pr merge <N> --squash --delete-branch --admin
```

This works because the operator has admin/maintainer rights on the repo. The `--admin` flag bypasses the branch protection rule.

## When NOT to use --admin

- Other contributors have requested changes (respect the review)
- CI is not fully green (the admin flag bypasses required checks too)
- The PR is a draft

## Never

- Assume auto-merge works — it's disabled at the repo level
- Force-push to `main` instead of merging through the PR
- Leave the feature branch un-deleted (`--delete-branch` cleans up)

## Confirmed approach

PR #76 (gitCommit prefix fix): all 8 CI checks passed, `--squash` blocked by policy, `--auto` rejected (repo-level disable), `--admin` succeeded → `c28e0fe` merged, branch deleted (Jun 30 2026).

# Skill-scoped inline tools — don't promote to registry as a workaround

When an eval shows the LLM picks the wrong tool (e.g. `platform.core.search` instead of
`security.find_rules`), promoting the skill-scoped inline tool to the **global registry**
is NOT an acceptable fix — even if it makes the tool available to the default agent's router.

## Why not

- As more teams ship Agent Builder skills, registry-wide promotion **does not scale**: every
  promotion pollutes the global tool surface available to every agent and every skill.
- It's a per-skill escape hatch, not a systemic fix. The user reverted a promote-to-registry
  patch (`b1f372b` → reverted manually Jul 9 2026) for exactly this reason.
- The right scalable solution is **per-skill tool scoping** — subtractive filtering
  (`SkillDefinition.excludeRegistryToolIds` + `ToolManager.removeTools` / `selectTools` filter),
  or an RFC for per-skill tool surface control — not global registration.

## Decision rule

| Situation | Wrong fix | Right fix |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| LLM picks `platform.core.*` over skill's inline tool | Promote inline tool to registry | Per-skill tool scoping / subtractive filter |
| Skill tools not visible to default agent's router | Promote to registry | Fix routing + registration; eval against default agent (natural routing) |
| Need a tool shared across multiple skills | Inline per-skill (default) | Registry ONLY if genuinely cross-skill platform primitive |

- Routing/L1 failures → see `feedback_eval_routing_registration_before_content.md` (registration before content)
- Evals must use default agent (natural routing) → same file, "Evals must exercise natural routing" section
- Plugin CLAUDE.md anti-pattern: "Default inline + API until CLI lands" / "do not register new tools for MCP/3P access"

name: feedback_sqlite_wal_pragma_readonly_guard
description: "db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL') on a readonly SQLite connection throws SQLITE_READONLY unless the DB is already WAL; guard it in readonly workers"
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-01
source: "treadmill DbWorkerPool 2026-07-01: readonly reader workers set WAL unconditionally; a freshly-seeded temp DB (rollback-journal mode) crashed the worker with SQLITE_READONLY, surfacing as a silent hang in the smoke test"
---

# Guard `journal_mode = WAL` on Readonly SQLite Connections

`journal_mode = WAL` is a **write** to the SQLite database file header.
On a connection opened `{ readonly: true }` it throws `SQLITE_READONLY`
UNLESS the DB file is already in WAL mode (readonly connections inherit
the mode from the file header, so the pragma becomes a no-op that
succeeds).

**Why:** In a reader-pool architecture, the main **writer** process
opens the DB writable and sets WAL once — that persists in the file
header. Readonly worker connections then inherit WAL. But if a worker
opens a DB that was never put in WAL (a freshly-created file, a
rollback-journal DB, or a test fixture seeded without WAL), the
unconditional `db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL')` crashes the worker at
boot before it serves a single query.

**How to apply:**
```ts
const db = new Database(dbPath, { readonly: true });
try {
  db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL'); // no-op when already WAL (inherited)
} catch {
  // readonly + non-WAL DB: the writer process owns setting WAL
}
db.pragma(`busy_timeout = ${ms}`);
```
- The writer process (not the reader) is responsible for setting WAL.
- Smoke tests that seed a temp DB must either (a) set WAL on the seed
  connection before closing, or (b) rely on the worker's guarded pragma
  above. Prefer (b) — it matches production where the DB may be in any
  mode.

**Never:**
- Set `journal_mode = WAL` unconditionally on a readonly connection.
- Assume a worker crash with an empty error message is a code-load
  failure — dump `JSON.stringify(err, Object.getOwnPropertyNames(err))`;
  this one surfaced as `{"code":"SQLITE_READONLY"}` with no `message`.

**Confirmed approach:** Validated by `db-worker-pool.smoke.test.ts`
which boots a real readonly pool against a seeded temp DB (PR #135).

name: feedback_static_contract_tests_over_render_tests
description: When vitest is node-only (no jsdom, .ts-only glob), verify "core unchanged + addition is conditional" via static source-parsing tests rather than standing up React Testing Library
type: feedback
---

# Static-contract tests beat render tests under node-only vitest

When the vitest config is `environment: 'node'` with a `.ts`-only
include glob (no `.tsx`, no jsdom), a React component render test would
require adding `@testing-library/react`, jsdom env, and a `.tsx` glob —
meaningful infra churn for a preservation check. The ponytail-compliant
alternative is a **static-contract test**: read the source file as a
string and assert on the contract the components depend on.

**Why:** Hit during T-4.7 of the EDD capsule initiative. The eval-cockpit
gained a Timeline panel + iteration-history hook (Phase 3); T-4.7 needed
to prove the CORE was unchanged (poll loop still calls original tools,
addition is conditional, no removals). Standing up jsdom for one
preservation suite was disproportionate. Instead, 10 static-contract
assertions on the source strings pinned the contract exactly:
- poll hook still calls `name: 'eval-cockpit-health'` (etc.) — proves
  the 6 original tools are still wired.
- poll hook does NOT contain `iteration-history` — proves the addition
  wasn't sneak into the poll loop.
- `useIterationHistory` matches exactly one `name: '...'` — proves the
  hook calls exactly one tool.
- App.tsx matches `params.skill_id ? (<TimelinePanel` — proves the
  panel is conditionally gated.

**How to apply:**
- Reach for static-contract tests when the goal is "prove the shape
  didn't change" rather than "prove the component renders correctly".
- Read the source with `readFileSync` and assert with `toMatch(/regex/)`.
- For tool-call sites, match `name: '<tool-id>'` literals.
- For conditional gates, match the actual JSX syntax — **read the source
  first**, don't assume (`&&` vs `? (` tripped me up once).
- Pair with a deferred visual smoke (Playwright/Canvas) for the
  rendering claim — the contract test covers shape, the smoke covers pixels.

**Never:**
- Don't use static-contract tests to verify runtime behavior (does the
  hook actually fetch?) — that needs execution, not parsing.
- Don't write a static-contract test against syntax you assumed; always
  grep the real source for the gate syntax first.

**Trade-off:** static-contract tests are refactoring-fragile (rename a
tool and the regex breaks) — but that's the POINT for preservation: a
rename SHOULD fail the preservation test so the change is reviewed.

**Confirmed approach:** Validated 2026-07-01 in
`packages/mcp-server/src/views/eval-cockpit/__tests__/preservation.test.ts`
(10/10 green, caught a real regex/syntax mismatch during authoring).

source: elastic-llm-benchmarker commit 000ff68 — single "fetch failed" at 22:50 marked Qwen run permanently failed and killed vLLM mid-suite after Stage 1 had cleanly passed
---

# Transient Network Errors Must Not Tear Down Pipelines

When a long-running pipeline polls an external API (Buildkite, GitHub, ES), a single transient network error (`fetch failed`, `ECONNRESET`, `ETIMEDOUT`) must **never** cascade into tearing down the entire pipeline. The poll loop should retry transient errors and only treat persistent failures as terminal.

## Failure mode

```typescript
// BROKEN — observed in scheduler.ts before fix
const pollPromise = pollWeeklyMatrix()
  .then(persist)
  .catch(async (err) => {
    // Any error → mark queue failed, tear down vLLM
    await queue.updateStatus('failed', err.message)
    await releaseInfrastructure()  // kills vLLM container
  })
```

A 1-second network blip at 22:50 UTC:
1. `fetch failed` thrown from `createBuild`
2. Propagated up through `pollWeeklyMatrix`
3. `.catch()` marked queue entry `failed`
4. Next `.then()` released infrastructure — killed the vLLM container
5. Buildkite build that was already running had no vLLM to reach
6. Run abandoned after Stage 1 had cleanly passed

**7 seconds of network blip wasted 90 minutes of pipeline work.**

## Correct patterns

### 1. Retry transient errors in the fetch wrapper

```typescript
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4
const BASE_DELAY_MS = 2_000

for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
  try {
    return await fetch(url, opts)
  } catch (err) {
    const transient = /fetch failed|ECONNRESET|ETIMEDOUT|ENOTFOUND/.test(msg) ||
                      /[45]\d\d/.test(status)
    if (!transient || attempt === MAX_ATTEMPTS) throw err
    await sleep(BASE_DELAY_MS * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
  }
}
```

### 2. Distinguish transient from fatal in the orchestrator

```typescript
.catch(async (err) => {
  const transient = /fetch failed|ECONNRESET|ETIMEDOUT/.test(err.message)
  if (transient) {
    // Log, leave queue active, leave infra running for resume
    logger.error('transient error — NOT tearing down', err)
    return  // queue stays active, vLLM stays up
  }
  await queue.updateStatus('failed', err.message)
})
```

### 3. Never let an empty error message propagate as "success-ish"

`ConnectionError` from `@elastic/elasticsearch` can have `message: ''` when the underlying socket died. Catch this explicitly — `if (!err.message) err.message = 'connection closed'` — or the queue entry will be saved with an empty error_message, which is invisible in dashboards.

## Why this matters

Pipeline orchestration code is the highest-leverage place for resilience. A bug here wastes **every downstream minute** — model loading (5-10 min), benchmark runs (5-10 min), Buildkite cold builds (15 min), eval phases (10-30 min). A single transient error that tears down the pipeline can cost 60-90 minutes per occurrence.

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **Catching everything uniformly** — treats transient and fatal the same way
- **Tearing down infra on any error** — destroys hours of work for a 1-second blip
- **Empty error messages** — make failures invisible in dashboards and logs
- **No retry in fetch calls** — one blip propagates immediately
- **`.catch()` blocks that always call `updateStatus('failed')`** — never consider that the error might be transient

## Confirmed approach

Commit `000ff68` (elastic-llm-benchmarker, Jul 1 2026):
- `buildkite-eval-trigger.ts`: `createBuild` retries transient errors 4× with exp backoff
- `scheduler.ts`: detached poll `.catch()` distinguishes transient from fatal; transient errors leave queue active and infra running
- `health-check.ts`: `isContainerRunning` retries SSH 3× before declaring crash

Same network blip that killed the run before now retries silently and the pipeline continues.

## Pairs with

- `verify-bug-fix-claims-before-pr.mdc` — verify the fix actually catches the blip before declaring it solved
- `proactive-anticipation.mdc` — pre-mortem should include "what if the network blips?"
- `feedback_host_saturation_kills_orbstack` — host-side cause of similar symptoms

Node `fetch()` **follows redirects by default**. A probe expecting `GET /legacy → 301` will see **200** from the final `/` page unless redirect handling is disabled.

**Never:**
- Assert 301/302 on a URL that redirects without disabling fetch redirect following
- Assume smoke failure on legacy route means redirect is broken — check probe config first

**Confirmed approach:** PR #112 — probe passes with `manualRedirect: true`; live `curl -I` confirms 301 → `/`.

- `autoAdvanceEpics()` G1–G5 in `orchestrator-loop.ts` — epic → feature → plan → activate → promote
- `docs/prd-proactive-work-intelligence.md` — problem statement; engine exists, **auto-execute safe subset** is the remaining 80%

Opt-in auto-execute for deterministic next-actions (`retry_job`, `activate_plan`, `advance_feature`) with allowlist env gate — **shipped PRs [#87](https://github.com/patrykkopycinski/patryks-treadmill/pull/87)–[#90](https://github.com/patrykkopycinski/patryks-treadmill/pull/90): retry + activate + PR apply-feedback (manual Do it / `*` auto); MCP `treadmill_execute_next_action`; ephemeral janitor + session reconciler — see `reference_treadmill_command_center_autonomy.md`**

|---|---|

| 150 agent templates / org chart | Single-operator SDLC; Paperclip-style hierarchy is overhead |

name: feedback_treadmill_daemon_cold_start
description: Treadmill daemon cold start — ES backfill, skill scan, and awaited boot work must not block :3100
type: feedback
confidence: proven
---

# Treadmill Daemon Cold Start — Don't Block :3100

The launchd daemon runs `tsx src/main.ts`; HTTP binds at the **end** of `create()` in `index.ts` (~1300 lines after DB open). Anything **awaited** or **synchronous** on that path delays `startApiServer` and makes `treadmill status` / health probes fail for minutes.

**Why:** 2026-06 session debugging "daemon not running" after brain-hands/aquifer merges. Root causes were stacked: (1) partial ES drift re-enqueued 1305 tasks every boot, (2) `scanProjectSkills(TREADMILL_PROJECT_ROOT)` walked the entire Kibana tree synchronously, (3) awaited ES warm-up/provision on the critical path. Watchdog killed the process when `/api/health/lite` timed out while the event loop was blocked.

## Validated fixes (merged PR #86 → `main`)

| Issue | Fix | File |
|-------|-----|------|
| Partial ES drift → full re-backfill | `shouldRunFullBackfill`: only when `esCount === 0` | `es-backfill.ts` |
| Backfill blocks boot | `void runBackfillIfNeeded(...)` — never `await` on boot path | `index.ts` |
| ES warm-up/provision | Whole ES boot block in `setImmediate(() => void (async () => { ... })())` | `index.ts` |
| Kibana skill scan | Scan **`daemonSourceRepo`** (treadmill), not `TREADMILL_PROJECT_ROOT` (kibana); inside deferred ES block | `index.ts` |

## Non-obvious JS trap

`void (async () => { scanProjectSkills(root); await index... })()` does **not** defer the walk — the async function runs synchronously until its first `await`. A 100k-dir tree walk still blocks the event loop before `create()` reaches `startApiServer`. Use **`setImmediate`** (or a worker) to defer sync work off the boot turn.

## How to apply

- Daemon won't answer on `:3100` after bounce → tail `~/Library/Logs/patryks-treadmill/ao-orchestrator.stdout.log`; look for last line before stall (often post-`es-issue-indexer` or mid-`create()`).
- Poll **`/api/health/lite`** (not full `/api/health`) during boot; allow **60–90s** before declaring failure.
- **Do not** `launchctl kickstart -k` in a tight loop during warm-up — each kill resets boot and looks like a hang.
- After source edits on `main`: rebuild orchestrator, single bounce, poll until green (see `rebuild-and-restart.mdc`).
- On-demand full-repo skill scan remains via `POST /api/scan-skills` — don't walk kibana at boot.

## Never

- `await runBackfillIfNeeded()` before HTTP listener
- `scanProjectSkills(process.env.TREADMILL_PROJECT_ROOT)` on boot when project root is a large monorepo
- Assume `void async IIFE` defers synchronous CPU/IO work
- Declare daemon dead after <60s of `health=000` during intentional restart

**Confirmed approach:** Reproduced on live daemon; fixes verified with health 200, `boot.phase=ready`, PR [#86](https://github.com/patrykkopycinski/patryks-treadmill/pull/86) merged.

name: feedback_treadmill_main_checkout_ship_when_daemon_hot
description: "Shipping a logic change to the treadmill MAIN checkout while the daemon runs from it — self-updater refuses dirty/diverged trees, so feat-branch-in-place + reconcile after merge"
type: feedback
---

# Shipping to the treadmill main checkout while the daemon is hot

When a logic change has to land on the treadmill **main checkout** (not a
sibling worktree) — typically because the change is already live and validated
in the working tree and a dependency was just decommissioned — the naive PR
flow can leave the running daemon on stale code. Use this flow.

## The self-updater is protective, not eager

`self-updater.ts` **refuses to touch the working tree** in three cases:
- **Dirty tree** — "Skipping update: working tree has uncommitted changes."
- **Local HEAD ahead** of `origin/main` — "nothing to fast-forward."
- **Diverged** from `origin/main` — "refusing to fast-forward (manual reconcile
  required)."

So while the main checkout has uncommitted changes (or is on a feat branch), the
self-updater is inert and cannot clobber the daemon's live code. That's the lever
that makes the safe flow work.

**Visibility (Jul 2026):** `treadmill status` and `/api/health.selfUpdate.blockedByDirtyTree`
now surface when a dirty tree blocks update (includes the ahead remote SHA). **`bounded-retry`**
stops infinite rebuild loops when a self-update build fails.

**Split concurrent WIP:** when the main checkout accumulates uncommitted changes spanning
independent concerns (e.g. a routing fix + unrelated diagnostics), ship separate `feat/` PRs —
bundling makes the tree stay dirty longer and blocks self-update until all WIP is reverted or merged.

## Safe flow

1. Commit the changes to a **feat branch created in the main checkout**
   (`git checkout -b feat/<slug>` — the working-tree changes come along).
2. `git push -u origin feat/<slug>` → `gh pr create` → `gh pr merge --auto
   --squash`. The daemon keeps running the correct code the whole time (its
   in-memory build is unaffected by the branch pointer).
3. After the PR auto-merges, **reconcile the main checkout**: `git checkout main
   && git pull --ff-only origin main`. Working tree now equals merged main;
   self-updater sees clean+current and stays a no-op.
4. Rebuild `dist/` + bounce (`treadmill stop`; launchd respawns) so the daemon
   picks up the merged build.

**Never** revert the main working tree to pre-change code (e.g. `git checkout
main` without the reconcile pull) while a decommissioned dependency is down — a
daemon restart in that window would run stale code pointing at the dead backend.

## Related gotcha (don't misdiagnose)

`/api/health` is slow (~2.9s) only on its **30s cache-miss** — it does
synchronous SQLite there (`safeCount` x6 + two `GROUP BY` over the sessions
table). That sync work momentarily stalls the event loop, so a **concurrent**
request to another endpoint (e.g. `/api/subsystem-health`, which is actually
in-memory and 2-37ms) can time out transiently, especially during post-bounce
warm-up. It is NOT a bug in the other route. `/api/health` is already mitigated
by the 30s cache + a no-DB `/api/health/lite` for the watchdog. Re-measure
before "fixing" a route that timed out once.

**Confirmed approach:** validated 2026-07-01 shipping the Firecrawl->CRW
migration (PR #136) — daemon stayed on live CRW code through the PR, reconciled
clean to `9642134`.

# PR Auto-Merge Branch Lifecycle

When a PR auto-merges via squash, GitHub deletes the remote branch (if `delete_branch_on_merge` is enabled). If you then `git push` the same branch name again, GitHub creates a NEW remote branch — but the auto-merge setting from the old PR is gone.

**Why:** Discovered when PR #120 auto-merged the first commit, then subsequent commits were pushed to the same branch name expecting auto-merge to still be active. A new PR (#121) had to be created manually.

**How to apply:**
- After `treadmill ship-feature` squash-merges a PR, the feature branch is deleted
- If you need to push more commits, either create a new branch or re-enable auto-merge on the new PR
- Check `gh pr view --json state` before pushing to a branch that was recently squash-merged
- If `allow_auto_merge` is false at the repo level, `gh pr merge --auto` silently fails

**Never:**
- Assume auto-merge persists after a branch is deleted and re-created
- Push to a branch name that was already squash-merged without checking PR state first

**Confirmed approach:** Observed across PRs #120/#121 in patryks-treadmill (Jun 29, 2026).

name: feedback_treadmill_remote_dispatch_race_and_autopause
description: Two compounding treadmill bugs made healthy remote Hermes dispatch on attached-worktree hosts look like "agent exited non-zero" — shared status-file race + auto-pause never resetting on reactivate
type: feedback
---

# Treadmill Remote Dispatch: Shared-Status-File Race + Auto-Pause Never Resets

Diagnosed and fixed 2026-07-08 during Daybreak S0 spike on `kibana-i9`
(attached-worktree, `daybreak-spike`). Fixed in `patryks-treadmill`
commit `209cdda`.

## Symptom

Automated `treadmill` dispatch of Hermes tasks to `kibana-i9` failed in
~1 second with `agent exited non-zero`, on every attempt, for every task.
Manually SSHing in and running the exact same `hermes-wrapper.py`
invocation by hand worked fine and completed successfully after ~23
minutes. The gap between "manual = works" and "automated = fails
instantly" was the tell that this was a monitoring/plumbing bug, not an
agent/model bug.

## Root cause 1 — shared status-file race

On **attached-worktree** hosts (single persistent worktree reused across
every job/attempt, as opposed to per-job ephemeral worktrees), every
attempt wrote its terminal status to the literal path `.ao/status.json`.
Retries and orphaned prior attempts share the SAME worktree. A stale
attempt's orphaned bash wrapper trailer
(`agentCmd && echo running || echo failed > status.json`) could still be
alive as a zombie process minutes after a NEW attempt started — and its
`echo failed > status.json` clobbered the fresh attempt's `running`
status within ~1s, long before the real (and eventually successful)
agent process finished.

**Fix:** attempt-scope the status path —
`status-<jobId>-attempt-<n>.json` — mirroring the existing
`agentStreamPath` convention. A stale writer then lands on a dead path
nothing reads instead of clobbering the live one. Local (per-job
worktree) dispatch never needed this: per-job worktrees + pid-file/pgroup
reaping in `launchLocalAgent` already prevent the analogous race there.
Orphan cleanup (`buildOrphanCleanupCommand` in `fleet-manager.ts`) was
also extended to `pkill -f` the attempt-scoped filename pattern so the
stale wrapper shells get reaped, not just the child processes.

## Root cause 2 — auto-pause never resets on reactivate

`countConsecutiveFailures()` walked a plan's **entire** job history
newest-first until hitting a `passed` job. A plan that already had ≥5
historical failures (all caused by bug #1 above) and no passed job since
would immediately re-trip `AUTO_PAUSE_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES` on the very
next orchestrator tick after `treadmill_activate_plan` — before a single
new job under the reactivated run could even dispatch. The operator had
no way to signal "give this a fresh run."

**Fix:** stamp `plans.activated_at` on every `activate()` call (schema
v65) and scope the failure count to jobs `created_at >= activated_at`.
"Activate" now means "fresh run", matching operator intent.

## Diagnostic pattern worth repeating

When automated dispatch fails near-instantly but the identical manual
invocation succeeds, suspect the **monitoring/status-reporting layer**
before the agent/model. Check:
1. Is the status file path shared across retries/attempts on the same
   host, or attempt-scoped?
2. Are there orphaned processes from prior attempts still alive and
   writing to files the current monitor reads?
3. After a fix + reactivate, does the plan immediately re-pause with
   zero new jobs dispatched? If so, the failure-streak counter is
   probably not scoped to the reactivation.

**Confirmed approach:** validated live — job `b7535412` ran 10+ minutes
without premature failure (previously ~1s), single clean process tree on
`kibana-i9`, correct attempt-scoped status file, plan stayed `active`
through reactivation with `activatedAt` correctly stamped.

name: feedback_treadmill_remote_static_gate_unscoped
description: patryks-treadmill remote static-gate execution (runStaticViaExecutor) had zero scoping logic and always ran full-repo checks even for zero-diff tasks — separate code path from the already-scoped local gate; PR #159 fixed mechanical-checks skip, PR #163 ported scoping to the remote path
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-11
source: treadmill scope-mechanical-checks-and-boot-reconcile + scope-remote-static-gate worktrees (Jul 10 2026)
---

# Remote static gate was never scoped — two separate implementations, only one got fixed first

A plan (`daybreak-s1-pd4b-component-alignment`, dispatched to `worker-m1max`) stalled ~11h on phase 3/5. Root-caused as a compounding issue, not a single cause:

1. **Real concurrency was 1, not 3** — `fleet.json` had `worker-m1max.maxConcurrentJobs: 3`, but the plan used a single `attachedWorktree`. Tasks pinned to an attached worktree reuse it verbatim and never consult per-plan concurrency, so all ~40 tasks ran strictly serially on 1 job slot even with headroom for 3. True parallelism on an attached-worktree host needs a **second registered `attachedWorktree` entry**, not `AO_INTRA_PLAN_PARALLEL`.
2. **Heavy fixed cost per task** — each static gate (Kibana jest/typecheck/build on the remote host) alone took ~270-380s, even for trivial verification tasks (`grep -q ...`, `test -f ...`).
3. Job reclamation desync (`reclaimStranded`/`reapBudgetExhaustedPending`) left stale `in_progress` `plan_tasks` when a job was reaped via the SQL-only path without propagating the failure back — needed manual reconciliation.

## The scoping bug (two separate implementations)

- `runStaticGate` (`gates/static.ts`) — the **local** path — already scopes `typecheck`/`lint`/`jest-changed`/`i18n-check` correctly to changed files and skips cleanly on empty diff.
- **But** `mechanical-checks.ts`'s three checks (`dead-code` 480s budget, `schema-coverage` 480s, `self-review` 300s) are appended unconditionally to every gate run and have **no branch in `buildScopedCommand`** — their names don't match the four scoped checks, so they always fall through to `return baseCommand` and run full-repo, every time, even with zero source changes. Fix (PR #159): skip these three when `changedFiles.length === 0`.
- **Separately**, `runStaticViaExecutor` (`unified-pipeline.ts`) — the **remote/fleet** execution path (used by this very plan) — had **zero scoping logic at all**, always running the raw full `check.command` regardless of diff size. This is a distinct implementation from the local `runStaticGate`, not a shared one — fixing the local path (PR #159) did nothing for remote-dispatched plans. Fix (PR #163): port `getChangedFilesViaExecutor` + `buildScopedCommandViaExecutor` into the remote path, mirroring the local scoping logic.

**Lesson: when a scoping/gating fix lands for one execution path (local), always check whether a parallel remote/fleet-dispatch implementation exists and needs the identical fix — treadmill's local vs. remote code paths are NOT shared by default.**

## Other fix in the same arc

Boot-time reclaim propagation: `plan_tasks` were not updated synchronously at daemon boot when `reclaimStranded`/`reapBudgetExhaustedPending` gave up on a stranded job, leaving stale `in_progress` rows. Fixed as part of PR #159 alongside a guard against overwriting tasks that aren't actually `in_progress` (mirrors the reconciler's State-C precondition — a task could already be `completed`/`skipped` if a zombie job finishes late).

Both PR #159 and PR #163 were manually squash-merged (`gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`) since this private repo has no auto-merge available.

Treadmill has two distinct subsystem patterns:

- Periodic scanners get their own dashboard fragments and API endpoints instead
- The distinction is: health trackers answer "is this subsystem working?" (failure ratio); scanners answer "what did this subsystem find?" (findings list)

description: patryks-treadmill npm test slowness root cause was a global git-secrets hook template (init.templatedir in ~/.gitconfig) firing pre-commit/commit-msg hooks on every test-created git repo/commit, not per-test git init overhead — fixed by clearing GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR in the spawned test process env
type: feedback
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-11
source: patryks-treadmill transcript f3c315c9 — npm test performance investigation
---

# Treadmill test-suite slowness: global git-secrets hook template, not git init

## Symptom
`npm test` in `patryks-treadmill` was slow, with per-commit operations inside test-created
git repos taking much longer than expected. The initial suspect was `git init` overhead
for each test fixture repo.

## Root cause
Not `git init` cost — a global `git-secrets` hook template (`init.templatedir` set in the
operator's `~/.gitconfig`) auto-installs `pre-commit`/`commit-msg`/`prepare-commit-msg`
hooks into **every** repo these tests create (since `git init`/`git clone` copies the
template dir's hooks into the new repo's `.git/hooks/`). Those hooks then fire on **every**
test-created commit. Measured tax: ~4x per commit (10 commits: 5.0s with hooks vs 1.2s
without).

## Fix (shipped, PR #167, merged)
One line in `packages/orchestrator/scripts/run-tests.mjs` — clear `GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR` in the
spawned test process's env before running the suite. This is local-only (CI has no such
global git config) and requires zero test-file changes.

## Generalizable lesson
When a test suite's git operations (init/clone/commit) are unexpectedly slow, check the
operator's global `~/.gitconfig` for `init.templatedir` or other global hook installers
before assuming the slowness is intrinsic to the git operation itself — a global hook
template silently taxes every repo the tests create, and the effect scales with commit
count, not repo count.

# Treadmill Memory Golden Validation — Lightweight Endpoint

Operator golden recall (hand-tuned hybrid queries, rank-1 `source_id` match) can be refreshed **without** reindex/backfill — when ES is idle.

**Why:** Jun 2026 post-merge ops — `treadmill memory-reindex --validate --daemon` blocked the orchestrator event loop for minutes; watchdog killed the process (health probe timeouts, launchd exit `-9`). Dashboard `goldenValidation` stayed `null` because the in-memory cache resets on every daemon death. Shipped [#104](https://github.com/patrykkopycinski/patryks-treadmill/pull/104): `POST /api/memory/validate-golden` runs the same probes as reindex's `--validate` tail (~10s when ES idle, read-only ES hybrid + optional Jina rerank).

**Caveat (Jun 29):** Immediately after `memory-reindex --validate`, the same endpoint can hang 120s+ under ES load. Prefer trusting reindex's `golden=N/N` line or use `--max-time 300`. See `feedback_validate_golden_curl_post_reindex_hang.md`.

## How to apply

```bash
# After daemon bounce or when Memory dashboard badge is empty
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3100/api/memory/validate-golden

# Verify
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3100/api/memory/stats | jq .goldenValidation
# expect passCount/required 5/5 when TREADMILL_ES_RERANK_INFERENCE_ID is set
```

- **`goldenValidation` is process memory only** — not persisted to SQLite. Every cold start needs one `validate-golden` call (or a full reindex with `--validate`, which is heavier).
- **Rerank mode:** follows `TREADMILL_ES_RERANK_INFERENCE_ID` in secrets; when set, search mode is `hybrid+rerank`.
- **Cold start:** allow 60–90s before health is green; if restart script polls only 60s, a second kickstart after warm-up may be needed (see `feedback_treadmill_daemon_cold_start.md`).

## Never

- Run `memory-reindex --validate --daemon` on a **live** launchd daemon when you only need the golden badge refreshed
- Assume `/api/memory/stats` shows golden results after rebuild without calling `validate-golden` or reindex-validate
- Tight-loop `launchctl kickstart -k` during warm-up — each kill resets boot and clears `lastGoldenValidation`

**Confirmed approach:** 2026-06-26 — 5/5 hybrid+rerank after `validate-golden`; stats + Memory view populated; endpoint merged in PR #104.
