# Model-family hardware fit for the benchmarker GPU VM (2×A100-80GB, 160GB total)

Research from a Jul 9 2026 discovery-queue-refill session, checking GLM-4.x and
Kimi K2 family candidates against the benchmarker's actual GPU VM before enqueueing.

## GLM family
- **GLM-4.5-Air** (110B total) — ~220GB in bf16, does NOT fit 160GB VRAM without
  quantization. The AWQ-FP16Mix variant was already benchmarked (in the completed-6
  pool) — don't re-enqueue as "fresh".
- **GLM-4.6-AWQ** (`QuantTrio/GLM-4.6-AWQ`, 360B total params, AWQ-quantized, ~50GB
  on disk) — **OOMs on 160GB total VRAM even quantized**. Confirmed live: deployed,
  started benchmarking, OOM'd. 360B is simply too large for this hardware regardless
  of quantization scheme — don't re-attempt without a bigger VM.
- **GLM-4.7-Flash** — needs bleeding-edge `transformers` (5.0+, git-main) that the
  standard `vllm/vllm-openai:latest` image doesn't ship yet (confirmed via an open
  vLLM GitHub issue). Skip until vLLM's base image catches up — don't force a custom
  image build for one model family.
- **GLM-5.2** exists on HF but wasn't evaluated for size/quant fit this session.
- Parser: `glm4_moe`/`glm45` — proven vLLM tool-call parser support for the family
  when the weights DO fit.

## Kimi K2 family
- **Dead end for this hardware across the board.** Even the "small" variant
  (`Kimi-K2-Instruct-0905`) is ~1TB in safetensors total — no quantization scheme
  gets that under 160GB.
- Newer generations (K2.5, K2.6, K2.7-Code) switched to a new architecture class
  (`KimiK25ForConditionalGeneration` / `kimi_k25`) that isn't in vLLM's supported
  parser list at all — a second, independent blocker beyond raw size.
- Per `prefer-latest-model-per-family`, `Kimi-K2-Instruct` itself is now 2+
  generations stale (K2.5/K2.6/K2.7-Code exist) — don't enqueue the old generation
  even if a smaller quant surfaces.
- **Do not add bare `kimi` to `fallbackSearchProbes`** — it over-matches unrelated/
  unsupported generations. If a future Kimi variant ever fits, target it by exact id.

## Devstral (viable, current-gen)
- `mistralai/Devstral-Small-2-24B-Instruct-2512` — 24B dense (~48GB bf16), comfortably
  fits 160GB, newest Devstral/Mistral-Small generation. This is the reliable
  "European rotation" candidate per `feedback_benchmarker_model_queue_floor.md`.

## Nemotron (checked, skipped)
- `nvidia/Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B-Instruct-HF` is stale — Nemotron is on gen 3 now
  (`NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16`, far higher downloads). But gen 3's
  architecture is `nemotron_h`, which is **not in vLLM's supported architecture
  list** — skipped rather than risk a guaranteed Stage 1 failure. Don't enqueue
  either the stale gen-1 or the unsupported gen-3 until vLLM adds `nemotron_h`.

## Discovery capability-registry invariant

Discovery and candidate filtering must derive supported architecture and tool-call-parser capability from one canonical registry. Independent hand-maintained whitelists drifted: supported `mistral3` and `glm4_moe` models were rejected before configuration fetch, while GLM-4.5 naming lacked `-Instruct` despite having a verified `glm45` parser. Parser capability must outrank weak name/tag heuristics.

## Practical takeaway
Before enqueueing a new model family on this GPU VM, check (in order): (1) total
param count vs 160GB even at 4-bit/AWQ (a rough floor is ~300B total params is
already too large regardless of quant), (2) whether the HF `config.json`
architecture string is in vLLM's supported list, (3) whether the tool-call parser
for that family is proven (hermes/mistral/llama3_json/glm45/etc.), (4) whether the
vLLM base image's `transformers` version is new enough for very recent releases.

# Benchmarker Model-Selection Gate Gaps (evidence-backed)

Four OSS models fully evaluated end-to-end (Stage 1 vLLM perf → Stage 2 3× Kibana
security suites → Stage 3 EIS) on 2×A100-80GB. Real results (reports regenerated
with the fixed per-suite scoring logic):

| Model | Arch | Total / Active | Ctx native | triage/rag/esql | Verdict | Throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| deepreinforce-ai/Ornith-1.0-35B | Qwen3.5-MoE (256e·8/tok) | ~35B / ~3B | 262144 | ✅✅✅ | **support/high** | 757 tps |
| Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | Qwen3.5-MoE (256e·8/tok) | ~35B / ~3B | 262144 | ❌❌✅ | investigate | 1089 tps |
| Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct | Qwen2 dense | 14B / 14B | 32768 | ❌✅✅ | investigate | 1144 tps |
| Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | Qwen2 dense | 7B / 7B | 32768 | ❌✅✅ | investigate | 1886 tps |

Report: `docs/model-benchmark-comparison-and-agent-builder-gaps.html`.

## The central proof: static gates cannot predict agentic quality

**Ornith-1.0-35B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B are the SAME base architecture** — byte-for-byte
identical `config.json` `text_config`: `hidden_size:2048, num_hidden_layers:40,
max_position_embeddings:262144, num_experts:256, num_experts_per_tok:8,
moe_intermediate_size:512`. Static gate view (param count, context, arch, VRAM) is
IDENTICAL. Behavioral result: **Ornith 3/3 (support) vs Qwen3.6 1/3 (investigate)**.
The entire delta is post-training (DeepReinforce RL/reasoning tune). No name/param/context/arch
gate can see this — only an actual eval separates them.

## The 4 gaps in `agentBuilderBaseline` (all 4 models fail the gate as written)

1. **Instruct gate is name-matching, not capability.** `checkInstructVariant()`
   (`model-candidate-filter.ts:581`) hard-rejects any id lacking `instruct/chat/-it/_it`.
   Rejects Ornith (the BEST model) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B — even though Qwen3.6 ships a
   `chat_template` and both serve via the hermes vLLM parser. **Fix:** detect
   `chat_template` (tokenizer_config.json / chat_template.jinja) as the real signal;
   demote name-match to a warning.
2. **Param gate is blind to MoE active params.** `checkParameterCount()`
   (`model-candidate-filter.ts:556`) uses TOTAL. Both MoE models pass the 7B floor on
   35B total but have ~3B active; the 3B-active MoE loses to the dense 7B on RAG.
   "A3B" literally = Active 3B. `estimateParameterCountFromHfConfig` never reads
   `num_experts`/`num_experts_per_tok` (declared in `HfConfigJson.text_config` but unused).
3. **Context gate trusts advertised, deploys native.** `checkContextSize()` +
   `enrichModelInfoFromHfConfig` takes `Math.max(card, config)`. Dense Qwen2.5-7B/14B
   are 32768 native, advertise 131072 via YaRN only. Gate passes on the card claim;
   vLLM then serves 32k unless rope-scaling flags are set → passing gate, degraded deploy.
4. **`minToolCallSuccessRate: 1.0`** (`config.ts:47`) is unrealistic for small models.
   ITL is ALREADY tiered by size (`maxItlP50MsTiers`, `config.ts:64`) — copy that pattern.
   Score post-repair (after `validate_tool_calls.ts` filter + one retry), matching prod.

**Strategic fill (Gap 5):** add a cheap behavioral tool-call probe BEFORE the full CI
gate — it's the only signal that ranks same-arch models. Then add a coding/agentic eval
suite (security suites over-index on domain knowledge; only esql ≈ codegen).

## CI-eval data shape (non-obvious, required to query results)

- `benchmarker-ci-evals` docs: top-level `score` is **null** even on PASSED builds; the
  real per-suite scores live in Buildkite artifacts, NOT in ES. **The reliable signal is
  the build `status` (passed/failed)**, one suite per build (`eval_suites:["..."]`).
- `regenerate-recommendation --model <id>` maps latest per-suite status → pass/fail and
  rebuilds the verdict from persisted data — **no GPU/CI re-run**. This is the fast path
  to "N fully evaluated models" when models already ran but reports are stale/bug-collapsed.
- `recommendation-reports` has no `generated_at` (sort on `@timestamp`); flags
  `stage1_passed/stage2_ran/stage2_passed/stage3_ran` distinguish fully-run from gate-rejected.

## Treadmill-coding routing (from these results)

Primary = **Ornith-1.0-35B** (only model passing agentic triage + structured gen; 757 tps
acceptable for autonomous loops). Fast tier = **Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct** (2.5× throughput,
passes structured gen, weak at multi-step reasoning). **Avoid Qwen3.6-35B-A3B** — 35B VRAM
for sub-7B agentic quality.

**Confirmed:** all numbers from real ES data + live HF config.json + gate code traced to source.

# Benchmarker CI on the Shared On-Demand Pipeline — Ownership & Operation

The benchmarker triggers its Stage 2 security-eval suites on
`kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`, which is **shared with every other
person triggering on-demand evals** (PRs, manual runs). Two things follow
that repeatedly mislead.

## 1. Build numbers interleave — a dedicated branch does NOT isolate them

Giving benchmarker its own Kibana branch (`benchmarker/ornith-evals`) ended
the `skip_queued_branch_builds` same-branch cancellation contention (see
`reference_cloudflared_quicktunnel_rotation`), and it isolates **commits**.
It does **NOT** isolate **build numbers** — those are pipeline-global.

Concrete run (2026-07-03): our three suites were builds **#199, #201, #203**
(non-consecutive). **#200 was `refs/pull/273461/head`** (a different
person's weekly-evals PR) that landed in the middle. **#202** was similarly
not ours.

**Never** assume `ourFirstBuild + N` is your Nth suite. Before treating a
build as yours, confirm via the read-only MCP `get_build`:
- `branch` == your dedicated branch,
- `creator.email` == you,
- `commit` / `message` == your benchmarker commit ("Benchmarker: <model>
  on-demand eval").

The daemon logs the exact build number it triggered
(`CI eval result saved {buildNumber, status}` and
`CI Evals: triggering on-demand build {suite}`) — trust the log's number,
not arithmetic.

## 2. Suites run as 3 SEPARATE sequential builds (not one matrix build)

`Scheduler.runCIEvals` iterates `suitesToRun` in a `for` loop
(`security-alert-triage` → `security-alerts-rag-regression` →
`security-esql-generation-regression`), one `createOnDemandBuildOrAdopt`
per suite. Each waits for **pipeline idle** before triggering (so an
unrelated build like #200 running delays your next suite — by design, not
a hang). Each build ≈ pipeline-upload → pre-build → **Build Kibana
Distribution (~20-40 min)** → **LLM Evals (~10 min)**. Full Stage 2 for 3
suites ≈ 1h40m wall clock. `detachPoll: true` runs this whole loop in the
background; the scheduler foreground just heartbeats.

## 3. Operational gotchas when watching a run

- **`start-local.sh` daemonizes.** The harness-tracked launch job (or
  `nohup` wrapper) **exits 0 after ~99s** when the launcher forks the real
  daemon into the background. A "task success" notification for the *launch*
  is NOT the benchmark finishing — the detached daemon (find via
  `ps aux | grep start-local.sh` / the cloudflared + ssh pids) keeps running
  for hours. Tail `.smoke-logs/ornith-daemon.log`, don't trust the launcher
  exit.
- **Heartbeat floods the log.** The scheduler prints
  `Scheduler: waiting for deferred Buildkite poll before dequeuing next
  model` every ~10s. Real events (suite pass, next-suite trigger, Stage 3)
  get buried. Read progress with
  `grep -vE "waiting for deferred Buildkite poll" .smoke-logs/ornith-daemon.log
  | tail`.
- **Happy-path terminal sequence** in the daemon log:
  `on-demand build completed {suite,status:passed}` ×3 →
  `Stored stage2 result {status:success}` →
  `EIS chat_completion endpoints already available` (Stage 3 CCM) →
  `Stored reasoning result {status:success}` ×2 →
  `Stored recommendation report {verdict}` →
  guard stopped → tunnel disconnected → container removed → GPUs freed.

**Related:** `feedback_buildkite_mcp_over_cli` (use read-only MCP for
build/job state), `reference_cloudflared_quicktunnel_rotation` (tunnel
persistence), `feedback_benchmarker_cross_host_daemon_contention` (a 2nd
daemon on the same VM is a different contention source).

# Benchmarker Stage-1 + Eval-Connector Root Causes (PR #3 / kibana #274606)

Surfaced by the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B E2E run on the i9 runner. Four distinct root causes, two repos. Distinct from the earlier resilience-fixes commit (`reference_elastic_llm_benchmarker_resilience_fixes.md`).

## 1. Stage-1 `exit code 137` mid-benchmark respawns — drop `--restart unless-stopped` from the INTERNAL docker run

- **Symptom:** Stage 1 dies with `exit code 137` (SIGKILL) / "CI smoke test failed" partway through the benchmark.
- **Root cause:** the internal `buildDockerRunCommand` (`src/services/vllm-deployment.ts`) set `--restart unless-stopped`. During Stage 1 the benchmark runs as a `docker exec` against the container; when vLLM OOMs/crashes, Docker **auto-restarts the container**, which kills the exec'd benchmark process mid-run.
- **Fix:** remove `--restart unless-stopped` from `buildDockerRunCommand`. **Do NOT** remove it from the customer-facing `buildDeployCommandWithToolCalling` (customers want the auto-restart).
- **Why Stage 2 is unaffected:** `CiEvalInfrastructureGuard.ensureRestartPolicy()` already runs `docker update --restart unless-stopped` (+ `docker start` on exit) to keep the container alive for the CI-eval polling window. So the keep-alive is applied *after* Stage 1, exactly when it's wanted — never during the benchmark.
- **Invariant check after build:** `grep -o unless-stopped dist/cli.js | wc -l` should be **2** (guard `docker update` + customer deploy command), never 3.

## 2. GPU VM disk fills to 100% — mount a shared HF-cache volume

- **Symptom:** later Stage-1 deploys fail with `disk_space Insufficient disk space` on the GPU VM.
- **Root cause:** without a volume mount, each container downloads model weights into its own writable layer; layers accumulate and never dedup.
- **Fix:** mount `-v vllm-hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface` (named Docker volume) on both the internal and customer deploy commands. Configurable via `VllmDeploymentOptions.hfCacheVolume` (default `'vllm-hf-cache'`, disable with `''`). Weights persist and dedup across deploys.

## 3. Eval 500 "Missing name for tool use" — set `enableNativeFunctionCalling: true`

- **Symptom:** Stage-2 Buildkite build fails with `Missing name for tool use` from Kibana's inference plugin.
- **Root cause:** our vLLM runs with `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser <hermes|mistral|llama3_json>` and emits **native OpenAI `tool_calls`**. But the `.gen-ai` connector used `apiProvider: 'Other'`, which defaults to **simulated** function calling — its inline parser throws on native tool-use output.
- **Fix:** set `enableNativeFunctionCalling: true` in the connector config on BOTH paths: `src/services/buildkite-connector-builder.ts` (`GenAIConnector` interface + payload) and `src/services/kibana-connector.ts`. The key is schema-accepted (`kbn-connector-schemas/openai/schemas/v1.ts`) and matches kbn-evals' own `generate_litellm_connectors.js`.

## 4. Eval 500 "maxContentLength size of 1048576 exceeded" — raise `maxResponseContentLength`

- **Symptom:** large-output subject models (e.g. 200-alert summary-mode `security-alert-triage`) fail on the connector→LLM hop.
- **Root cause:** Kibana's `xpack.actions.maxResponseContentLength` defaults to **1 MiB**.
- **Fix (Kibana side, not benchmarker):** add `--xpack.actions.maxResponseContentLength=20mb` to the shared eval Scout config `src/platform/packages/shared/kbn-scout/src/servers/configs/config_sets/evals_tracing/stateful/classic.stateful.config.ts`. Scoped to the eval Kibana; production keeps the default. Landed on `elastic/kibana:fix/weekly-evals-matrix` (PR #274606).

## Validation

- Benchmarker: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run build`, 923 vitest pass, eslint 0 errors. PR #3.
- Deployed to i9 runner: rsync 3 src files → `npm run build` (nvm node v24.17.0) → verified compiled `dist/` (`enableNativeFunctionCalling` present, `vllm-hf-cache` present, `unless-stopped`=2) → graceful `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.i9.benchmarker`.

# Benchmarker Stage 2 Scoring + Report Regeneration (commit d196889)

Ornith-1.0-35B passed all three Kibana on-demand eval suites (triage, rag-regression, esql) but the recommendation report showed **investigate / medium** with every suite scored 0. Root cause was three independent data bugs, not a model or CI failure. Fixed and verified: Ornith regenerated to **support / high**, 3/3 suites score 1.0, Stage 3 reasoning restored.

## The three bugs

| # | File | Bug | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `src/scheduler/scheduler.ts` (`pollWeeklyMatrix`) | Per-suite on-demand builds run in a loop, but aggregation resolved artifacts from **only the last build** (`lastResult`) and `mapBuildkiteResultToStage2(..., suitesToRun, ...)` keyed the single score by `evalSuites[0]`. Earlier suites' scores came back `null` → `0` in `suiteResults[].score` → below the 0.8 gate. | Resolve **each suite's own** artifacts inside the loop, build a per-suite `Stage2Result` via `mapBuildkiteResultToStage2([suite], ...)`, then `mergeStage2Results(perSuiteStage2)` (an existing, tested helper that unions each suite's scores map + suiteResults and derives overall status). |
| 2 | `src/api/queue-server.ts` | Dashboard API read only `ES_API_KEY`; `.env` defines `ELASTICSEARCH_API_KEY` (the `esUrl` line already had the fallback). ES client had no auth → `security_exception`. | `esApiKey: process.env.ES_API_KEY ?? process.env.ELASTICSEARCH_API_KEY`. |
| 3 | `src/services/elasticsearch-results-store.ts` (`getLatestReasoningResult`) | Query used `term: { model_id }` + `term: { status }` against `benchmark-reasoning-*`. Reasoning docs land in a **date-suffixed, dynamically-mapped** index where `model_id`/`status` are analyzed `text` (with a `.keyword` subfield), so `term` on the raw field **never matched** — 20 real Ornith reasoning docs were invisible to the read. | Match mapping-robustly: `bool.should` over both `model_id`/`model_id.keyword` and `status`/`status.keyword`, `minimum_should_match: 1`. |

## Resume-path scoring regression (Jul 2026)

The scheduler's all-suites-completed resume fast-path must set both `scores[suite] = 1` and `suiteResults[].score = 1` for every passed suite. Omitting the field persists `null` to Elasticsearch; the recommendation builder then defaults it to `0`, yielding a false `investigate`/`reject` verdict despite passing CI. Keep the resume-result construction in the shared Stage 2 mapper and cover it with a regression test.

## Key meta-learning: live in-memory vs offline ES read

Bug #3 never manifested during the live run because the scheduler builds the report from the **in-memory `run.stage3Result`** populated by the Stage 3 worker in the same process. It only surfaces on any **offline read-back from ES** (the `regenerate-recommendation` command, the dashboard, a resume). When debugging a "field looks present but query returns 0", suspect **text-vs-keyword**: `match_all` shows the doc with the exact string, but `term` fails because the resolved (often auto-created, date-suffixed) index dynamically mapped the field as `text`. Test with `term: { field.keyword }` before assuming data absence.

## `regenerate-recommendation` CLI (new)

`node dist/cli.js --config config/local.json regenerate-recommendation --model <id>` rebuilds a recommendation from **persisted** Stage 1/2/3 data — no build re-run. Reconstructs a minimal `PipelineRun` (Stage 1 metrics + vLLM config from the prior report, corrected Stage 2 from persisted per-suite CI builds via the fixed mapper, Stage 3 via `getLatestReasoningResult`), calls `buildRecommendationReport`, saves. All inputs read from ES — nothing fabricated. Use after any scoring-logic fix to give already-evaluated models their corrected verdict. Prints `verdict before → after` and per-suite scores.

## Gotchas hit during this work

- **`recommendation-reports` and `benchmark-reasoning` are exact index names, not `-*` datastreams for the write/templated index**, but reasoning docs actually resolve to `benchmark-reasoning-<suffix>`. `getLatestRecommendation` queries the exact index (`recommendation-reports`, keyword-mapped → `term` works); `getLatestReasoningResult` queries `benchmark-reasoning-*` (dynamic index → text). Same field name, different mapping per read path.
- **Shell env leak into vitest**: sourcing `.env` (`set -a && . ./.env`) into the persistent shell exports `BUILDKITE_KIBANA_BRANCH`, which vitest inherits and which overrides `config/smoke-full.json` **even with `skipDotenv: true`** (skipDotenv only skips the file, not already-set `process.env`). This falsely fails `config.test.ts` expecting `fix/weekly-evals-matrix`. Re-run with `env -u BUILDKITE_KIBANA_BRANCH` to confirm it's an artifact, not a regression.
- **Config schema is branch-scoped**: `tunnel.provider` enum on `fix/gpu-vm-lease` is `['ngrok','cloudrun','load_balancer']` — no `cloudflared` (that lives on `feat/cloudflared-tunnel-provider`, 2 commits, unmerged). `config/local.json` sets `cloudflared`, so read-only CLI commands need `TUNNEL_PROVIDER=ngrok` to load config on non-cloudflared branches. The daemon that ran Ornith was built from the feat branch.

## Validation

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; `npx vitest run` 932 passed / 14 skipped (the 1 "failure" was the env-leak artifact above; clean env → 16/16 in config.test.ts).
- `npx eslint` on all four files: 0 errors (pre-existing warnings only).
- Ornith `regenerate-recommendation` run end-to-end against live serverless ES: `investigate/medium → support/high`, suites `triage=1 rag=1 esql=1` all pass, stored report id `8912fb09-…`.

## Known follow-up (not fixed this cycle)

- **Write-path root cause of bug #3**: reasoning docs land in a dynamically-mapped date-suffixed index instead of the keyword-templated `benchmark-reasoning`. The read fix fully restores consumers, but an index template (or write-to-exact-index) would prevent the text mapping in the first place and let other `term` consumers work. Requires an index template + reindex of existing docs — deferred; the mapping-robust read is the durable consumer-side fix. Driver: `src/services/es-index-mappings.ts` (add index template for `benchmark-reasoning-*`).

# Buildkite `state=failing` is NOT terminal — don't poll-exit on it

A `bk build view <n>` poll loop that treats `failing` as a terminal state will
fire its "build done" notification while the build is still running (~65 jobs
in flight, only 2-3 failed so far). `failing` just means "at least one job has
failed while the build continues" — it later resolves to `failed` (or
`passed` if failed jobs are retried/soft-fail) once every job finishes.

**Terminal states only**: `passed`, `failed`, `canceled`, `blocked`. Do not
include `failing`, `running`, `scheduled`, or `canceling` in the exit
condition of a build-completion poller.

```bash
case "$STATE" in
  passed|failed|canceled|blocked)
    echo "BUILD_DONE state=$STATE"; exit 0;;
esac
```

**Corollary**: a `failing` build with a few failed jobs is worth triaging
immediately (e.g. checking for a shared root cause like a transient Vault/CI
infra outage — `dial tcp ...:8200: i/o timeout` at the pre-command hook is a
common transient-infra signature, not a suite/model regression), but don't
conflate "worth triaging now" with "build is done."

## Never

- Treat `bk build view` `state=failing` as a terminal/exit condition in a
  polling script — it will fire long before the build actually finishes.

# Stale/uncommitted `package-map.json` can silently block Kibana typecheck/push

In a Kibana worktree, `src/platform/packages/private/kbn-repo-packages/...`
ships a generated `package-map.json` (or similar path) that normally gets
refreshed by `yarn kbn bootstrap`. If a package was added/moved without a
full bootstrap, the stale map causes a typecheck failure that blocks pushing
a commit — the error doesn't obviously point at "regenerate the package map"
on first read.

**Fix (fast path, no full bootstrap needed):**

```bash
node -e "
import('./src/dev/kbn_pm/src/commands/bootstrap/regenerate_package_map.mjs')
  .then(m => m.regeneratePackageMap ? m.regeneratePackageMap() : null)
"
```

Then re-run the failing typecheck and retry the push. This is much faster
than a full `yarn kbn bootstrap` when the only drift is the package map.

**Confirmed root cause** (Kibana PR #274606, `weekly-evals-matrix` worktree):
`src/platform/packages/private/kbn-repo-packages/package-map.json` is a
gitignored, locally-generated registry cache. After merging `upstream/main`
into a long-lived worktree, this cache can miss a package that arrived via
the merge (e.g. `@kbn/as-code-utils`) even though `node_modules` itself was
freshly bootstrapped — the type-checker's dependency resolver (`ts_project.ts`)
then throws `invalid kbn_references in <project>: @kbn/<pkg> does not point
to another TS project` on an unrelated-looking project. **After merging
`upstream/main` into a long-lived worktree, regenerate the package map (or
run a full bootstrap) before attempting a push — don't assume
`yarn kbn bootstrap` alone self-heals it.**

## Never

- Assume a typecheck failure referencing `kbn-repo-packages`/package-map
  content requires a full bootstrap — try `regenerate_package_map.mjs`
  directly first.
- Assume a fresh `node_modules` bootstrap also refreshed the package-map
  cache after merging `upstream/main` — verify/regenerate it explicitly
  before pushing from a long-lived worktree.

## `regeneratePackageMap`/`regenerateTsconfigPaths` need `discovery()`'s output, not empty args

Both `regeneratePackageMap(log, packageManifestPaths)` and
`regenerateTsconfigPaths(tsConfigRepoRels, log)` require args computed by
`discovery()` (`src/dev/kbn_pm/src/commands/bootstrap/discovery.mjs`) —
calling `regeneratePackageMap()` with no args throws
`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'filter')` inside
`get_packages.js`. Correct one-shot invocation (no full bootstrap needed):

```bash
node -e "
async function main() {
  const { discovery } = await import('./src/dev/kbn_pm/src/commands/bootstrap/discovery.mjs');
  const { regeneratePackageMap } = await import('./src/dev/kbn_pm/src/commands/bootstrap/regenerate_package_map.mjs');
  const { regenerateTsconfigPaths } = await import('./src/dev/kbn_pm/src/commands/bootstrap/regenerate_tsconfig_paths.mjs');
  const { packageManifestPaths, tsConfigRepoRels } = await discovery();
  const log = { warning: (...a) => console.log('[warn]', ...a), info: console.log, debug: () => {}, success: console.log };
  await regeneratePackageMap(log, packageManifestPaths);
  await regenerateTsconfigPaths(tsConfigRepoRels, log);
}
main().catch(e => { console.error(e); process.exit(1); });
"
```

**Both caches must be regenerated together** — they're separate gitignored
files (`src/platform/packages/private/kbn-repo-packages/package-map.json`
vs. `packages/kbn-ts-projects/config-paths.json`) and drift independently.
Confirmed on `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` (2026-07-16): after regenerating only
`package-map.json`, `type_check --project
x-pack/solutions/security/packages/kbn-evals-suite-security-ai-rules/tsconfig.json`
still failed with `invalid kbn_references in
@kbn/evals-suite-security-ai-rules: @kbn/security-evals-rule-data-snapshot
does not point to another TS project` — same symptom shape, different
missing cache. Check both before assuming the fix landed.

## Never (addendum)

- Regenerate only one of the two caches (package-map vs. tsconfig
  config-paths) after adding a new package — a `does not point to another
  TS project` error after a package-map fix means the tsconfig cache is
  *also* stale and needs the same treatment.

# Kibana pre-push hook lints untracked stray build artifacts, not just your diff

A push can fail at the `check_changes.ts` ESLint step with a wall of
prettier/license-header errors on files you never touched. Root cause: the
pre-push hook lints **all untracked files in the worktree**, not just the
files in your diff. Stray generated `.d.ts` build artifacts left over from
an earlier ad-hoc `tsc -b` run (e.g. under `src/platform/plugins/private/*/`
or a solution plugin's schedules dir) count as untracked and get linted,
producing dozens of failures unrelated to the actual PR.

**Fix:** `git status --porcelain` to find the stray untracked files, confirm
they're generated build output (not real changes), then `rm -rf` them and
retry the push.

## Never

- Assume every lint failure at a Kibana pre-push hook is caused by files
  in your own diff — check `git status` for stray untracked generated
  artifacts first, especially after ad-hoc `tsc -b` runs in the worktree.

name: reference_buildkite_pr_cloud_deploy_lookup
description: Find a Kibana PR's persisted Cloud QA deployment (URL + creds + image SHA) from the Buildkite `cloud` annotation
type: reference
---

# Locating a PR's Persisted Cloud QA Deployment

When a Kibana PR carries labels **`ci:cloud-deploy`** + **`ci:cloud-persist-deployment`**,
CI stands up an ESS Cloud QA deployment that survives past the build — the
ready-made target for a reviewer/PM demo. You don't need to build anything; you
need to *find* it.

## Where the connection details live

They are NOT in a dedicated API — they're in a **Buildkite build annotation**
with `context: "cloud"`.

```
list_annotations(org_slug="elastic", pipeline_slug="kibana-pull-request", build_number="<N>")
```

The MCP payload is `{ headers, items[] }` (NOT a bare array). Contexts seen on a
typical build: `ctx-gobld-metrics`, `ctx-gobld-agent-provider`,
`test-group-*`, **`cloud`**, `test_failures`, `ci-stats-report`. Parse the item
whose `context == "cloud"`; its body (strip HTML) contains:

```
Kibana:        https://kibana-pr-<PR>-<hash>.kb.<region>.gcp.elastic-cloud.com
Elasticsearch: https://kibana-pr-<PR>-<hash>.es.<region>.gcp.elastic-cloud.com
Credentials:   vault read -address=https://secrets.elastic.co:8200 \
                 secret/kibana-issues/dev/cloud-deploy/kibana-pr-<PR>
Kibana image:        docker.elastic.co/kibana-ci/kibana-cloud:<ver>-SNAPSHOT-<SHA>
Elasticsearch image: docker.elastic.co/kibana-ci/elasticsearch-cloud-ess:<ver>-SNAPSHOT-<SHA>
```

## Two high-value facts from the annotation

- **The Kibana image SHA tells you which commit is actually deployed.** Match it
  against the PR head (`git rev-parse HEAD`) to prove the persisted deploy runs
  the code under review — not a stale earlier push. A red CI build can still
  have a healthy, current deployment (the deploy step ran before the flaky jobs
  failed).
- **Access is the `elastic` superuser + Vault password**, not SSO. Log in at the
  Kibana URL as user `elastic` with the `password` field from the Vault read
  (`vault login -method=oidc` first, one-time/day). For a headless API key, mint
  one against `${ES_URL}/_security/api_key`.

## Quick health check (no auth)

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 15 \
  https://kibana-pr-<PR>-<hash>.kb.<region>.gcp.elastic-cloud.com/login
# 200 = up
```

## Note on the `-security` Vault suffix

The base annotation path is `.../cloud-deploy/kibana-pr-<PR>`. Serverless
*security-project* creds sometimes live at `.../kibana-pr-<PR>-security` (used by
the response-actions `recreate-*-env.sh`). If the base path 404s from Vault, try
the `-security` suffix.

**Confirmed approach:** Used on elastic/kibana#272111 (build 463251) — resolved
`https://kibana-pr-272111-774f55.kb.us-west2.gcp.elastic-cloud.com`, verified
image `9.5.0-SNAPSHOT-9119c95` matched PR head, `/login` → 200, even though the
build was red on 3 unrelated flaky jobs.

name: reference_cloudflared_quicktunnel_rotation
description: cloudflared quick-tunnel URLs rotate on every restart and orphan in-flight CI eval builds with ENOTFOUND — local DNS guard doesn't cover the remote consumer
type: reference
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-03
source: elastic-llm-benchmarker Ornith Stage 2 — builds #188–191 all failed on ENOTFOUND
---

# cloudflared Quick Tunnels Rotate URLs → Orphan In-Flight CI Builds

The benchmarker exposes the GPU-VM vLLM to Buildkite CI evals through a
public tunnel, injected into the CI Kibana connector at build-trigger
time. Migrating from ngrok to **cloudflared quick tunnels** fixed the
`ERR_NGROK_334` reserved-domain collision but introduced a different
failure of the same class.

**The failure (observed on Ornith #188–191, all failed):**
The CI eval's `POST /api/agent_builder/converse` returned
`500 Internal Server Error — Error calling connector: Unexpected API
Error: ENOTFOUND - getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND
<name>.trycloudflare.com`. The injected hostname no longer resolved
(`dig +short` empty), while the daemon's *current* tunnel was a
**different** hostname.

**Root cause:** A cloudflared quick tunnel mints a **new random
`*.trycloudflare.com` hostname on every `cloudflared` start**, and the
old hostname stops resolving the instant the process that owns it exits.
Any daemon/tunnel restart, reconnect, or crash between connector
injection and eval completion (~30 min for a security suite) orphans
every in-flight build's connector → `ENOTFOUND` from the remote CI
agent. During heavy debugging (many daemon bounces) this is near-certain.

**Why the local DNS guard is insufficient:** `waitForDnsPropagation`
(added in `src/services/tunnel-service.ts`) polls `dns.resolve4` on the
**local macOS** box so an early `getaddrinfo` doesn't poison the OS
negative cache. That protects local `fetch` probes, but the actual
consumer is the **remote Buildkite GCP agent** — the local guard says
"resolvable" while the remote still fails once the URL rotates.

**Durable fixes (in priority order):**
1. **Named Cloudflare tunnel** (stable hostname surviving restarts) —
   needs a CF account/token + one DNS record; a mid-run daemon bounce
   reconnects to the *same* hostname. This is the clean answer.
2. **In-scope code guard (no credentials):** daemon must refuse to
   rotate/restart the tunnel while a Buildkite build it triggered is
   in-flight, and re-inject the current URL on reconnect. **← IMPLEMENTED
   + VALIDATED, see below.**
3. Stable ngrok reserved domain also survives restarts, but had its own
   ghost-endpoint 334 collisions on ungraceful stop — a named CF tunnel
   is cleaner.

## VALIDATED FIX (2026-07-03) — persistence + detach + reuse-first reconnect

Fix #2 was implemented (no CF credentials needed) and **held end-to-end
across the full Ornith-35B Stage 2 run: one tunnel survived all THREE
sequential ~40-min CI builds (#199 triage, #201 rag, #203 esql; ~1h40m
total), externally reachable the whole time.** Post-run the recommendation
report was generated and the daemon torn down cleanly.

Three non-obvious mechanics in `src/services/tunnel-service.ts`
`CloudflaredProvider` that made it work — miss any one and the URL still
rotates:

1. **Spawn detached + `unref()`** (`spawn(..., { detached: true })` then
   `child.unref()`) so the `cloudflared` process **outlives the daemon
   process**. Without this, a daemon bounce kills the tunnel with it.
2. **Persist state to a file** at
   `~/.elastic-llm-benchmarker/cloudflared-<localPort>.json` =
   `{ pid, url, localPort, establishedAt }`. On next `connect()`,
   `checkExisting()` reads it, verifies the pid is alive (`kill(pid, 0)`)
   AND the hostname still resolves (`dns.resolve4`), and **reuses the same
   URL** instead of minting a new one. Override dir with
   `BENCHMARKER_TUNNEL_STATE_DIR` (used to isolate unit tests).
3. **`reconnect()` for cloudflared calls `connect()` (reuse-first)**, not
   a fresh spawn — so the in-flight-build guard's periodic reconnect can't
   rotate the URL.

Liveness signals during a run: `ps -p <pid>` on the persisted cloudflared
pid + the SSH `-L <localPort>:localhost:8000` forward pid; `curl
https://<host>/v1/models` from anywhere on the internet returns the model
list. `--max-model-len auto` resolved to **262144 (256K)** for Ornith-35B
on 2×A100-80GB.

Still worth doing eventually: **fix #1 (named tunnel)** remains the clean
answer for a persistent 24/7 daemon — the quick-tunnel host is still
ephemeral if the cloudflared process itself dies (not just the daemon).

**Diagnosis shortcut:** `ENOTFOUND`/`ECONNREFUSED`/404 on the tunnel host
in the eval job's converse `[cause]` = **infra** (tunnel dead/unreachable),
not model quality. Fetch it via `tail_logs` (see
`feedback_buildkite_mcp_over_cli`).

**Related:** benchmarker also collides with the operator's own matrix
work when both trigger on the same `kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`
pipeline / `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` branch (`skip_queued_branch_builds`
cancels same-branch builds). Give benchmarker evals a dedicated branch.

name: reference_crw_scraper_integration
description: "CRW (fastCRW) integration gotchas — Firecrawl-compatible but SearXNG sidecar required, nested data.results shape, health probe on /health not /"
type: reference
---

# CRW (fastCRW) Scraper Integration

CRW is the lightweight self-hosted web scraper that replaced Firecrawl for
treadmill web-research (`~/Projects/crw-selfhost`, `docker compose -f
docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d`, port 3000, ~210MB running vs Firecrawl's
~2.5GB). It advertises a Firecrawl-compatible `/v1/search` + `/v1/scrape` API,
but the compatibility is shallow — four non-obvious differences bit during the
migration:

## 1. `/v1/search` requires the SearXNG sidecar

A bare `docker run ghcr.io/us/crw` container answers `/v1/scrape` but **fails
every `/v1/search`** — search federates through a SearXNG sidecar. You need the
full compose stack (crw + searxng + lightpanda), not a single container.

## 2. Response shape differs — nested `data.results[]`

Firecrawl v1 `/v1/search` returns `data` as a **flat array**. CRW returns
`data.results[]` (nested). A parser must accept both:

```ts
const items = Array.isArray(payload.data) ? payload.data : payload.data?.results;
```

CRW also puts the per-result summary under `snippet` (Firecrawl uses
`description`).

## 3. Health probe — `/health` returns 200, `/` returns 404

Self-hosted Firecrawl returns 200 on the base URL `/`. CRW returns **404 on
`/`** and 200 only on `/health`. A naive Firecrawl-style base-URL probe
false-negatives, which (in treadmill) tripped the self-heal loop into trying to
resurrect the decommissioned backend. Probe `/health` first, base URL as
fallback.

## 4. `query_expand_variants` is a latency lever; treadmill only reads results

`config.docker.toml` `[search] query_expand_variants` fans out N concurrent
rewrite queries (default baked to 3 for answer accuracy). Treadmill consumes
only the **ranked results** (title/url/description), never CRW's calibrated
"answer", so it can trade the last accuracy point for reliability: dropping
3 -> 2 shortened the slow-query tail and lifted the web-research success ratio
0.875 -> 0.917 without meaningful recall loss.

## Compose already health-gates the stack

`crw` `depends_on: searxng: { condition: service_healthy }` + searxng's own
`/healthz` healthcheck (10s interval) + `restart: unless-stopped` on all three
services mean a "CRW up but SearXNG down" half-up state is prevented at the
compose layer and auto-recovered. No boot-time smoke probe is needed — it would
duplicate five existing health layers.

**Env compat:** the env var kept its `FIRECRAWL_*` name (`FIRECRAWL_API_URL`,
`AO_CRW_DIR`) for backwards compatibility; treadmill's tool tracker still labels
it `firecrawl` internally.

**Confirmed approach:** validated end-to-end 2026-07-01 — full research scan,
20 insights, successRatio 0.917 after the variants tune (PR #136).

# Daybreak gate evaluation — two-axis model

A key conceptual clarification for the **Evaluation and Trust** workstream: testing
the Daybreak worker/gate system splits into **two orthogonal axes**, each needing
its own methodology. Conflating them (testing only output quality) leaves the
control-flow gates unverified — a perfect reasoning engine behind a buggy gate is
unsafe (fails open).

## Axis 1 — Output / reasoning quality ("is the verdict good?")

- **What:** does the AI's proposal/verdict/evidence make sense?
- **Technique:** LLM-judge evaluators, scored trajectories (`@kbn/evals`), Scout
  multi-step flows.
- **Where:** the **worker testing pyramid** (L1–L6: unit → contract → integration →
  Scout UI-journey → on-demand matrix → weekly matrix). L4 (HITL prompt-state) and
  L5 (evaluators) gate C5 `security-multi-step` out of weekly exports until wired.
- **Docs:** `docs/daybreak-worker-testing-pyramid.md` +
  `docs-site/worker-testing-pyramid/index.html` (dark-mode SVG artifact).

## Axis 2 — Gate-mechanism correctness ("does the gate block/allow/route?")

- **What:** given input X, does the gate actually block/allow/route the way it
  should — **independent of whether the underlying reasoning was good**.
- **Technique:** **deterministic, exhaustive tests with zero LLM calls** — pure
  control-flow assertions. Runs on every CI build, keyed to the thing each gate
  claims to guarantee.
- **Gates under test (three families):**
  - **Family A — worker hooks** (7-hook contract: dedup gate, output guard, etc.):
    each hook is a claim ("I dedup", "I guard output"); test asserts the claim
    holds for the specified input → outcome mapping.
  - **Family B — Approval Gate primitive** (the shared platform
    `waitForApproval`/`waitForInput` + AB `confirmation` policy): test the
    fail-closed behavior, the stale-submit 409 (CAS), the autoclose path.
  - **Family C — process gates** (Entry / Pilot / Launch / Expansion): test the
    ship-readiness gate mapping fires the right checklist per stage.
- **Docs:** `docs/daybreak-gate-test-plan.md` +
  `docs-site/gate-test-plan/index.html` (methodology-first rebuild: per-gate claim
  → technique → test location → pass proof → run cadence).

## Why the split matters

The first deliverable built (worker-testing-pyramid) only covered Axis 1. The user
clarified: "by evaluation pyramid plan I meant how we are going to evaluate/test
each of the gates." Gate-mechanism correctness is a **different axis** that needs
its own test suite — if you only test output quality, a gate that fails open is
invisible until production. Treat gates as **software control flow**, not judgment
calls.

name: Daybreak Watch vs Worker vs Workflow three-layer model
description: D10-ratified model — Watch=tier, Watch Orchestrator=executing parent workflow (one per Watch), Worker=domain workflow invoked by Orchestrator. Supersedes the Jul 14 "Watch=non-executing grouping" framing.
type: reference
---

## Three layers (updated Jul 15, 2026 — D10 ratified)

Decision [D10](https://github.com/elastic/project-daybreak/blob/main/docs/daybreak-decision-log.md) (Jul 14, DECIDED, Yuliia/Tehila/Michael/James) **supersedes** the earlier "Watch is a non-executing naming/grouping construct" framing. The new runtime model:

> **The Orchestrator sequences; Workers produce evidence; the Watch is the product tier those components implement.**

| Layer | What it is | Cardinality / notes |
|-------|------------|---------------------|
| **Watch** (tier) | Customer-facing product tier — mandate, autonomy, allowed scopes, which Workers may run. Named, always-on unit of agentic security work (Watch Floor, Dark Watch, etc.). | 1 per product capability area |
| **Watch Orchestrator** | A specially configured Elastic Workflow — **one per Watch** — that schedules, triggers, and coordinates Workers. Does **not** do domain work. Owns `run-as` identity, creates the Investigation Conversation, owns HIL/approval pause points. | exactly 1 per Watch |
| **Worker** | An Elastic Workflow invoked by the Orchestrator (`workflow.execute`/`workflow.executeAsync`) to perform domain work (enrich, correlate, act). Produces evidence; does not own investigation container or Watch-level HIL. | 1..N per Watch |

## Why this model (not self-scheduling Workers)

- Single `run-as` identity per investigation (the Orchestrator's Service Account)
- One Investigation Conversation per Watch run (not one per Worker execution)
- Throughline shows proposals from the Watch run, not a queue of raw Worker executions
- Coherent HIL step owned by the Orchestrator, not scattered across Workers
- Contract rule: **list Investigations (Conversations with Watch provenance), not raw WorkflowExecutions**

## CWL POC contract alignment

The Common Worker Layer POC (Garrett Spong, PR #27 RFC) projects **Watch === tagged workflow (1:1 for inbox projection)** — where the tagged workflow *is* the Watch Orchestrator and child `workflow.execute*` targets are Workers. This is compatible with D10. The contract carries only a `ProposalStub` until [#17942](https://github.com/elastic/security-team/issues/17942) ratifies the Proposal schema.

- Managed id convention: `system-inbox-watch-floor`, `system-inbox-watch-officer`, etc. Tags: `watch`, `watch-floor`/`watch-officer`/`watch-dark`/`watch-deep`. Owned by plugin id `inbox`.
- Callables come from the executable graph (`skill://…` on `ai.agent`, `workflow.execute*`) — display overrides only; never invent skills the YAML does not invoke.

## Doc precedence

- **D10 + Watches Architecture** (`daybreak-watches-architecture.md`) — canonical runtime model
- **CWL RFC** (PR #27) — POC contract for Watch implementers
- **Kibana PR #277576** — reference implementation (inbox projection)
- Garrett PR #17 = CWL POC SoT; Nir PR #11 = product vocabulary — both subordinate to D10

## Deprecated framing

- **"Watch Commander"** human-role term → use analyst/Watch Officer instead (D10 follow-up: remove from personas/legacy prose)
- **"Watch is non-executing / Watch = 1:N grouping"** (Jul 10–14 docs) → superseded by D10
- **"Worker = runtime workflow, Watch = UX only"** → Watch now has a runtime realization (the Orchestrator)

## Related

- `reference_daybreak_cwl_proposal_worker_ownership.md` — CWL owns Worker + Proposal schema (ProposalStub until #17942)
- New hard blockers surfaced by Platform Gap Analysis: service-account/`run-as` execution identity (Daybreak can't defer like Nightshift) + background/system agent runs (AB has no no-human-turn trigger yet)

# Dev Machine Fleet & Role Assignment

The user has three Macs available for Kibana development. Assign work by matching the machine's dominant strength to the workload, not by "newest = everything."

| Machine | RAM | Arch | Role |
|---------|-----|------|------|
| **M4 Max** | 48 GB | arm64 | **Interactive / primary** — editing, TS server, unit tests, typecheck. Fastest P-cores, but lowest RAM of the three. |
| **M1 Max** | 64 GB | arm64 | **Heavy / RAM box** — ES + Kibana server, Fleet, FTR/functional suites, long Jest runs. Slightly slower cores than M4 but the *most RAM*. Also set up (Jul 3 2026) as a **second headless EDD runner** (`worker-m1max`, 100.67.93.90, user `mac`) mirroring the i9 — see `reference_m1max_apple_silicon_runner`. |
| **Intel i9 MacBook Pro** | 32 GB | x86_64 | **Disposable background runner** — unattended, "done when it's done" jobs. Being set up (Jul 2026) as a **headless EDD skill-dev runner** (see `reference_headless_macos_runner_setup`). Slowest, thermal-throttles under sustained load. Also the only x86 box → x86 verification. |

## Non-obvious role-assignment rule

**Give the "heavy/RAM" role to the machine with the most RAM even if its cores are slower.** Kibana dev is RAM-bound (ES + Kibana + FTR + TS server + browser can hit 20–40 GB), and heavy runs (FTR, full Jest, stack hosting) are duration-tolerant, not latency-sensitive. So the 64 GB M1 Max beats the 48 GB M4 Max for hosting the stack, and freeing the M4 from stack-hosting recovers its scarce RAM for the snappy interactive loop. This is why the "best" machine (M4 Max) is *not* the one that runs the stack.

## Adding a third machine — diminishing returns

An Intel/32 GB laptop is strictly behind both Apple Silicon boxes for interactive or heavy-RAM work. It earns its keep only as: (1) fire-and-forget CI-style runner for slow suites, (2) x86 verification box, (3) low-priority parallel-PR/scratch box. Don't make it a first-class dev machine.

name: reference_diagnose_event_loop_saturation_sample
description: "Diagnose Node event-loop saturation on macOS with `sample <pid>`: SyncProcessRunner::Spawn = sync child_process block; uv__io_poll = healthy idle"
type: reference
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-01
source: "treadmill daemon saturation investigation 2026-06-30 → 2026-07-01: sample <pid> distinguished sync-spawn blocking (SyncProcessRunner::Spawn → kevent) before the fix from normal idle (uv__io_poll → kevent) after; then isolated a second cause (dead worker pool → main-thread SQLite fallback)"
---

# Diagnosing Node Event-Loop Saturation with `sample` (macOS)

When a Node HTTP daemon accepts connections but never services them
(curl times out with 0 bytes while the process stays alive in state
`R`), the event loop is blocked. macOS `sample` reads the main thread's
call stack and tells you WHAT is blocking.

## Command
```bash
sample <pid> 4 -mayDie     # 4-second sample; -mayDie tolerates a busy process
```
If `sample <pid> N` returns empty output, retry with `-mayDie` and a
longer window; a pegged process sometimes rejects the first probe.

## Reading the output — the decisive frames

| Main-thread top frame | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `node::SyncProcessRunner::Spawn → uv_run → uv__io_poll → kevent` | A `spawnSync`/`execSync`/`execFileSync` is in flight, blocking the loop | Convert that call site to async (`runGitAsync`/`runGhAsync`/`execFile`+promisify) |
| `uv_run → uv__io_poll → kevent` (no SyncProcessRunner) | **Normal idle** — loop is waiting for I/O | The block is NOT a sync spawn; look elsewhere (busy DB on main thread, tight CPU loop, GC) |
| Heavy frames in a DB/SQLite native addon on the main thread | Synchronous DB work on the hot path | Move to a worker pool (and verify the pool actually booted) |

## The two-cause pattern (this incident)
1. **Before fix**: `SyncProcessRunner::Spawn` dominated → sync spawns on
   HTTP routes. Fixed by converting to async.
2. **After fix**: `sample` showed `uv__io_poll` (idle) yet HTTP still
   saturated intermittently. The block wasn't ON the sampled stack —
   it was a **dead worker pool** falling back to main-thread SQLite,
   serializing reads. `sample` ruled OUT sync spawns, which redirected
   the investigation to the worker pool.

## Corroborating signals (check alongside `sample`)
- `[ao-watchdog] health probe failed (N/5)` climbing → confirms
  unresponsiveness window.
- Daemon self-audit `EVENT_LOOP_JITTER` / `MEMORY_GROWTH` warnings.
- Probe latency histogram: alternating fast (~20ms) and timeout (5s+)
  responses = intermittent block, not a hang.

## Key lesson
`sample` is as useful for what it RULES OUT as what it confirms. A clean
`uv__io_poll` stack under saturation is a strong signal the block is
off-main-thread (worker crash, native addon, downstream service), not a
sync call — don't keep hunting sync spawns once the stack goes idle.

type: reference

updated: 2026-07-02
source: skill-dev 3686518a — weekly build #51, significant-events/eis-anthropic-claude-4-6-sonnet job 019f1f3d-cfdd-475c-ab0f-aac0a08cd4ff, line 1699 (verbatim quote below)

# EIS Claude Rejects Assistant-Message Prefill

Sending a conversation to the EIS connector
`.anthropic-claude-4.6-sonnet-chat_completion` that ends on an **assistant**
message (assistant-message *prefill*, used to steer the model's next token)
returns a hard 400 from the ES inference layer
(`ElasticInferenceServiceUnifiedChatCompletionResponseHandler`):

```
Received a bad request status code for request from inference entity id
[.anthropic-claude-4.6-sonnet-chat_completion] status [400].
Error message: [This model does not support assistant message prefill.
The conversation must end with a user message.]
```

So any caller that builds a request ending on an assistant turn hard-fails on
this model even though it works on other providers. In weekly #51,
**only `claude-4-6-sonnet` failed** significant-events; opus, 4.7-opus, all
gemini, all gpt-5.x and gpt-oss-120b passed — so it is a sonnet-specific
provider rejection, and it only bites when the model happens to emit a
content-only turn (see below).

## Origin — CORRECTED 2026-07-02 (earlier note said `nl_to_esql`; that was WRONG)

`significant-events` does **not** route through `nl_to_esql`. Verified call
chain: `identify_ki_queries.ts:144` → `executeAsReasoningAgent`
(`@kbn/inference-prompt-utils`), a ReAct-style reasoning loop.

The trailing assistant message comes from the reasoning agent's
`completeNextTurn` re-invocation in
`kbn-inference-prompt-utils/src/flows/reasoning/execute_as_reasoning_agent.ts`
(~L355): when the model returns **content with no tool calls**, the flow
re-sends `prevMessages.concat(assistantMessage)` (no trailing tool message, so
the request **ends on the assistant turn**) with `stepsLeft: 0` to force the
final output. For claude-4.6-sonnet on EIS that trailing assistant turn is
rejected as prefill. (The normal tool-loop path ends on a `tool` message →
maps to Anthropic "user" → fine; only the content-only completion path trips
it, which is why it's model-behaviour-dependent and intermittent across models.)

This is the **same shape** as Automatic Import's LangGraph ReAct loop in
elastic/kibana#268293 — a reasoning/agent loop, not a hand-built prefill and
not `nl_to_esql`.

## Correct fix (central, not per-suite)

Two options, both owned by search-kibana / inference, NOT security-matrix:
1. **Adapter guard** — in the Kibana inference chat-complete adapter (or EIS
   response handler), for models that reject prefill, convert/strip a trailing
   assistant turn or append a minimal user continuation before send; or catch
   the specific prefill-400 and retry once with a sanitized conversation.
2. **Reasoning-flow guard** — in `executeAsReasoningAgent`, never send a
   request that ends on an assistant message; append a synthetic user
   "continue"/tool turn on the `completeNextTurn` re-invocation. Fixes all
   reasoning-agent callers but not LangGraph (#268293) — so (1) is the more
   universal "central" fix.

## Watch for it

Symptom is a 400 mentioning "assistant message prefill" — not a scoring or
trajectory failure. It appears for any reasoning/agent loop (or a hand-built
prefill) on sonnet, in any suite. Distinct from the transient
`SocketError: other side closed` / `fetch failed` that also appears in long
(>1h) runs when Kibana/EIS wobbles, and distinct from the judge-side
`google-gemini ... Service temporarily unavailable` transient.

# elastic-llm-benchmarker daemon: never hard-kill during in-flight CI evals

## The rule
Never hard-kill (`pkill`, `launchctl kickstart -k`, raw SIGKILL) the `elastic-llm-benchmarker` daemon while a model has an in-flight Buildkite Stage 2 CI-eval poll. The daemon's `reclaimStaleEntries` logic treats any non-graceful exit as an orphaned run: the in-flight model gets reset to `pending` and **re-runs from Stage 1**, discarding potentially hours of prior work and re-triggering the expensive Stage 2 CI eval from scratch.

## Correct reload procedure
1. Use the graceful `stop-local.sh` path (sends SIGTERM), never a hard kill.
2. `detachPoll: true` means the actual Buildkite build keeps running independently of the daemon process — the daemon is just waiting for a safe checkpoint before it exits.
3. The graceful drain + launchd respawn cycle can legitimately take **several minutes** (observed: ~4-7 min in one case). This is expected behavior, not a hang — don't panic-kill it early.
4. After respawn, launchd's `KeepAlive` config determines whether it auto-restarts on clean exit; verify via logs (`Received SIGTERM. Stopping scheduler...` then a later boot line) rather than assuming.

## R9_API_KEY (9router auth) wiring
- Goes in `~/.treadmill/secrets.env`, no quotes, plain `KEY=value` line.
- `run-daemon.sh` sources it via `set -a; . secrets.env; set +a`; `model-router.ts`'s `interpolateEnvVars` expands `${R9_API_KEY}` into the `r9-claude` profile's `apiKey` field at daemon load time.
- Never write the live key yourself — it's a live credential; prompt the operator to paste it in.

## Treadmill + 9router routing verdict (settled)
Use 9router (`r9-claude` profile, exposes Claude Opus 4.8) as **primary for judgment-heavy roles only** — plan-generation, PR-review, verification — **with `fallbackTo: copilot-default`**. Do NOT do a wholesale Copilot→9router replacement: 9router is a documented single point of failure ("has silently wedged before" per the operator's own `ao-config.yaml` notes). Keep high-frequency, cheap roles (`fast`, `plan-chat`) on direct Copilot to avoid 9router's ~2k-token overhead per call.

## `ornith-1.0-35b-mtplx` naming caveat (treadmill/benchmarker context)
The "MTP" in `mtplx` implies multi-token-prediction/speculative decoding, and the upstream model card does document a real 1.53x speedup (76→116 tok/s on M3 Max) — **but only when served via the dedicated `mtplx` runtime** (`mtplx start`). When served through plain LM Studio (`localhost:1234`, the operator's actual setup), the MTP sidecar is inert and `-mtplx` performs identically to `-mlx`, just with a larger download footprint. Don't assume the speedup applies just because the model name is loaded.

## Local model concurrency constraint
The operator can only load **one model at a time** in LM Studio (RAM-constrained, single local model policy). Don't design routing configs that assume two local LM Studio models running simultaneously — route reasoning-heavy tasks to cloud (9router/Copilot) instead of a second local model.

**Never:** hard-kill a daemon with an in-flight CI-eval poll to "save time" on a reload — the reclaim-to-pending cost is far higher than the wait.

# elastic-llm-benchmarker Resilience Fixes (commit 000ff68)

Three files were patched to prevent transient network errors from tearing down the pipeline. The Qwen3.6-35B-A3B run on Jun 30 2026 was abandoned mid-suite when a single `fetch failed` blip at 22:50 UTC cascaded into vLLM teardown — Stage 1 had cleanly passed (ITL=8.66ms, throughput=1089 tok/s).

## Files

| File | Fix |
|---|---|
| `src/services/buildkite-eval-trigger.ts` | `createBuild` retries transient errors (fetch failed, ECONNRESET, ETIMEDOUT, 408, 429, 5xx) up to 4× with exp backoff (2s, 4s, 8s, 16s). 4xx (except 408/429) surface immediately. |
| `src/scheduler/scheduler.ts` | Detached `pollPromise.catch()` distinguishes transient from fatal. Transient errors log and return without `updateStatus('failed')` or `releaseInfrastructure()`. Queue stays active for resume. |
| `src/services/health-check.ts` | `isContainerRunning` retries SSH `docker inspect` up to 3× with 5s delay. If all attempts fail, assumes container still running (returns `true`) instead of falsely declaring container_crash. |

## Validation

- All changes typecheck clean (`npx tsc --noEmit`)
- Applied on Jul 1 02:00 run: Stage 1 passed cleanly, Stage 2 detached poll did not tear down on transient errors
- The `isContainerRunning` fix prevented false `container_crash` during the 9-minute vLLM model load phase (45 SSH-inspect attempts during load)

## Known follow-ups

- The on-demand Buildkite pipeline (`kibana-evals-on-demand-llm-evals`) is shared with other teams. A non-benchmarker build can hijack the agent, and the daemon correctly waits via `waitForPipelineIdle`. This is by design, not a bug.
- The Kibana `fix/weekly-evals-matrix` branch (PR #274606) is required for `BENCHMARK_MODEL_ID` vLLM connector injection. Until that lands on main, builds must run on this branch or LiteLLM generation overwrites the injected connector.
- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has real eval limitations: invalid tool-call syntax under the `hermes` parser, and context-length overflows on RAG-sized attachment bundles. These are model quality issues, not code bugs.

cloud/serverless project (e.g. a PR cloud deploy), do **not** reuse the RSA
`run_gcp_fleet_vm.js` tooling wholesale — it targets a *local* ES over
Tailscale and stands up its **own** Fleet Server. A serverless project already
provides a managed Fleet Server + public ES, so ~80% of that tool is dead
weight (reusing it means *removing* features — a sign the abstraction doesn't
fit).

**Correct shape:** self-contained runbook — cloud Fleet REST API → GCP VM →
direct `elastic-agent install --url <managed-fleet> --enrollment-token <tok>`.
No Tailscale, no self-hosted Fleet Server.

**Reuse from RSA scripts (branch `agent-builder-prebuilt-skills`,
`x-pack/solutions/security/plugins/security_solution/scripts/endpoint/`):**
- The **Defend package-policy body** (from `common/fleet_services.ts`
  `addEndpointIntegrationToAgentPolicy`): input type `ENDPOINT_INTEGRATION_CONFIG`,
  `config._config.value = { type:'endpoint', endpointConfig:{ preset:'EDRComplete' } }`,
  package `{ name:'endpoint', version:<from GET /api/fleet/epm/packages/endpoint> }`.
- The Fleet route set: `POST /api/fleet/agent_policies`,
  `POST /api/fleet/package_policies`,
  `GET /api/fleet/enrollment_api_keys?kuery=policy_id:"…"` (→ `items[0].api_key`),

**Connectors:** serverless projects ship preconfigured EIS connectors —
converse via default `elastic-ai-agent` resolves one automatically; omit
`connector_id` unless the deployment needs it explicitly.

**Converse contract:** `POST /api/agent_builder/converse`, body
`{ input, agent_id, connector_id? }`, response `{ conversation_id, steps[],
response:{ message } }`. Detect skill activation from `steps[]`: a `load_skill`
tool_call or `filestore.read` of `…/<skill>/SKILL.md`, plus the skill's own
tool ids.

**Runbook location:** operator tooling → `context/changes/<id>/demo/` in the
skill-dev plugin, NOT committed into the Kibana PR.

JSON parsers), `seed-ransomware-cloud.md` (ransomware-kill-chain →
logs-endpoint.events.*), `generate-activity.sh`, `converse-smoke.sh` (4/4

# `generate-matrix` Auto-Generates the PM Improvement Backlog

`evaluation { action: "generate-matrix", git_branch, time_window, output_dir }`
returns `{ html, json, summary, warnings }`. The `json` report is not just the
raw cell grid — it already contains the analysis a PM handoff needs. Don't
re-derive it by hand.

## Structured fields in `json`

- `models[]` — each has:
  - `cells` — `{C1..C7}{L1..L5}` → `{ score10, rawMedian, sampleSize,
    notApplicable, notApplicableReason, ... }`
  - `compositeScores` — `{ externalScore (C1–C4 L3 mean), internalScore
    (C1–C4 L1–L4 mean), agentBuilderScore, recommendation }`
  - **`improvementPlan`** — `{ externalScore, internalScore, recommendation,
    topPriorities[], executiveSummary }`. Each `topPriorities` entry is
    `{ rank, category, layer, categoryLabel, layerLabel, score10, scoreBand
    (bad|warn|ok), lever, headline, action }`. The `lever` maps to an owner.
- **`managementBrief`** — `{ title, scoringExplainer, leverGuide }`.
  `leverGuide` maps each lever (`skill-authoring`, `eval-suite`, `routing`,
  `tool-schema`, `test-data`, `ci-coverage`, `model-selection`) to a
  human `label`, `owner`, and `description` — ready-made owner assignment.
- `categories`, `layers` — label lookups. `modelComparison`, `tokenCost` —
  cross-model + cost rollups.

## Reading it (tool output is megabytes — parse, don't read)

The tool result inlines the full HTML, so it lands in an agent-tools file with
MB-long lines. Parse programmatically:

```python
raw=open(F).read(); d=json.loads(raw[raw.find('{'):]); rep=d['json']
# rank systematic weak cells across frontier models:
#   for each C×L, mean(score10) over the 5 frontier model ids, sort ascending
```

## Practical finding shape (this matrix, 14d branch rollup)

The weak cells cluster in **routing** (L1 activation, L2 trajectory), not
**content** (L3 = 9.3–9.8 everywhere). So the PM narrative writes itself:
"content is strong, routing is the lever." Ranked backlog came straight from
`improvementPlan.topPriorities` + the cross-model per-cell mean.

## Filters

Same as `export-token-cost`: `git_branch` + `time_window` for a branch rollup
(weekly `build_url` filter is empty until Buildkite exports scores to golden —
see `feedback_matrix_golden_cluster_score_lag`). Active deployment must be
`golden-evals` (has the `evaluationsKbnApiKey` for `.evaluation-scores*`).

name: reference_git_hook_distribution_pattern
description: Git hooks in .git/hooks/ are per-clone — distribute via tracked scripts/install-hooks.sh (heredoc-emit + chmod + idempotent), not symlinks
type: reference
updated: 2026-06-30
source: ao-workspace pre-commit wiring session
---

# Git Hook Distribution Pattern

Git hooks in `.git/hooks/` are **per-clone** — not version-controlled. A hook
written directly into `.git/hooks/pre-commit` exists only on the machine that
created it.

## Canonical distribution pattern

1. Write the hook body into a **tracked installer script** at
   `scripts/install-hooks.sh` (heredoc-emit + `chmod +x`).
2. Make the installer **idempotent** (safe to re-run; overwrites).
3. Document the one-line install step in README: `bash scripts/install-hooks.sh`.
4. Other machines pull the repo, run the installer once, and the hook is live.

## Don't put hook logic in a tracked file and symlink

Symlinks from `.git/hooks/pre-commit` → `../../scripts/my-hook.sh` work, but:
- Windows clones break (symlink semantics differ).
- The hook then runs with cwd = the symlink's dir, not the worktree root —
  fragile path assumptions.

Heredoc-emit into `.git/hooks/pre-commit` via installer script is more portable.

## See also

- `reference_bash_source_dirname_bug.md` — the specific path-resolution bug that
  the `git rev-parse` anchor in this installer fixes.
- `feedback_rule_frontmatter_lint.md` — the lint this hook runs.

name: reference_github_pr_apply_suggestion_api
description: Apply a GitHub PR review "```suggestion```" block server-side via the Contents API instead of a local worktree edit + bootstrap + push — ~1 min vs ~40 min on Kibana
type: reference
confidence: strong
source: PR #273049 Claude-reviewer suggestion + prior Kibana PR hygiene observations
---

# Applying PR Review Suggestions via GitHub API (not local worktree)

When a reviewer (bot or human) posts a fenced ```` ```suggestion ... ``` ```` block on a
PR comment, default to applying it as a commit directly on the PR branch via the GitHub
Contents API — **not** a local worktree edit + `yarn kbn bootstrap` + `tsc` + push. GitHub
has **no native apply-suggestion endpoint**; the web UI button synthesizes the commit
client-side. Replicate that:

1. `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}?ref={branch}` → `{sha, content(base64)}`.
   The `?ref=` query param is **mandatory** whenever the path isn't on the default branch
   of the content repo — always true for external-fork PRs, where you must target the
   **fork repo** (`head.repo.full_name`), not the upstream `elastic/*` repo.
2. Decode base64, apply the suggestion text as a line-targeted string replacement.
3. `PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}` with `{message, content(base64), sha, branch}`
   → commit lands directly on the PR branch ref.
4. For atomic multi-file suggestions, use the Git Database API instead:
   `git/blobs` + `git/trees` + `git/commits` + `refs/heads`.

Reusable helper: `~/.local/bin/gh-apply-suggestion`.

**Speed win:** this skips the ~25-min `yarn kbn bootstrap` + ~20-min `tsc` type-check +
pre-push-hook loop that the local-worktree path incurs — one `gh api` call vs. a
multi-minute pipeline. Verified: PR #273049's `--anomaly-threshold` range-validation
suggestion took ~40 min via local worktree when the Contents-API path would have been ~1 min.

**When to still use the local worktree path:** only when the suggestion needs behavioral
verification (running the affected test to confirm it actually passes) before pushing.
For pure refactor / rename / type-narrowing / formatting suggestions, trust the reviewer
and apply server-side directly.

**Caveat — snapshot tests:** if the suggestion touches code guarded by jest snapshots /
Argos / Lost Pixel, applying server-side won't regenerate them. Follow up immediately with
a tiny regen commit (`node scripts/jest <path> -u` scoped to that file's nearest
`jest.config.js`, pushed via the same API path) or CI fails on the stale snapshot.

## Kibana PR hygiene (paired conventions)

- When a feature PR touches files owned by another team's CODEOWNERS (`kbn-evals`,
  `agent_builder`, `kbn-scout` platform paths), **split those into a dependent PR that
  merges first**, then rebase the feature PR — minimize the required-reviewer set, not
  just the diff size.
- On a merge-blocking Agent Builder skill PR, **defer new/changed eval-suite work to a
  follow-up PR** and prove flag-on behavior with a **local demo** (kbn-cell or Cloud QA)
  so the skill can merge without waiting on eval infra.
- **Never put LangSmith/vendor dataset or run IDs in Kibana PR descriptions** — trigger
  evals via labels and match the weekly connector set.
- **Cloud QA PR-demo login uses Vault SSO creds** for the PR deployment, not hand-rolled
  passwords.

name: reference_golden_score_read_path_results_not_failing_examples
description: Read post-revamp golden eval scores via MCP evaluation.results (Kibana API); list-runs/failing-examples read legacy index and falsely report "no score documents"
type: reference
confidence: strong
updated: 2026-07-03
source: skill-dev 3686518a — reading on-demand build #193 (security-ai-rules) C2 L2 find-rules trajectory from golden cluster
---

# Reading golden eval scores: use `evaluation.results`, not `list-runs`/`failing-examples`

When reading scores for an on-demand or weekly build from the golden cluster
(`kbn-evals-serverless-…`, `deployment { action: "use", name: "golden-evals" }`),
the score docs live in the **post-revamp `.evaluation-scores*` datastream**,
readable only through the **Kibana evals API** (needs `evaluationsKbnApiKey`).

## The trap (cost several tool-calls to discover)

- `evaluation { action: "list-runs", args: { suite_id, branch } }` shows the run
  but with **`scoreCount: 0`** — it reads legacy `kibana-evaluations*` (empty
  post-revamp) and its `traceQueryHint` points at the legacy index.
- `evaluation { action: "failing-examples", args: { run_id } }` returns
  **`"has no score documents"`** — it queries by legacy `run_id`, but revamp
  docs key on `execution_id_norm` / `suite_id_norm`, so a legacy-run_id lookup
  is empty even when scores exist.

**Do NOT conclude "the run has no scores" from either of those.** The scores
almost certainly exist; you queried the wrong plane.

## The working read path

```
evaluation { action: "results", args: { suite_id: "<suite>", limit: 60 } }
```

`results` "tries the Kibana evals API first, then ES, then CLI" — the API path
returns the revamp scores. Output is large (written to an agent-tools file).
Parse with jq: each `.scores[]` doc has
`{ runId, suiteId, exampleIndex, input, evaluatorName, score, passed, label,
explanation, traceId, datasetName }`.

Useful slices:
```bash
jq -r '.scores[].datasetName' f | sort | uniq -c            # datasets present
jq -r '.scores[].evaluatorName' f | sort | uniq -c          # evaluators present
jq -r '.scores[] | select(.datasetName=="<ds>" and .evaluatorName=="Trajectory")
       | "ex\(.exampleIndex) [\(.label)] \(.score) — \(.explanation)"' f
```

Gotcha: `.input` is **sometimes JSON, sometimes plain text** — `.input|fromjson`
throws on the plain-text rows. Guard with `try (.input|fromjson.prompt) catch .input`
or just slice `.input[0:90]`.

## Interpreting routing-suite scores (security-ai-rules `rule-generation-routing`)

Two evaluator-reading gotchas that will mislead a naive read:

1. **Trajectory `label` is the real signal, `score` alone is polluted.**
   `label:"N/A"` rows (rule-creation routing + distractors) are coerced to
   `score:0` but are NOT failures — the explanation says "scored via
   ExpectedToolCalled/ForbiddenToolNotCalled, not trajectory" or "no tool
   trajectory annotation". Only `label:"poor"|"good"` rows are real find-rules
   trajectory measurements. **Filter `label!="N/A"` before averaging any
   trajectory cell** (matrix aggregation must too).

2. **`ForbiddenToolNotCalled=1.0` is a decoy on inventory examples.** Its
   forbidden set is per-example-role: on find-rules *inventory* examples it
   forbids `security.create_detection_rule` (don't create when asked to list),
   **NOT** the ES|QL tools. So a model that wrongly routes to
   `platform.core.generate_esql`/`execute_esql` still passes
   ForbiddenToolNotCalled. Only the **Trajectory `explanation`** (coverage
   `0/2`, "Missing tools: …find_rules", "Extra tools: …generate_esql,
   execute_esql") exposes the ES|QL misroute. Read the trajectory explanation,
   never the aggregate pass flags.

## Also true

- A **green on-demand build ≠ recovered score** — non-hard-gated evaluators
  (trajectory) let the build pass while the cell stays 0. Always read the
  actual score, not the Buildkite state.
- `list-runs` is still fine for **finding the run id + commit + branch**; just
  don't trust its `scoreCount`.

## skill-dev `getRunScores` / live eval smoke trap

When skill-dev plugin code reads scores directly from ES (e.g. Phase 4 live-eval
smoke, `getEvalResults` / `getRunScores`), revamp docs use
`metadata.execution_id` and `metadata.suite_id` — **not** legacy top-level
`run_id` / `suite.id`. Filtering on legacy fields returns **0 scores** even
when Playwright exited 0 and golden cluster has data. Same class of bug as
`list-runs`/`failing-examples` — fix the filter plane, don't chase skill content.
Example input shape is often `{ question: "..." }` — parsers must match that,
not a JSON-stringified object key.

# Headless macOS Laptop Runner Setup

How to turn a spare MacBook (e.g. the Intel i9, see `reference_dev_machine_fleet`) into a lid-closed, SSH-only background job runner. Ordered by the non-obvious traps.

## The bootstrap chicken-and-egg (do this FIRST, physically)

**Fresh macOS has Remote Login OFF**, so you cannot provision it remotely — the very first setup must happen sitting at the machine. This forces a two-phase setup: Phase 1 physical (enable SSH + no-sleep), Phase 2 everything-else over SSH from the primary machine.

- Enable SSH: System Settings → General → Sharing → **Remote Login** ON (allow the admin user). CLI `sudo systemsetup -setremotelogin on` often needs Full Disk Access on modern macOS → the GUI toggle is the reliable path on a fresh box.

## Clamshell / closed-lid no-sleep (the key trick)

macOS normally requires an external display + power + keyboard to run with the lid closed. To run **headless with the lid closed and NO external display**, keep it on AC power and set:

```bash
sudo pmset -c disablesleep 1   # THE trick: allows clamshell w/o external display
sudo pmset -c sleep 0
sudo pmset -c displaysleep 0
sudo pmset -c disksleep 0
sudo pmset -c powernap 0
sudo pmset -c autorestart 1     # auto power-on after power loss
sudo pmset -c womp 1            # wake for network access
```

`disablesleep 1` is the non-obvious flag — without it the machine sleeps the moment the lid shuts regardless of the other settings.

## FileVault reboot trap + unattended-login recipe (VALIDATED Jul 2 2026)

If **FileVault is ON**, after any reboot the disk stays encrypted/locked and the GUI
never logs in until someone unlocks at the physical login screen — so user LaunchAgents
(the EDD stack) never start. (Note: `sshd` is a *system* daemon and DOES start at boot
regardless of GUI login, and Tailscale runs as a system NetworkExtension — so SSH access
itself survives a reboot even without login; only the *user session* is gated.)

Full unattended reboot-survival recipe for a trusted-LAN spare (all validated on the i9,
`sudo` is passwordless via a sudoers drop-in):

```bash
# 1) FileVault OFF (decrypts in background; status flips to Off immediately)
sudo fdesetup disable -inputplist <<'PLIST'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Username</key><string>USER</string>
  <key>Password</key><string>PASSWORD</string>
</dict></plist>
PLIST

# 2) Auto-login user + /etc/kcpassword (XOR-obfuscated password; key is 11 bytes)
python3 - <<'PY'
key=[0x7D,0x89,0x52,0x23,0xD2,0xBC,0xDD,0xEA,0xA3,0xB9,0x1F]
pw=[ord(c) for c in "PASSWORD"]
out=[b^key[i%11] for i,b in enumerate(pw)]
i=len(out)
while len(out)%12!=0: out.append(0^key[i%11]); i+=1
open("/tmp/kcp","wb").write(bytes(out))
PY
sudo cp /tmp/kcp /etc/kcpassword && sudo chown root:wheel /etc/kcpassword && sudo chmod 600 /etc/kcpassword && rm /tmp/kcp
sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow autoLoginUser -string USER
```

Verify after `sudo shutdown -r now`: `who` shows the user on `console` (autologin worked),
`launchctl list | grep <agents>` shows them running. On the i9 the launchd Kibana
supervisor then does `colima start → wait ES healthy → start Kibana (source)` on its own,
so the whole EDD stack is serving ~2-3 min after boot with zero human touch.
(Alternative that keeps encryption: `sudo fdesetup authrestart` unlocks for exactly one
reboot — but useless after unexpected power loss, so not for a truly unattended box.)

## Stable addressing

Set a clean LocalHostName (Sharing pane) and reach it via **Bonjour `<name>.local`** (e.g. `kibana-i9.local`) instead of chasing DHCP IPs. Then `ssh-copy-id` the primary machine's existing key and add a `Host` alias to `~/.ssh/config`.

## Phase 2 (over SSH, from primary machine)

Xcode CLT → Homebrew → `nvm` + Node from the target repo's `.nvmrc` → git clone → `yarn kbn bootstrap`. For the EDD workload specifically: a **dedicated** cell stack on cell-allocated ports (never the shared dev ports), frontier-model EIS connectors (see `feedback_eis_ccm_provisioning_remote_cell`), and a job-queue runner.

**For reboot survival, use `launchd` user agents, NOT tmux.** The i9 runs two LaunchAgents (`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.i9.edd-runner.plist` = job-queue runner; `com.i9.edd-kibana.plist` = Kibana-source supervisor that ensures `colima` + cell ES/EDOT are up then starts Kibana), both `RunAtLoad` + `KeepAlive`. Docker cell containers use `restart: unless-stopped`. Combined with the autologin recipe above, the entire stack returns after a reboot with no human touch. tmux only survives disconnects, not reboots.

## Cross-refs

- `reference_dev_machine_fleet` — which machine plays this role and why
- `skill-dev-eval-driven-loop` — the EDD workflow this runner hosts (dedicated stack, reserved ports, frontier models)
- `feedback_daemon_launch_via_tmux` — tmux for long unattended runs
